I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee   on Industry,  having   been   authorised  by the  Committee,
hereby present this   One Hundred Seventy Fourth  Report  on Operational Effectiveness of PMRY, REGP and KVI Schemes in Bihar, Jharkhand,
West Bengal and Maharashtra  (Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries).
 
2.         The Committee visited Ranchi and Patna on 2
nd and 3rd October, 2004 and interacted with the representatives of respective State
Governments, industrial federation / associations and the banks on the working of KVIC, REGP and PMRY in Jharkhand and Bihar.  The Committee
further visited Kolkata on 17th January, 2005 and Mumbai on 23rd January, 2005 and interacted with the representatives KVICs / NGOs / Banks and
Government of West Bengal and Maharashtra to take stock of the ground realities regarding the working of PMRY, REGP and KVIC in West Bengal
and Maharashtra.  The present report has been prepared on the basis of the Committee's interaction during its study visit in select States and the
background note as provided by the Ministry of ARI.

Prime Minister Rozgar Yojna (PMRY)
 
1.1     The Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) scheme was launched on 2nd October, 1993 in the country. The objective of the scheme is to
assist educated unemployed youth from the weaker section of the society in setting up micro enterprises in all economically viable activities as per
the parameters of the scheme .The scheme is implemented in both urban & rural areas of the country from 1994-95 onwards.
 
1.2       The objective of the Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) is to mitigate the problem of unemployment amongst the
educated unemployed youth belonging to weaker sections of the society through setting up of self employed tiny units.
The annual target of employment generation under the PMRY is as per the target envisaged for the Scheme in the Xth
Plan document of the Planning Commission which envisages to create 50 million person years of gainful employment
opportunities over the Xth Plan. Accordingly, a target of 1.65 million person years over the Xth Plan or an annual target of
employment of 3.3 lakh persons or 2.20 lakh units per annum has been envisaged under the PMRY.

2.2     Optimum utilization of funds released under the PMRY Scheme is ensured.  The release/utilization of funds under
the Scheme is based on the performance/achievement of target by the State/UTs.  The funds released to State/UTs are
reconciled regularly and surplus/deficit amount is adjusted to ensure full and optimum utilization of funds released
under the Scheme. To ensure achievement of target under the Scheme implementing agencies are requested to plan out
the activities of sponsoring, sanctioning and disbursement as per the quarterly schedule of sponsoring sanction and
disbursement prescribed while communicating annual targets to State/UTs/Banks. Consequent upon the decision taken
in the recently held review meeting, the State/UTs and banks have been requested to monthly monitor the achievement of
targets set under the Scheme.

3.2       The performance of PMRY in the States of Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal and Maharashtra, although slight     improvement has there during
2004-05 as compared to the last year for the corresponding period. The performance of PMRY in these States has been further accelerated after the
visit of the Committee.  It may be seen that the achievement (disbursements as reported by the RBI) in the States of Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal
and Maharashtra has gone up from 10, 105, 662 and 3143 Nos. at the time of visit of the Committee to 2130, 4510, 2013 and 5771 Nos. respectively
after the visit of the committee.
 
3.3       The Committee is not at all satisfied with the performance of PMRY in the States of Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal and
Maharashtra, although slight     improvement has been  there during 2004-05 as compared to the last year for the corresponding period. 
The Committee observes that it is desirable that Ministry of ARI  in tandem with the Ministry of  Finance, banks and state Government 
should keep monitoring over timely and effectively implementation of Schemes under its purview and accordingly apprise the Committee.
 
  
3.4     The analysis of the performance under PMRY during the last three years based on the reports received from RBI shows that  besides
other reasons, performance under the Scheme in States is positively correlated with the recovery of loan over dues under the Scheme. Other
reasons for failure of Scheme are competition from Central/State Govt. Schemes offering higher subsidy, difficulty in getting the desired
target group due to higher level of per capital income, non viable projects, reluctance on the part of banks to sanction and disburse loan,
militancy, etc.  The Committee, therefore, is of view that the Ministry of ARI in tandem with the banking division, Nationalized Banks and
the State Governments of Bihar, Jharkhand , West Bengal and Maharashtra should take suitable steps ensuring compliance with under -
mentioned yardsticks for better functioning of PMRY in these states:-
(a)
   Minimise the rejection ratio  by banks against no. of application received.
(b)   Avoid the stoppage/delay of disbursement  in  PMRY loans on flimsy   grounds
(c)    Quick disposal of application on the part of DICs  and forwarding the same  to banks
(d)   Coverage  of SC/STs under the scheme as per the  norms  stipulated by Government of India.

4.0       Working of Khadi Industries in West Bengal, Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Bihar
4.1       The financial assistance provided under khadi sales rebate and Interest Subsidy has largely helped the khadi sector
to enhance its performance over the previous year.  While the Interest Subsidy propelled the flow of working capital from
banks, the rebate element helped khadi institutions to boost sales and to get relief from the  blockage of working capital to
a certain extend. The Rebate and Interest subsidy are two important components used for the furtherance of the khadi
programme. The rebate is a promotional expenditure provided on  khadi sales for neutralizing the cost due to higher wage
component thereby to boost its sales. Similarly, the quantum of Interest Subsidy provided on funds availed from
Commercial Banks against ISEC issued by KVIC helps to enhance credit flow to khadi programme.
 
4.2     KVIC has launched an Insurance Scheme for the welfare of khadi workers which brings a sense of social security
among the khadi workers.  The portion of khadi grant is paid to Insurance Company as KVIC’s share of the premium
under this scheme. Similarly, KVIC has launched a Product Development, Design Intervention and Packaging (PRODIP)
for the betterment of khadi sector.  Certain part of khadi grant is utilized for this purpose also which in turn helps for the
furtherance of khadi sector.
 
4.3    During its  study visit to Ranchi, Patna, Kolkata, Mumbai, the Committee took stock of the ground realities of the working of Khadi and Village
Industries in these select States.   The Committee got an opportunity to interact with the representative of NGOs/Industrial Associations of the
respective States and the representative of the respective state Governments.

4.5       The Committee  desires to know the reasons for drastic reduction in funds allocated for khadi programme for Bihar which has been
earmarked to the tune of Rs.160.70 lakhs in B.E. 2005-06 in comparison to Rs.346.51 lakhs during 2004-05.  The Committee recommends

4.6       West Bengal
 
4.6.1    The Committee was informed that the West Bengal has established its status under Khadi programme for its unique art and craftsmanship.
The climatic condition and abundant local resources have widened the scope for the development of Khadi programme in the State. The districts of
Malda, Murshidabad, Nadia, Birbhum, Bankura, Hooghly, Purulia have the extensive coverage of the Khadi programmes, especially for silk &
Muslin Khadi.
 
 
 
 
4.6.2    The Committee was informed that Mulberry cocoon cultivation in the districts of  Malda, Murshidabad and parts of Birbhum had been
increased adequately and as a result of which, silk reeling and weaving unit have been concentrated in those localities. Further, a good number of
skilled artisans are also available in those area. As such, the scope of silk Khadi activities in those areas have been expanded considerably. Jiagunj,
Raghunathganj, Piarapur area of Murshidabad district is famous for the Garad varieties, while the Bishnupur in Bankura district is famous for the
exclusive Baluachari design. Besides Mulberry silk, Matka Silk, Tassar Silk are produced in good quality and in huge quantity also. In production of
silk Khadi the state contributes 36.37 per cent  of total silk Khadi production in KVI sector and ranks in 1st position in overall performance under
KVIC.
 
4.6.3    The Committee was further informed that another prestigious product of West Bengal is Muslin Khadi. Muslin Khadi has reached to its
fineness to the extent of 500 metric count and there is no competitor of this industry. The main characteristic of this industry is large-scale
employment of women artisans. Around 8,000 women artisans in the state are engaged in this industry. Muslin Khadi Industry has grown in the
districts of Murshidabad, Nadia, Burdwan and Malda.  In production of Muslin Khadi, the state ranks at the top contributing 55.25 per cent of the
total production of Muslin Khadi in KVI sector.

4.9       The Committee is of the opinion that since Maharashtra has been the leading state for economic activities, it is utter surprise that out
of one hundred three khadi institutions, eighty two Khadi institutions fall inot the 'D' category.  The Committee is constrained to note that
the achievement in the state has been much less than the targets set out in action plan.  KVIC has to look into the reasons and do its best to
achieve the desirable results. The KVIC should therefore, initiate appropriate steps for improving the Khadi industries in Maharashtra
where Khadi is doing its business far below the level of expectation. The Ministry of ARI should also intervene and appropriate directions
should be issued to chalk out Action Plan for promoting and proliferation of Khadi Industries in the State.
 
4.10     Bihar
 
4.10.1  Consequent to the   division of Bihar in the year 2000  almost the entire Industrial and rich mineral base along with many of the power
projects of the erstwhile state of Bihar  went to the newly  created   State  of Jharkhand, leaving Bihar an Industrially backward state.  The fact that
Bihar remained largely an agricultural  state   necessitated the  formulation   of a new Indusial Policy, 2003 for Bihar in order to give a boost and
impetus  to industrial growth.  However, with a large agricultural base and available huge manpower resources, Bihar, with a rich historical and 
cultural heritage, has good potential for agro processing, bio technology, tea processing,   software technology, tourism  and other allied industries 
along with handloom, sericulture and handicrafts. Insufficient infrastructure   development, inadequate supply of power, frequent floods, low flow of
capital investment  from outside, adverse C.D. Ratio are some of the major impediments in the industrial growth of the State.  Competition from
well-established products and services from other States and through imports such as through Nepal pose a threat to the viability of the local
industry.  But the State Government is alive to the situation and is trying hard to remove these impediments in conjunction with the Government of
India for creating a more conducive environment for industry and investment.
 
4.10.2  The Committee was apprised that the State Government have taken a series of steps for improving the investment and industrial climate in the
State, which  mainly  included the announcement of the Industrial Policy, 2003; announcement of the Stores Purchase Preference Policy, 2002;
reconstitution of Industrial Area Development Authority and establishment of the amalgamated Bihar Industrial Area Development Authority; and
restructuring of Public Sector Undertakings in the State.
 
4.10.3  Some of the recent developments that have taken place in the State on the industrial side include setting- up  of new units, and opening of
closed industrial  units   such as  Katihar Jute Mill, Rameshwar Jute Mill etc.  The State Government have also set up a Software  Technology   Park
in Patna which has stated  functioning.   On   the  food  processing side the Agri Export Zone has been notified and exports of Litchi has increased  
nearly eleven fold from a level of 35 MT in the year  2000-01 to 396 MT in the year 002-03.  It has also being decided to include Honey and
Vegetables in the Agri Export Zone.  A separate Agri processing side, adequate training ,  EDP courses etc.   are being  organized   to promote the
development of  food processing industries.  Similarly, having regard to the good potential for Tea in Bihar, especially in Purnea,   Kishanganj and

Araria districts, a special   package has been  announced  by the State Government for  promoting the establishment of  Tea  processing unit in the
State.  The first such  tea  processing units  has already commenced production in the State.   Two cluster development programmes have been taken
up under the Government of India  scheme, one in Patna districts for brass and E.P.N.S. items and other in Munger for gun making.
 
4.10.4  The State Government  have given priority to promotion of infrastructure for industry.  Some of the major initiatives include setting - up of
the Software  Technology Park, establishment of Growth Centres,  setting up of the Export Promotion Industrial Park at Hajipur, the  proposed Air
Cargo Complex at Patna, the establishment  of the Central Institute  of Plastic Engineering and Technology at Hajipur  etc.  Similarly, all efforts are
being made to develop and improve the infrastcture in existing Industrial areas and industrial estates   through the Bihar Industrial Area Development
Authority.
           
 
4.10.5  The Committee has been apprised that Bihar has about  1.32 lakhs weavers and nearly 34,000 Handlooms and Power looms Programmes for
development of  clusters of  weavers, establishment of  work-shed, provision of looms and equipments and other measures have been undertaken,   A
comprehensive handloom development project involving a total cost of Rs.8709.80  lakhs  has been prepared and sent to the Government of India for
approval.  Similarly, on the Sericulture side, schemes are being implemented for promotion and development of Tasar, Mulberry and Eri both by the
State  Government and through the Central Silk Board (CSB).  These  include    a composite Tasar and  Eri Development project for  Banka and
Jamui districts  by the CSB at   a  total cost of Rs.1434.00 lakhs and a mulberry project in Purnea and   Kishanganj districts at a cost of Rs.140.00
lakhs.  A Special composite project for sericulture development in the State   for Rs.3709.00 lakhs  has been sent to  the Central Government for
approval.
 
           
4.10.6  The Committee has been apprised that there is a large sugar industry in the State.   The total area under sugarcane in the State during the year
2002-03 was  R.2.54 lakh  hectares with sugarcane  production of   nearly 119 lakh tonnes.  There are  10 sugar mills functioning in the State, all of
them  in the private  sector,  with a combined capacity of nearly   37,700 TCD.  The production of sugar during  the year 2002-03 in   the State was 
4.08 lakhs tonnes.
 
4.10.7  The State Government is thus putting in all efforts for industrial development and promotion   of investment   in the State both in the
manufacturing and the services sector.  The Industrial Policy  2003 provides  the policy framework for the various schemes  that are being
implemented  with this objective.   The  special  package announced in  1997  for industries in the North-East by the Union Government   and for
Utranchal and Himachal Pradesh recently, needs to be provided for Bihar at the earliest.
 
4.10.8  The Committee understand that in post partition phase (since the year 2000),  Bihar  remained  an industrially  backward  state with
insufficient and poor infrastructure development , inadequate supply  of power, low capital flow, adverse C.D. ratio.  The announcement of 
new industrial  policy has not made any observable  headway.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view  that  the Central Government  in
tandem  with the state government has to start  from the stretch  for launching effective   industrial  growth and development  of the  state. 
Since the state  has   largely been remained  an agricultural state.  A   new beginning    can be  made in the areas of Agro -rural  industries
by initiating following course of action:-
 
(i)
                 Due  impetus to anciliarisation  of Jute industry in Purnea, Katihar, Araria, and Kishanganj to extract  benefits of opening up of
Katihar Jute Mills;
(ii)               De-centralisation of setting up of software technology  park in each district of the state;
(iii)             Promotion and proliferation of  tea processing units in Kishanganj, Purnea and Araria;
(iv)             Institutional and logistic  support to Agro -Rural Industries, specially  Sugar Mills and its  backward linkages;
(v)               co-ordination with Central Silk Board (CSB) for development of TAsar, Mulberry, Eri development in Bhagalpur , Banka,
Jamui, Purnea and Kishanganj;
(vi)             Promotion of Handloom and powerloms programmes for development  of clusters of weavers, establishment of work shed   at
Panchayat level of each districts.  Government may approve the composite schemes  for  development   of Handloom and
sericulture in the state; and
(vii)           Having regard to the fact that Bihar is an industrially backward  state, the  special package announced in  1997  for industries in
the North-East by the Union Government  and for Utranchal and Himachal Pradesh recently, needs to be provided for Bihar at
the earliest.

4.10.11            The Committee is of view that Bihar, after the partition and separation of Jharkhand, remained basically an agricultural
state, that too not very organised, and the state being bereft of any large scale or even medium scale industries, the only option that remains
with the state  is the accelerated promotion and proliferation of agro - rural industries and Small Scale and Medium Enterprises which have
the benefit of requiring  low investment and providing vast potential for employment generation.  Therefore, the Committee  strongly
recommends that the Ministry of ARI and SSI should come together in chalking out district- wise Development Strategy, based on

4.18     Working of REGP in West Bengal, Jharkhand, Maharashtra and Bihar
 
4.18.1  As per the recommendations of High Power Committee, KVIC introduced the Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) for
financing viable. Village Industries Projects.  Under this scheme, Margin Money @ 25% of the project cost up to Rs. 10 lakhs and 10% of the
difference of project cost up to  Rs. 25 lakhs over and above Rs. 10 lakhs is provided for setting up viable Village Industries projects.   For certain
categories of entrepreneurs such as women, physically handicapped, ex-servicemen and those belonging to SC/ST/OBC, minority communities,
North Easter Region, including Sikkim, hill border and tribal areas, Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Lakshdweep etc. margin money is @ 30% for
projects up to Rs. 10 lakhs.  The Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) is implemented with the active involvement of 27 nationalized
scheduled commercial banks, their Regional Rural Banks.  Now this programme has deeply percolated  its roots in the countryside and got unique
identity.

effort for effective implementation of REGP in West Bengal , Jharkhand, Maharashtra and Bihar. Further from 2002-03, the payment of margin

the State Governments of Bihar, Jharkhand , West Bengal and Maharashtra should take suitable steps ensuring compliance with under -

CHAPTER – I
 
MICRO ANALYSIS OF PROBLEMS AND PROSPECTS OF SSI
 
(A)              ORISSA
 
Orissa is endowed with mineral resources like manganese, coal, iron ore, bauxite etc. Besides it has a vast coastline which provides the potential for harnessing marine
resources. Yet the state represents a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty. The quick estimate of Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) the State suggest that primary
sector constitutes nearly 38% of NSDP followed by Service sector (28%). Secondary sector (17%) and Tertiary sector (17%) in other words the rate of shift from agrarian
economy to industrial one is quite marginal for the State.
 
1.1 Liberalization and Globalization has changed the face of state economy and has thrown great challenge for SSI and they no longer operate under protected  environment,
but have to face harshness of competition both from within the country and outside. Such change requires technology up gradation, modernization, backward and forward
integration, skill development and better marketing. This requires funds for fixed capital and working capital need and the shortage of these funds seriously affects the SSIs
of Orissa leading to sickness.
 
1.1.1 The committee was apprised that Super Cyclone occurred in Orissa during the 1999 also greatly affected the SSI Units of Orissa. SISI, Cuttock  has undertaken a study
to diagnose the factors responsible for sickness in Orissa by taking some samples of sick S SI units which were identified for revival. The major reason for inadequate
working capital is the poor equity limit, lack of financial strength of landing institution and high interest rate. The major reasons for sickness of SSI units in the states are :-

(i)         Shortage of working capital & timely availability of working capital
(ii)        Immature/unplanned marketing strategy
(iii)       Non-availability of right type of raw materials at a reasonable price, the SSI units           are       not able to provide continuously the similar type of product with
same         cost.
(iv)       Sick units commonly faced the problem of cost over run of the project. thereby             delayed commercial production.
(v)        Low capital utilisation
(vi)       Use of inappropriate or obsolete technology by SSI units
(vii)      Shortage or irregular supply of power, changes of industrial policies, delay in      getting payment labour problem, natural calamities etc. also inhibit the SSI units   in
showing healthy trends of growth in Orissa.
 
1.1.2 The Committee interacted with the representatives of Orissa Industries Association and Orissa Young Entrepreneurs Association in the presence of representatives of
Ministry of SSI, Government of Orissa and the Banks, The Committee came across that Orissa is having only 2% of SSI units in India and the share of Orissa in total Bank
finance to SSI units is only to the tune of 1.08 %. The associations pointed our following solutions for improving SSI sector in the state :-
 
(i)         The rehabilitation package should be implemented promptly within a time frame to revive the unit. It is fact that inadequate finance and untimely finance by the
banks whether term loan or working capital is responsible for sickness of SSI steps should be taken to strengthen the forum of SLIIC and the promotional agencies and the
financial institution to do pro-active role to overcome the difficulties faced by the units.
 
(ii)        As SSI units in Orissa were affected badly due to super cyclone, a special liberal package to the affected units by extending all types of concession, and also
extending the period of repayment should be drawn in consultation with Reserve Bank of India.
 
(iii)       Priority should be given by Nationalized Banks to finance potential SSI unit in a particular area.
 
(iv)       Compromised settlement of NPA: As the response from SSI unit in Orissa for NPA settlement is encouraging. So more time should be given to cover more number
of NPA units.
 
(v)        Different financial linked schemes like CGTSI, CLCSS, NEF, Composite Loan scheme, SME find of SIDBI Should be popularized in Orissa as most of the
entrepreneurs are not aware of these schemes.
 
(vi)       The innovative financing like venture capital, factoring services etc. should be popularized which will improve the position of the unit to get finance easily.
 
(vii)      Orissa State Financial Corporation which is the chief term loan provider to SSI unit in Orissa is in urgent need of financial restructuring, so as to clean up their
balance sheet. The mechanism of state government, SIDBI and the IDBI have to play a proactive role in this.
 
(viii)      There should be a liberalised OTS Policy by Financial Institutions for sick SSI.
 
(ix)       The forum of State Level Inter Institutional Committee i.e. SLIIC should be made more effective. The decision of the SLIIC should be made compulsory
implementation by other agencies concerned with revitalization of their units.
 
1.1.3 The Committee was informed by the representative of Orissa State Financial Corporation Employee’s Union that following relief an concession may be granted to the
state :-
 
(i)         Impress upon the SIDBIJIDBIICommercial Bank to waive the entire interest that has accrued on Financial Assistance to OSFC w.e.f. 1.11.99 to 30. 06. 2004.
(ii)        The interest payment of Rs.160.53 crores already made by OSFC to TDBIJSIDBI/ Banks may be adjusted against principal liabilities of these institutions after such
waiver of interest.
 
(iii)       To impress upon SIDBI to continue with refinancing under SMEs Fund, which is already made available to SIDBI by the Union Government.
 
(iv)       Development strategy for promotion of SSI units in economically backward district like Bolangir and Koraput, Kalahandi and extension of income tax and central
Excise exemption on the lines of North East and Uttranchal and Himachal Pradesh.

1.1.4    The Committee observes that Orissa demonstrates a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty as the state, despite having mineral and marine resources, has been
bereft of sustainable industrial growth and economic development. The Committee finds that the cherished Charter of the Planning Commission which was “to combine a
rapid rise in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing production and offering opportunities to all for
employment in the service of the community”, has not seen the light of the day in the state. The state has been devoid of planned development giving rise to the
economically backward district like Bolangir, Koraput and above all the Kalahandi.
 
1.1.5      No major efforts have been made to put the state on the industrial development track, and therefore there is the lack of ancialirisation of industries in the Small and
Medium sectors. Besides, the general problems like lack of Infrastructural development and marketing assistance and shortage of timely and adequate credit flow etc., the
state has also been the victim of natural calamities like super cyclone in 1999 which have actually devastated the Small scale industrial set up and thus arrested the industrial
growth and promotion and proliferation of small and medium enterprises in the state.
 
1.1.6    The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the financial institutions should come forward for providing timely and adequate credit flow to the entrepreneurs for
accelerated industrial growth and promotion of SMEs in the state. The Committee recommends that concerted efforts must be undertaken for popularization of venture
capital, factoring services and other financial linked schemes like CGYTSI, CLCSS, NEF and SME Fund of SIDBI.
 
1.1.7      The Committee further recommends that following key areas must be selected for effective action:
 
(i)        Strengthening the functional aspects of state level inter-institutional Committee (SLIIC) and promotidnal agencies;
 
(ii)    Financial restructuring of Orissa State Financial co-operation by seriously considering the proposal of adjustment of interest payment to the tune of Rs. 160.33 crore
against principle liabilities besides wavering of the interest;
(iii)        Extension of income tax and central excise exemption for setting up of SMEs in economically backward districts like Bolangir , Koraput and Kalahandi on NER,
Uttranchal and Himachal Pradesh line;
 
(iv)     Special liberal package to super cyclone effected SSI units like rehabilitation package and one time settlement (OTS).
 
(B) GUJARAT
 
1.2        Small Scale Industry in Gujarat has witnessed impressive development. There are
over 10,000 SSI registrations granted every year during last decade. As per 3rd Census,
Gujarat accounts for 11.2% of working SSI units in the country. The performance of S
industry in Gujarat, therefore, has been very impressive. The State Government has introduced various schemes to provide support to SSI as part of Gujarat Industrial Policy
2003. Providing interest subsidy @ 5% to new as well as existing SSI units for undertaking.  The small scale industry is facing difficulties with regard to credit flow from
financial institutions. The Committee was informed as under:
 
(i)         The investment in small scale sector is over Rs.450 crore. The credit flow from nationalised  banks does not match with investment taking place in SSI. Against the
total turn-overn of over Rs. 12,000 crore per annum by SSIs in Gujarat, the credit flow is hardly Rs. 1500 cr. The industry, therefore, suffers from inadequate credit flow.
 
(ii)        Higher rate of interest on term loan prevents availability of funds, as higher rate of interest, about 13% interest per annum is charged.
 
(iii)       Credit Guarantee Scheme for SSI has not become popular with banks and SSIs continue to face difficulties in providing collateral guarantee.
 
(iv)       Credit  Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation  of SS1s take off of this scheme has been negligible in Gujarat . The banks are not providing
assistance under the scheme, thereby depriving SSI units of the scheme introduced by Government of India.
 
(v)        Assistance for Cluster Development in Gujarat, there are 83 product clusters in small scale sector e.g. Rajkot for diesel engine; Jamnagar for brass parts industry;
Morbi for ceramic industry; Surat for power loom industry. Accounting for over 43% of investment, 48% of production and 47% of employment in overall figures of SSIs.
However, only one cluster has been taken up for assistance by Government of India under the scheme. There is a need to cover clusters in the state.
 
(vi)       Raw material shortage the small scale industry, especially the engineering industry, has been facing problem of availability of steel. The SSI requires about 2,70,000
MT of steel, 40,000 MT of rounds and 50,000 MT of wire rods problems of availability of steel.

(C) KARNATAKA
 
1.3       Karnataka has been pioneer in industry. In recent times, Karnataka has emerged as the knowledge and technology capital of the cQuntry making rapid strides in the
economy of the sate. IT and related industries, biotechnology and strong research and development institutions have given Karnataka a pride of place in the global market.
Growth of small-scale industries in Karnataka has been very rapid since 1982-83. As on 3 1’ March, 2003, 2,98,218 small scale industrial units have been registered with the
Directorate of Industries and Commerce. It is estimated that the investment is to the order of Rs.616374 lakhs providing employment for about 17,22,190 persons. Largest
concentration of small scale industries is in Bangalore Urban District, which is 53,665 followed by 27,084 units in Belgaum  District, 18149 units in Mysore district and
17,615 units in Tumkur district. Koppal has 3,451 in small-scale industries.
 
1.3.1 Problem being faced by SSI Sectors in Karnataka
 
(i)         Inadequate quality power supply,Lack of transportation in rural areas, lack of assured marketing facilities and huge domestic market still lie untapped,
 
(ii)        Raising inputs cost as compared to price of finished goods resulting into stagnant SSI sector;

1.4.12              Status of Power supply to Industries
 
1.4.13         The Committee was apprised that Bihar has an installed capacity of around 3000 m.w. Thermal power accounts for over 90 per cent of the total generating
capacity in the state. Implementation of various power projects have been in different stages. These projects cover thermal power at Nabinagar, Chandil , Patna, Kursela and
Tenughat and Hydel Power at KoelKaro, Kadwan and Sankha. Government of India recently announced a package of new schemes worth Rs. 12,036 crores for the State
including assistance to power projects. Several pithead thermal projects are also on the anvil. The Eastern Region of the country (installed capacity 9000 m. .w.) with 6000
m.w. of power operates in an integrated mode as a single system. With the central share available from this system and inequity due to trade equalisation policy, the supply
of power has been erratic in Bihar. The State Government is aptly placing highest priority on the development of power sector in its economic planning to bridge the demand
gap. It is also encouraging private sector participation in power generation and power distribution in the State. Setting up of captive power plants, to meet the existing as well
as future demand for power of industrial units, is being encouraged in the state. Installation of Diesel Generating sets by entrepreneurs are also permitted for running the
enterprises. With the encouraging power policy pursued by the State Government, th industrial activity in the state would pick up in the years ahead.

(ii)        It is evident that nationalised banks are not taking adequate interest in advancing loans to SSIs. They still demand collateral securities up to the loan amounting to
Rs.25 Lacs which is against the norms. Necessary instructions to banks may be issued.
 
(iii)       In order to improve the global competitiveness of the domestic industries and also to provide for quality infrastructure, the Govt. of India has launche  Industrial
Infrastructure Up-gradation Scheme. The scheme lays down that 25% of the total cost of the project would be borne by other stakeholders of the respective cluster with a
minimum industry contribution of 15% of total project cost. It is suggested that the provision of 25% contribution as above may be relaxed and State Govt. or State Govt.
Institutions may be allowed to contribute the above share.
 
(iv) SIDBI provides guarantee against composite loan of Rs.25 Lacs under Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries. Under this scheme only a few special RRB,s
NSIC, NEDFI, SIDBI & few commercial banks who have entered into an agreement with the Guarantee Trust are authorised  to operate the scheme whereas SFCs have been
kept out. It is therefore, necessary that all the SFC’s and commercial banks may be permitted to participate in the implementation of the scheme.
 
(v)        It would be in the fitness of things that one consolidated & integrated code of rules should be applicable to the SSI units, so that they may not face complexities of
rules and hardship and utilize their time for productive purposes.

view that the main issues concerning the Indian SSI sector pertains to rehabilitation of the existing units by providing assistance at concessional rates, advanced

2.2       Working of credit linked Capital Subsidy Scheme
 
2.2.1    Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation in Small Scale Industries has been started by DC(SSI) in year 2000 which provides 12% subsidy
(subsequently raised to 15% ) to selected sub sectors on institutional finance for technology upgradation . The technology related needs for process modification and product
diversification can be fulfilled by SSI sector through the scheme. Action is being taken to enhance the scope of this scheme to cover more areas by O/o DC(SSI).
 
2.2.2    The purpose behind introduction of CLCSS is to motivate and facilitate SSI units to upgrade their technology through infusion of institutional credit. The strategy
adopted for this purpose is to provide 12% upfront capital subsidy on institutional finance availed to facilitate technology upgradation in small scale sector. The ceiling of
loans eligible under the scheme is presently Rs. 40 lakh.
 
2.2.3    The corpus fund created under the scheme is Rs. 600 crore for years of operation from Oct. 2000 to Sept. 30, 2005. Till February 2005, an amount of Rs. 23.86 crore
has been utilized under the scheme which includes an advance of Rs. 5 crore to SIDBI and Rs. 3 crore to NABARD for operationalising  the scheme. The slow progress
under the scheme is due to general inhibition on the part of SSI units to go for technology upgradation . The announcement made under General Budget for the year 2004-05
for enhancement in the rate of subsidy and the ceiling of loans eligible under the scheme will help to make the scheme popular among the SSI units.

2.3       Working of Credit Guarantee Scheme
 
2.3.1    The Credit Guarantee Scheme was launched with a view to alleviate the problems of collateral security faced by the small enterprises, particularly first generation
entrepreneurs, and to remove the impediments in flow of credit to Small enterprises sector. The problems in the implementation of the scheme pertains to low level of
awareness about the scheme amongst the field level officers of MLIs, negative mindset of the MLIs due to greater volume of administrative work in the small enterprises
lending and may be their bad experience in the past on a similar scheme, bankers’ traditional/usual comfort with collateral security and perceived high risk nature of small
enterprises sector. These problems of the bank branches need to be seriously addressed by the management of the banks. By enhancing the awareness about the scheme
among the field level officers of MLIs through seminars/training, the progress under the scheme could be improved. Furthermore, expeditious enhancement of the Corpus
Fund up to the envisaged level of Rs.2500 crore under the scheme would increase the comfort level of participating MLIs and encourage them to avail the scheme on a much
wider scale.
 
2.3.2    Since inception, 49 banks/institutions (i.e., 27 public sector banks, 11 private sector banks, 8 regional rural banks, NSIC, NEDFi and SIDBI) have become Member
Lending Institutions under the Scheme. As on 28 Februaiy 2005, a total of 22,684 proposals were approved for guarantee cover for an aggregate loan ofRs.484.61 crore. Of
this, so far 81 claims have been received from MLIs for settlement involving an amount of Rs. 1.70 crore. The scheme would continue till the end of Tenth Five Year Plan
and decision to continue it further would be taken thereafter.
 
2.3.3    The Credit Guarantee Scheme aims to alleviate the problem of collateral security among the small enterprises, particu’arly to tiny enterprises. To cover the entire tiny
sector, which is defined as units having investment in plant and machinery upto Rs.25 lakh, the Group of Ministers in its meeting held on 16th August, 2004 decided to raise
the loan limit under the scheme from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs.25 lakh. The proposal to further enhance the loan limit from Rs.25 lakh to Rs.50 lakh under the scheme is under
consideration of the Government.

2.10     Export Potential of SSI products
 
2.10.1 The export-import data obtained from Department of Commerce, Ministry of commerce and Industry indicate that India’s imports from China have increased to some
extent from Rs.5559 crores during 1999-2000 to Rs.18625 crores during 2003-2004. However, exports of India to China have grown significantly from Rs.2336 crores
(1999-2000) to Rs.13579 crores in  2003-2004.
 
2.10.2    The Committee was apprised that MIs. A.C. Nielsen on behalf of Ministry of
done an evaluation study. As per the findings the said study, major potential export mar for SSIs exports are US, EU and Japan. The potential export-worthy items in the SSI
sec have been categorized into three broad categories:
 
(i)         Potential items produced by SSI units amongst the top 100 items imported by major markets, which do not figure in the top 100 items exported from India to these
major markets:- The product groups that hold potential for SSI exports are agriculture, marine and allied products along with engineering! electrical! electronic product
group. The study identifies Japan as a potential market for exporting agriculture, marine and allied products whereas the European union and the US can be tapped for
enhancing SSI exports of engineering/electrical and electronic items.
 
(ii)        Potential items produced by SSI units amongst the top 100 items imported by major markets, which do not figure in the top 100 items exported from India to these
major markets:- The major thrust areas for SSI exports are agriculture and allied, chemicals, plastic items, leather and textile product groups. The study identifies the US and
EU as the potential markets for textile whereas Japan would be the ideal destination for export of chemicals product groups.
 
(iii)       Potential items produced by SSI units amongst the top 100 items imported by major markets, which do not figure in the top 100 items exported from India to these
major markets:- The potential for SSI is in various product groups like agriculture, marine and allied, chemicals and allied, leather items, textiles and other items. The EU
has been identified as the potential market for textiles including sports equipments whereas export of leather items holds potential for the US and the EU.
 
2.10.3  There is consistent increase in the percentage share of SSI exports in the field of electronics and computer softwate. The percentage share has increased from 13.12%
to 23.93% in 2003-2004 over the previous year. As regards the steps undertaken to increase the export potential of SSI sector, the Development Commissioner (SSI)
promotes participation of SSI units in product specific as well as general exhibitions in India and abroad every year. Besides this, training in export marketing and packaging
for exports is also provided to SSI units. Sector Specific Market Studies are conducted for selected SSI categories. In addition, publicity material for overseas publicity are

2.11     Challenges of globalization and liberalization
 
2.11.1  The Committee desires that the Government should take measures for preparing SSI sector to meet the challenges of globalization and liberalization under the WTO
regime. However, the basic concern of the Committee is the protection and promotion of domestic SSI sector under the prevailing global market economy. Therefore, the
continuous and concrete efforts should be made by the Government to protect the domestic Small Scale Industries from the on-slaught of adverse impact of globalization and
liberalization through appropriate tariff adjustment, anti dumping measures and other safeguards. Simultaneously the process of strengthening SSI sector and acquiring the
requisite competitive resilience should be .enhanced on the ground level. The Committee is in agreement with the views of SSI associations I federations that the Ministry of
SSI should make efforts for Streamlining and strengthening the Anti-dumping mechanism
 
(i) Conversion of Quantitative restriction (QRs) into rationalised tariff regime for providing protection to the domestic SSIs;
 
(ii) Implementation of VAT and safeguard duties to protect domestic producers in consonance with WTO provision; and
 
(iii) Expeditious disposal dumping cases are anti-dumping actions thereto, in view of almost all SSI products under open general license (OGL) list.
 
212      Legal framework
 
2.12.1  The Committee desires that legal framework affecting the Small Scale Industries must be satisfactory in order to give fillip to the promotion and development of
Small Scale Industries Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa, Jharkhand. The following issues may be taken up on priority basis and the Ministry of SSI should pursue
with the concerned Ministries: -
 
(i)         A single Unified Act governing the rules pertaining to retrenchment and layoffs and social benefits for employees.
 
(ii)        Enactment of Single Comprehensive Small Enterprises Development Act for SSEs similar to the Industrial Development and Regulation (IDR) Act.
 
(iii)       Comprehensive Social Security Scheme for widening the social safety nets.
 
(iv)       Amendment in the provision of the Delayed Payment Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertaking Act 1993 as amended in 1998 and the relevant provisions of
the Companies Act i.e. mandatory provision requiring the large enterprises to show in the entries of their Balance sheets the amount due for payment to the SSI units to
enable SSI units/suppliers to get payments as agreed upon.
 
(vi)       The SSI sector needs the Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Act, therefore, that the Ministry of SSI should continue to pursue for legislation of the Limited Liability
Partnership Act in the interest of Small Scale Sector.
 
2.12.2 The Committee views that small scale industries is the engine of growth, therefore, SSI units must be given the space to grow into medium enterprises. In the context
of globalisation there is a growing feeling in certain quarters that India should also adopt the SME Concept World over, policies are devised to meet the requirement of small
and medium enterprises (SME). The Committee desires that the steps should be initiated for formulating policies for Medium Enterprises and adequate institutional
arrangement and mechanism should be setup for working of medium enterprises in the national economy.

COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
ORISSA
 
            The Committee observes that Orissa demonstrates a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty as the state, despite having mineral and marine resources, has been
bereft of sustainable industrial growth and economic development. The Committee finds that the cherished Charter of the Planning Commission which was “to combine a
rapid rise in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing production and offering opportunities to all for
employment in the service of the community”, has not seen the light of the day in the state. The state has been devoid of planned development giving rise to the
economically backward district like Bolangir, Koraput and above all the Kalahandi.
(Para 1.1.4)
 
            No major efforts have been made to put the state on the industrial development track, and therefore there is the lack of ancialirisation  of industries in the Small and
Medium sectors. Besides, the general problems like lack of Infrastructural development and marketing assistance and shortage of timely and adequate credit flow etc., the
state has also been the victim of natural calamities like super cyclone in 1999 which have actually devastated the Small scale industrial set up and thus arrested the industrial
growth and promotion and proliferation of small and medium enterprises in the state.
(Para 1.1.5)
           
            The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the financial institutions should come forward for providing timely and adequate credit flow to the entrepreneurs for
accelerated industrial growth and promotion of SMEs in the state. The Committee recommends that concerted efforts must be undertaken for popularization of venture
capital, factoring services and other financial linked schemes like CGYTSI, CLCSS, NEF and SME Fund of SIDBL
(Para 1.1.6)
 
The Committee further recommends that following key areas must be selected for effective action:

(ii)        Financial restructuring of Orissa State Financial co-operation by seriously considering the proposal of adjustment of interest payment to the tune of Rs. 160.33 crore

INTRODUCTION
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry having been
authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and Seventy Sixth
Report of the Committee on the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005.  
2.The Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill 2005 was introduced  in  the Lok Sabha on the 12
th May 2005 
and was referred ( Annexure I) to the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry by the Hon’ble
Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 27
th May 2005 under Rule 270 (b) of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the
Council of States for  examination and report thereon.
3.The Committee held eight  sittings in all spreading over twenty hours on the Bill. A Press Communique dated the 15
th
June 2005, inviting the views/suggestions of the individuals, organisations, experts, institutions, etc. interested in the
subject matter of the Bill, was issued.   In its meeting held on the 21
st  June 2005 , the Committee heard the presentation
of the Secretary, Ministry of SSI, Government of India on the Bill and held preliminary discussion thereon. The
Committee decided to hear the views of all State governments and major industry associations, on the provisions of the
Bill.
4.       In response to the Press Communique, sixty four written memoranda were received, out of which thirty six
memoranda  were found to be relevant to the subject matter of the Bill. (List at Annexure-II)

provisions of the Bill. (Annexure-III)
6.     The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill on 29
th July, 2005.
7.     The observations and recommendations of the Committee have been incorporated at appropriate places in the
Report.

1.0       Background

1.1       At present the small scale industry is defined by notification under Section 11 B of the Industries (Development
and Regulation) Act, 1951. Section 29 B of the Act provides for the list of items reserved for SSI sector.  There was a
long standing demand from the small scale industries (SSI) sector for a single legislation for the sector, instead of
multiple laws, rules, regulations and administrative directives so far applicable to it and to minimize the visits
ofinspectors enforcing these multiple laws etc.
1.2       The Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI), Hyderabad was entrusted a study by the Government in
March, 2000.  The ASCI submitted its report in March 2002.   The draft Bill suggested by the ASCI was circulated in
April 2002 for wide dissemination of its contents and  was  also placed for consideration of  the Small Scale Industries
Board at its 47th   meeting held on 04
th  July 2002 at New Delhi under the Chairmanship of Minister of State for SSI. 
The feed-back received from the members of the SSI Board was examined and based on these the ASCI submitted a
final draft Bill in February 2003.  This draft Bill was again circulated to the members of the SSI Board on 25
th  June
2003 for their comments. 
1.3       A Cabinet Note on the draft Small Enterprises Development (SED) Bill was circulated among the
Ministries/Departments concerned for their comments twice, first in December 2003 and later in July 2004.  After
detailed examination of the comments of all concerned, the SED Bill, 2004 was submitted to the Cabinet Secretariat on
17
th  November 2004.  At the behest of the Cabinet Secretariat, a meeting of the Committee of Secretaries (CoS) was
held on 23rd  November 2004.  In light of the recommendations of the CoS, the draft Bill and the Cabinet Note was
modified and again circulated among the Ministries/Departments concerned on 07th  December 2004.
1.4       Based on the comments received from different Ministries/Departments,  on this draft (SED) Bill, the matter was
further examined and the Small and Medium Enterprises Development (SMED), Bill 2005 was circulated amongst the 
Ministries/Departments concerned on 14th  March 2005. After taking into account their views to the extent possible, the
SMED Bill, 2005 was submitted to the Cabinet Secretariat on 27th  April 2005 and approved by the Cabinet on 4th  May
2005.  The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 12th  May 2005.
1.5       The Bill aims at facilitating the promotion and development and enhancing the competitiveness of small and
medium enterprises and seeks to-
provide for statutory definitions of “small enterprise” and “medium enterprise”;
provided for the establishment of a National Small and Medium Enterprises Board, a high-level forum consisting of
stakeholders for participative review of and making recommendations on the policies and programmes for the
development of small and medium enterprises;
provide for classification of small and medium enterprises on the basis of investment in plant and machinery, or
equipment and establishment of an Advisory Committee to recommend on the related matter;
empower the Central Government to notify programmes, guidelines or instructions for facilitating the promotion and
development and enhancing the competitiveness of small and medium enterprises;
empower the State Governments to specify, by notification, that provisions of the labour laws specified in Clause9(2)
will not apply to small and medium enterprises employing up to fifty employees with a view to facilitating the
graduation of small enterprises to medium enterprises;
make provisions for ensuring timely and smooth flow of credit to small and medium enterprises to minimize the
incidence of sickness among and enhancing the competitiveness of such enterprises, in accordance with the guidelines
or instructions of the Reserve Bank of India;
empower the Central and State Governments to notify preference policies in respect of procurement of goods and
services, produced and provided by small enterprises, by the Ministries, departments and public sector enterprises;
empowering the Central Government to create a Fund or Funds for facilitating promotion and development and
enhancing the competitiveness of  small enterprises and medium enterprises;
empower to prescribe harmonized, simpler and streamlined procedures for inspection of small and medium enterprises
under the labour laws enumerated in Clause 15, having regard to the need to promote self-regulation or self-certification
by such enterprises;
prescribe for maintenance of records and filing of returns by small and medium enterprises with a view to reduce the
multiplicity of often-overlapping types of returns to be filed;
make further improvements in the Interest on Delayed Payments to Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings
Act, 1993 and making that enactment a part of the proposed legislation and to repeal that enactment.
Chapter-wise  Provisions of the Bill
2.0       The Bill consists of 33 Clauses spreading over seven Chapters. A brief description of the provisions of the Bill,

            Chapter 1
2.1      Preliminary
2.1.1    It contains Clauses 1and 2 dealing with Short title and commencement and Definitions.
2.1.2    The Bill explicitly focuses on facilitating the promotion and development and enhancing competitiveness of
small and medium enterprises.
Chapter II
2.2       National Small and Medium Enterprises Board
2.2.1    It contains Clauses 3-6 pertaining to National Small and Medium Enterprises Board, its composition, functions
and related provisions.
2.2.2    As a high-level forum consisting of all sections of stakeholders for participative review of and making
recommendations on the policies and programmes for the development of small and medium enterprises and issues
related thereto, constitution of the National Small and Medium Enterprises Board (in lieu of the currently existing non-
statutory body, known as the SSI Board), its functions and related matters have been provided for.  The size of the
Board has been limited to 30 members with due representation of State Governments, Union Territory (UT)
Administrations, Central Ministries, RBI, SIDBI, NABARD, IBA, associations of small and medium enterprises
(including associations of women entrepreneurs) and eminent persons from the field of economics and industry. 
The Clause 5 suggests functions of the Board aim at making it effective in its advisory and recommendatory role
Chapter III
2.3       Classification of Enterprises, Advisory Committee and Memorandum of Small and Medium Enterprises
Definition of Small Enterprise and Medium Enterprise
2.3.1    In the Clause relating to definitions in the draft Bill, the “small enterprise” (SE) and “medium enterprise”(ME)
have been defined.  Detailed criteria for defining such enterprises have been spelt out in Clause 7 and 8 of this Chapter. 
Different investment limits for the manufacturing and service-providing small and medium enterprises have also been
specified in Clause 7(1) in recognition of the fact that the investments in plant, machinery and equipment for these two
segments of SEs and MEs differ and are generally less for the services segment .
2.3.2    Advisory Committee
2.3.3    The Clauses 7 (2) to 7 (6) of Chapter III provide for constitution and functions of an Advisory Committee by the
Central Government to fine tune and recommend the classification of SME Sector. The factors to be kept in view by the
Advisory Committee in making recommendations on this subject have been enumerated in Clause 7(5). In order to
provide for flexibility in tune with the global and domestic changes in this dynamic sector, it has also been provided in
Clause 7(6) that the Central Government may, from time to time, vary the criterion of investment, consider
criteria/standards in respect of employment or turnover of the enterprises and include in such classification micro or tiny
enterprises or village enterprises, as part of small enterprises so that the interests and specific problems of micro (tiny)
and village/rural enterprises are taken into account.
2.3.4    Memorandum of Small and Medium Enterprises
2.3.5    The Clause 8 provides for the mechanism of signing Memorandum of Small and Medium Enterprises. The
Committee was informed that the  Third All India Census of Small Scale Industries (2001-02) shows that a very large
proportion of SSI units are either unaware of the existing  provisions of registration or unwilling to bear the transaction
cost involved in obtaining registration; as a result, a vast majority of SSI units are currently operating as unregistered
ones.  Gradual relaxation of State control over economic activities in the private sector has further reduced the need for
registration.
 2.3.6   As per the suggestions from SSI associations it has been provided in Clause 8 of this Bill that any person, who
intends to establish a small enterprise, may, at his discretion file a memorandum of small enterprises with the authority
prescribed by the State government. However any person, who intends to establish a medium enterprise, shall
mandatorily file a memorandum of medium enterprises with such an authority as notified by the Central government. 
2.3.7    This Clause also provides that any person who, having established a small enterprise before the commencement
of this Act, had or had not obtained a registration certificate may, at his discretion, file the memorandum. Even now, all
non-SSI units, except for those governed by licensing provisions under the I(D&R) Act, have to file the Industrial
Entrepreneur’s Memorandum (IEM) prescribed under Press Note No. 4 of 1998 dated 15.6.1998. Therefore, this Clause
further provides that any person who, having established a small enterprise before the commencement of this Act, had
or had not filed the IEM, shall, within ninety days from the commencement of this Act, file the memorandum.
Committee was informed that filing of such a memorandum has not been prescribed as a necessary condition in the
SMED Bill for availing of the benefits of promotional schemes of the Government for the sector.

Chapter IV
2.4       Measures for Promotion, Development and Enhancement of Competitiveness of Small and Medium Enterprises
2.4.1    The Clause 9(1) is an enabling provision for the Central Government to facilitate the promotion and
development and enhancing competitiveness of small and medium enterprises, particularly of the former, by way of
skill development, marketing assistance, infrastructure and cluster development with a view to strengthening backward
and forward linkages.  For such purposes, this Clause empowers the Government to specify, by notification, such
programmes, guidelines or instructions, as it may deem fit.
2.4.2    With a view to making the operation of these enterprises hassle-free to some extent and also facilitating
graduation of small enterprises to medium enterprises, Clause 9(2) provides that a State Government may, by
notification, provide that the provisions of the Employees’ Liability Act, the Weekly Holidays’ Act, Employment
Exchange (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act and the Apprentices Act shall not apply to small and medium
enterprises employing upto fifty employees in that State. The States currently administer these Acts and hence the
proposed empowerment is procedurally required .
2.4.3    Credit Facilities to Small and Medium Enterprises
2.4.4    It has been proposed in Clause 10 that the credit facilities for small and medium enterprises shall be progressive
and such as may be specified in the guidelines or instructions issued by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time, to
ensure timely and smooth flow of credit to such enterprises, minimise the incidence of sickness among and enhancing
the competitiveness of such enterprises. 
 2.4.5   The Committee was informed that the Government was considering to enhance the credit flow to SSI sector on
the lines with agriculture and that the RBI was in process of reviewing, consolidating and liberalizing its guideline on
credit for SME Sector.
2.4.6    Procurement Preference Policies
2.4.7    Clause 11 provides that Central/State Governments and UT Administrations may notify preference policies in
respect of procurements of goods and services, produced and provided by small enterprises by their respective
Ministries, Departments, aided institutions and public sector enterprises.
2.4.8    Funds for Promotion and Development  of Small and Medium Enterprises Development :
2.4.9    It has been provided in Clauses 12 to 14 that the Central Government may constitute one or more Funds for
promotion and development and enhancement of competitiveness of the Small and Medium Enterprises and there shall
be credited thereto any grants made by the Central Government, after due appropriation by Parliament by law in this
behalf.  The Fund shall be utilized exclusively for the measures specified in sub-Clause (1) of Clause 9.  Administration
of the Fund, coordination and ensuring timely utilization and release of sums, by the Central Government, will be done
through rules to be prescribed under the provisions of Clause 14. The National Small and Medium Enterprises Board
can advise the Central government over the use of such Fund.
Chapter V
2.5       Inspection of SMEs and Related Matters
 2.5.1   The Committee was informed of the study conducted by the Administrative Staff College of India,  that SSIs are
required to comply with 50 laws and deal with 64 inspectors.  A recent study (2004) conducted by FICCI has revealed
that the number of inspectors under the laws listed in the study report is 43 under labour laws, 24 under laws governing
manufacturing, 18 under environmental laws and 6 under Central Excise Act and State Sales Tax Acts.  Moreover, the
number of inspectors with powers of imprisonment, sealing the units and stopping operation are 20, 12 and 21
respectively.
2.5.2    In order to reduce the adverse effects of “Inspector Raj”, the Bill provides that inspections under the 7 labour
laws listed in Clause 15 shall be carried out in such manner and by such authority as may be prescribed.  The idea here
is to prescribe harmonized, simpler and streamlined procedures for inspection with due regard for the need to promote
self-regulation or self-certification by small and medium enterprises.
2.5.3    Further, in order to reduce the multiplicity of often-overlapping types of returns to be filed, Clause 16 provides
for maintenance of such records and filing of such returns, as may be prescribed, by small and medium enterprises .
Chapter VI
2.6       Delayed Payment to Small Enterprises
2.6.1    The Clauses 17 to 24 deal with the issue of delayed payment to the SSI units by the buyers.  Delayed payments
to small scale industries supplying goods or providing services to buyers have been a major cause of sickness in the SSI
sector.  The Interest on Delayed Payments to Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings Act, 1993 was enacted
to tackle this problem.  This Act was further amended in 1998 to provide for constitution of Industry Facilitation
Councils as a forum for resolution of disputes between the buyers and suppliers covered by the Act.  It was felt later that

further amendments were necessary to make the Act more effective.  Therefore, the provisions of the above-mentioned
Act have been modified accordingly and incorporated fully in Chapter VI of this Bill.  As a result, the said Act will
stand repealed as soon as SMED Act comes into force.
Chapter VII
2.7       Miscellaneous Provisions
2.7.1    In view of the latest observations of some Ministries/Departments questioning the need to designate specific
officers of the Central and State Governments as authorities under the proposed legislation and of specifying their ranks
in the erstwhile Clauses nos. 7 and 8 have been deleted and a general provision included in the new Clause 27.
2.7.2    The penalties are proposed to be provided (Clause 28) for violation of some of the Clauses of the proposed law.
Sufficient care has been exercised to ensure that the penalties are restricted to serious violations and the prescribed
punishment is not too harsh. Every order notified under sub-sections (1) of section 9 and every rule made by the Central
Government under the proposed legislation are proposed to be placed for consideration of both Houses of Parliament, as
provided in Clause 30 of the Bill.

4.0       While considering the Bill, the Committee observed that the Bill does not refer to the Tiny sector, which
constitutes a large segment of the small-scale sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tiny sector should
be duly incorporated in the Bill.  Accordingly, the Committee felt that appropriate Clauses may be incorporated in the
Bill to define the Tiny Sector  and also the consequential changes may be made in the  relevant Clauses of the Bill.  
5.0       Clauses by Clause consideration
Clause 2
5.1       The Clause seeks to define the various expressions used in the Bill.
5.2.1    The Committee is of the view that the definition of “Appointed day” in Clause 2(b) and “the day of acceptance”
and deemed acceptance” in explanation thereto does not provide the desired relief to the small supplier from the vice of
delayed payments.  The period of ‘30 days’ as provided in the Bill needs to be reduced.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that it should be reduced to 15 days.
5.2.2    The Committee considers the phrase “ in relation thereto” in Clause 2 (e) as superfluous and accordingly
recommends its deletion. 
5.2.3    The Committee recommends that the term `industrial’ in Clause 2 (g) and 2 (l) may be replaced with “
enterprises” so as to include both manufacturing and service enterprises both in small and medium  sector.
5.2.4    In Clause 2 (m) the Committee recommends for inclusion of ‘Tiny enterprises’ to  so as avail the benefits of the
provisions the Bill as referred to in Clause 8(1).
5.2.5    In addition to existing categories of suppliers as indicated in Clause 2 (m) the Committee recommends for the
inclusion of  `any commission, company, cooperative society, society or trust registered as such under the relevant Act
and engaged in selling of goods or services produced or rendered  by such enterprises’.
5.2.6 The Committee recommends that the Tiny Sector may be suitably defined in this Clause.
5.2.7    Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 3

head office in Delhi. If further lays down that the Minister in charge of the Ministry or Department of the Central

addition, it lays down the composition of the Board consisting of the Vice-Chairperson, member-Secretary, and 27

of the members of the Board, the manner of filling vacancies, frequency of meetings of the Board, association of other

5.3.1    The Committee was of the considered view that the National Small and Medium Enterprises Board (NSMEB)

5.8       The Clause seeks to lay down the requirement for filing of memorandum of small enterprise or medium
enterprise with the authority specified by the State Government or the Central Government under the provisions of this
Clause.  It also empowers the Central Government, to notify, the procedure of filing of the memorandum and the
authority with which the memorandum shall be filed by a medium enterprise.  This Clause also confers powers on the
State Government to notify the authority with which a small enterprise may file the memorandum.  It also enables the
Central Government to notify the procedure to be followed by the above-mentioned authorities for the purposes of this
Clause.
5.8.1    The Committee feels that in order to have clearer scenario in the tiny, small and medium Enterprises sector in
the country, it is necessary that such units must be registered. It will enable the Government to discern the trends in the
sector and take appropriate policy initiatives. The Committee, therefore, recommends for filing of Memorandum by the
tiny, small and medium enterprises mandatory. It will enable the units to avail the benefits of Government’s schemes.
5.8.2    The Committee however, emphasizes that the filing of Memorandum should be simple and after a given period
if no objection is raised by the relevant authority, the unit should be deemed as registered. As regards the industry
referred to in proviso to clause 8 (i)   such Memorandum may be filed with in one hundred and eighty days instead of
ninety days as provided in the Bill from the commencement of this Act.
5.8.3    Subject to such changes,  the Clause was adopted.
Clause 9
5.9       The Clause seeks to enable the Central Government to notify programmes, guidelines or instructions for
facilitating the promotion and development and enhancing the competitiveness of small enterprises and medium
enterprises.  It also empowers a State Government to provide, by notification, that the provisions of the Employers’
Liability Act, 1938, the Weekly Holidays Act, 1942, the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of
Vacancies) Act, 1959 and the Apprentices Act, 1961 shall not apply to small and medium enterprises employing up to
fifty employees in that State.
5.9.1    The Committee observes that as the Clause 9 (1) provides for the measures for the promotion and development
of small and medium sector and recommends that this Clause should also specifically include the ` tiny sector’ under the
coverage of such measures.
5.9.2    Further, the Committee is of the view that there is a need to encourage the women entrepreneurs in tiny, small
and medium enterprises. Therefore, the Clause 9(1) should have specific mention of women enterprises to underscore
the need for special incentives for women entrepreneurs.
5.9.3    The Committee acknowledges that competitiveness of Small and Medium Enterprises sector is severely
constrained by the outdated, inefficient technologies. Upgraded technologies are an imperative for these enterprises to
withstand the competition. Therefore, the Committee recommends that technology up-gradation as a vital input must be
reflected in Clause 9 (1) for the promotional measures.
5.9.4    The Committee is also of the view that the growth of tiny and small sector is stunted by the insufficient
infrastructural support and availability of critical inputs at reasonable prices. Therefore,  there should be specific
mention of such measures to overcome these constraints in the Bill.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends that
Clause 9 should provide for the railways  to earmark a definite percentage of its freight capacity for the transportation of
raw material meant for tiny, small and medium  enterprises as well as for the transportation of the products of such
units.  Similar mention may be made in the Clause 9 seeking the steel manufacturers and coal producers to reserve
definite percentage of their production for the tiny and Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) sector.
5.9.5    Subject to above changes,  the Clause was adopted.
Clause 10
5.10     The Clause seeks to provide for the credit facilities to the small and medium enterprises as may be specified in
the guidelines or instructions issued by the Reserve Bank of India.
5.10.1  The Committee was of the view that credit facilities under RBI guidelines have existed for several years without
much of avail. The Committee also took cognizance of the views expressed by the State Governments and industry
associations on the inadequacy of bank credit at concessional rates to the tiny, small and medium enterprises despite

repeated RBI guidelines in this regard.  Implementation of RBI guidelines by banks has been major concern of the
Committee. While appreciating that this  Clause  of the Bill recognizes the need to clear such bottlenecks, the
Committee recommends to give greater force of law to the provisions of this Clause. The Committee accordingly
suggests that term ‘ credit facilities’ may be replaced with the phrase ‘ The policies and practices in respect of credit to
the tiny’  
5.10.2  Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.

5.11     The Clause seeks to empower the Central Government or the State Government  to notify preference policies in
respect of procurement of goods and services, produced and provided by small enterprises, by its Ministries,
departments or its aided institutions and public sector enterprises.
5.11.1  The Committee recommends that Tiny enterprises may be included along with the small and medium enterprises
5.11.2  Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.

5.12     The Clause seeks to enable the Central Government to constitute, by notification, one or more Funds and credit
thereto any grants made to the Central Government under the provisions of Clause 13.
5.12.1  The Clause was adopted without any change.

5.13     The Clause seeks to empower the Central Government to credit to the Fund or Funds, such sums of money as the
Government may provide after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this behalf.
5.13.1  The Clause was adopted without any change.

5.14     The Clause seeks to empower the Central Government to administer the Fund or Funds in such manner, and also
entrusts that government with the responsibility for the coordination and ensuring timely utilization and release of sums
with such criteria, as may be prescribed.
5.14.1  The Committee was of the view that in order to facilitate that such Funds are utilized by the tiny, small and
medium enterprises all over the country, it was necessary that States too should establish similar funds with matching
contribution by Center and State governments. The Committee suggested that such provision should be made while
formulating Rules for this Clause under this Act.
5.14.2  Furthermore, the States should use these funds to finance R&D for the SME and Tiny enterprises.
5.14.3  The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 15
5.15     The Clause seeks to provide that notwithstanding anything in relation to inspection contained in the Payment of
Wages Act, 1936, the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948, the Factories Act, 1948, the Employee’s Provident Fund
and Miscellaneous Provision Act, 1952, the Maternity benefit Act, 1961, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, the Inspection of a small and medium enterprises shall be carried out in such manner,
with regard to the promotion of self-regulation or self-certification by the small and the medium enterprises, and by such
authority, as may be prescribed.
5.15.1  The Committee recommends for inclusion of Tiny sector at appropriate places in the Clause.
5.15.2  Subject to the  change,  the Clause was adopted.
Clause 16
5.16     The Clause seeks to provide that every small and medium enterprise responsible for maintenance or such
records, filing of such returns with such authority and in such forms, as may be prescribed.
5.16.1  The Clause was  adopted without any change.
Clause 17
5.17     The Clause seeks to specify the liability of buyer of goods and services from a supplier to make payment
therefore on or before the dated agree upon between the two parties in writing or, where there is no agreement in this
behalf, before the appointed day.  The proviso to this Clause seeks to limit the period agreed upon between the supplier
and the buyer in writing to seventy-five days from the day of acceptance or the day of deemed acceptance. 
5.17.1  The Committee felt that there was a need to expedite the payment due to tiny and small enterprises to enable
them to timely settle their liabilities with Banks without affecting their credit ratings. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the small and tiny suppliers should get their payment within Forty –Five days instead of Seventy-five
days from the day of acceptance or deemed acceptance as mentioned in proviso to this Clause.
5.17.2  Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 18
