5.18     The Clause seeks to specify the date from which and the rate at which interests will be payable by the buyer to
the supplier in case of the former failing to make payments of the amount to the supplier, as required under section 17.
5.18.1  The Committee was of the view that the rate of interest payable by the buyer on delayed payment should be high
enough to prevent delays in payment to tiny and small suppliers. The Committee, therefore, recommends that such
interest rate should be three times the bank rate instead of nine percent plus bank rate as prescribed in this Clause.
5.18.2  Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 19
5.19     The Clause seeks to make the amount due from a buyer, together with the amountof interest calculated in
accordance with the provisions of section 18, recoverable by way or a suit or other proceeding under law.
5.19.1  The Committee was of the view that the recourse to recovery of  amount by way of suit is  against the interest of
the supplier as it takes long time and involve other procedural complexities.  Perhaps,  this was the reason that Industrial
Facilitation Council (IFCs) have to be constituted to settle the dispute amongst the parties.  Industrial Facilitation
Council (IFCs) being set up under this Bill without having power to execute its award does not provide any relief to the
supplier.  The Committee, therefore, is the view that recovery through civil suit has to be avoided instead Industrial
Facilitation Council (IFC) be empowered with the powers to execute the awards.
5.19.2  The Committee, therefore, recommends  that this Clause could be deleted and the subsequent Clauses be
sufficiently strengthened by conferring upon the Industry Facilitation Councils the similar powers as vested with the
Consumer Forum,  to execute its award.
5.19.3  The Clause  was found redundant,  hence may be deleted.
Clause 20
5.20     The Clause seeks to provide for the jurisdiction of the Industry Facilitation Council for acting as an arbitrator or
conciliator in respect of  making  the amount due from a buyer, together with the amount of interest calculated in
accordance with the provisions of section 18, recoverable.
5.20.1  The Bill provides for setting up of one or more Industry Facilitation Council by State Governments under Clause
22 specifying its jurisdiction. The Committee then considered the situation of inter-state disputes and recommended that
the Industrial Facilitation Council of the State where the supplier is located, shall have the jurisdiction over such inter-
state cases. Such provision should be reflected specifically in this Clause.
5.20.3  The Committee was also of the view that  this Clause should fix a time limit for the Industrial Facilitation
Council to decide on the references made to it.   The Committee suggests that reference made to Industrial Facilitation
Council (IFCs) be decided within ninety days.
5.20.4  Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 21
5.21     The Clause seeks to debar any court or other authority from entertaining an appeal against any decree, award or
any other order unless the appellant (not being a supplier) has deposited with it seventy-five per cent of the amount in
terms of the decree, award or other order.
5.21.1  The Committee felt that filing appeal against any award made by an arbitrator like Industrial Facilitation
Council   was a right of the buyer that can not be infringed by such provisions as given in the Clause.  Further, the
condition imposed on buyer to deposit seventy five per cent of the amount due would critically affect the buyer without
providing any relief to supplier.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that such a condition may be removed from
this Clause. The Committee also noted that the Bill does not specify the Forum where such an appeal against the award
could be filed.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that such appeal against the award of Industrial Facilitation
Council may be made in the High Court  of that State and the clause may be amended accordingly.
5.21.2  Subject to such changes, the Clause adopted.
Clause 22
5.22     The Clause seeks to make it mandatory upon each State Government to establish one or more Industry
Facilitation Councils for the purposes of this Bill.
5.22.1  The Clause was adopted without any change.

5.23     The Clause seeks to lay down in detail the structure of the Industry Facilitation Council consisting of now less

the Industry Facilitation Council, the manner of filling vacancies of its members and the procedure to be followed in the
discharge of their functions.
5.23.1  The Committee suggests while constituting the IFCs the Tiny Sector should represented along with Small and
Medium Enterprises. Subject to change the Clause was adopted.

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND GENERAL OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A
GLANCE
 
8.1       The Committee during the course its interactions with various stake-holders including the representatives of
State Governments and the industry associations observed that there was a general approval of the Bill. However,
certain States and industry associations sought greater elaboration of the provisions of Bill particularly on the enabling
Clauses for promotion, development and enhancement of competitiveness of the tiny, small and medium enterprises. 
The Committee expressed its support and approval to the Bill, as the tiny, small and medium enterprise sector, which  is
an engine for social change and economic growth  needed a separate legislation according to its specific requirements.
8.2       The Committee appreciates that this Bill is an important initiative to relieve the tiny and SME sector of multiple
inspection regime. The Committee recommends that the government should take cognizance of the views expressed by
the State governments and industry association seeking a progressive trend towards self-certification and self-regulation.
The Committee also views that the inspections should be gradually replaced with a check-list of do and don’t to be
monitored by a single inspector. 
8.3       The Committee recommends that the Ministry of SSI should hold wide consultations with the industry
associations and State Governments while framing the rules, so as to incorporate the views of the State Governments
who shall be executing the provisions of the Bill. The Committee also recommends that Ministry should take a view of
the suggestion that enterprises with an investment upto Rupees one crore in plant and machinery, should be given some
preferential treatment while framing the rules.
8.4       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should widely published the provisions of the Act and the
corresponding processes / procedures for the public information.  Having formulated the enabling rules, the Ministry
should continue to monitor their execution by agencies at local level and should ensure that the agencies evolve
processes / procedures that are simple and in-consonance with the objectives of the Act.  The Committee underscores
the need for streamlining the rules and procedures while administering the provisions of the Act.  There must not be any
disjoint or contravention in the rules of procedures and processes at various levels and among various agencies.
8.5       The Committee also recommends that in order to encourage tiny, small  and medium enterprises to adhere to
pollution control norms, as per the Order dated the 10
th December 1997 of the Department of Industrial Policy and
Promotion, the cost of pollution control and R&D devices should not be included while calculating the investments in
plant and machinery. Similar exemption should be made with respect to industrial safety devices to promote such units
to adopt industrial safety norms.
8.6       Considering the significantly high incidences of sickness in tiny, small and medium enterprises, the Committee
was of the view that the Bill should also deal with the exit norms for the tiny and SME units. The Committee
recommends that Government should look into the matter and find out simpler exit mechanism at least for tiny and
small enterprises, after they have settled their dues and liabilities under the supervision of Industrial Facilitation
Council.

While considering the Bill, the Committee observed that the Bill does not refer to the Tiny sector, which constitutes a
large segment of the small-scale sector. The Committee, therefore, recommended that the tiny sector should be duly
incorporated in the Bill.  Accordingly, the Committee felt that appropriate Clauses may be incorporated in the Bill to
define the Tiny Sector  and also the consequential changes may be made in the  relevant Clauses of the Bill.
The Committee then took up Clause by Clause the SMED Bill 2005 and made its recommendations and observations.
Clause 2
The Committee was of the view that the definition of “Appointed day” in Clause 2(b) and “the day of acceptance” and
deemed acceptance” in explanation thereto did not provide the desired relief to the small supplier from the vice of
delayed payments.  The period of ‘30 days’ as provided in the Bill needed to be reduced.  The Committee, therefore,
recommended that it should be reduced to 15 days.
The Committee considered the phrase “ in relation thereto” in Clause 2 (e) as superfluous and accordingly
recommended its deletion. 
The Committee recommended that the term `industrial’ in Clause 2 (g) and 2 (l) may be replaced with “ enterprises” so
as to include both manufacturing and service enterprises both in small and medium sector.
In Clause 2 (m) the Committee recommended for inclusion of ‘Tiny enterprises’ so as to avail the benefits of the
provisions the Bill as referred to in Clause 8(1).
In Clause 2 (m) the Committee recommended for the inclusion of  `any commission, company, cooperative society,
society or trust registered as such under the relevant Act and engaged in selling of goods or services produced or
rendered  by such enterprises’.
The Committee recommended that the Tiny Sector may be suitably defined in this Clause.
Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 3
The Committee was of the considered view that the National Small and Medium Enterprises Board (NSMEB) should
have widest possible representation from all the States.  While constituting the Board the Government should ensure
that all the States are represented and more than one representation from a State may be avoided.  The Committee
accordingly recommended as under:
(i)         Number of Ministers of State Governments as provided in the Clause 3(3) (c) may be increased from five to six
and out of them one representation be provided to one of the North Eastern States.  Principle of rotation may be
followed while nominating the State Governments in the Board.
(ii)        In order to ensure greater representation of the industry associations in the Board, the Committee recommended
that membership under Clause 3(3) (k) be increased from ten to twenty representing associations of tiny, small and
medium enterprises.
(iii)       In order to give Board the benefit of expertise on technological issues that were vital for the development of
Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), the Committee further recommended to increase membership under Clause 3
(3) (i) from two to three so as to include eminent experts from the field of science and technology along with those from
the fields of economics and industry.  However, the Committee underlined that such experts should be truly independent
of government.
(iv)       In order to give Board the benefit of parliamentary input, the Committee recommended that the Chairman of the
Department related Parliamentary Committee dealing with Small and Medium Enterprises may also be nominated to the
Board,  in the ex-officio capacity.
The Committee welcomed the provision in the Clause 3(8) empowering the chairperson of the Board to invite at his
discretion the Ministers / Administrators of State/U.T. Governments and representatives of Associations of tiny, small
and medium enterprises in the meeting of the Boards.  The Committee, however, was not in favour of restricting the

176th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/176threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:46]
number of such meetings to two.  The Committee, therefore, recommended that the limit of ‘not more than two 
meetings’ for inviting non-members to the Board should be replaced with  ‘at least two’ meetings with a view to
facilitate consultation with wider spectrum of stake holders in the Board.
Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 4
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 5
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 6
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 7
The Committee noted that tiny enterprises have not been classified along with small and medium enterprises.  The
Committee strongly felt that tiny enterprises may also be classified under this Clause.  The Committee, accordingly,
suggested that (i) the enterprises engaged in the manufacture or production of goods where the investment in plant and
machinery does not exceed twenty five lakh rupees and;  (ii) the enterprises engaged in providing or rendering of
services where the investment in plant and machinery does not exceed the 10 lakh rupees be classified as tiny enterprise
under this Clause.
The Committee also felt that the tiny, small and medium enterprises should be adequately represented as individual
sectors in the proposed Advisory Committee.  The Committee, accordingly, recommended that the strength of Advisory
Committee be increased from five to nine so as to include three representatives of the State Governments instead of two
as provided in the Bill and one representative each from association of tiny, small and medium enterprises.
The Committee was also of the view that the scope of functions of Advisory Committee may be enlarged.  It should also
examine the matters referred to it by the National Small and medium Enterprises Board in connection with discharge of
the latter’s functions under the Act and submit its report to the latter.  The Central Government may seek the advice of
the Advisory Committee on the matters falling under the purview of the relevant Clauses of the Act.
The Committee was of the opinion that as the tiny, small and medium enterprises were being defined in accordance with
standard parameters of investments in plant and machinery only; inclusion of other parameters would be superfluous. 
Hence, the Committee recommended deletion of ‘ land and building’ in the Clause.   
Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 8
The Committee felt that in order to have clearer scenario in the tiny, small and medium Enterprises sector in the
country, it was necessary that such units must be registered. It would enable the Government to discern the trends in the
sector and take appropriate policy initiatives. The Committee, therefore, recommended to make filing of Memorandum
by the tiny, small and medium enterprises mandatory. It would enable the units to avail the benefits of Government’s
schemes.
The Committee however, emphasized that the filing of Memorandum should be simple and after a given period if no
objection was raised by the relevant authority, the unit should be deemed as registered. As regards the industry referred
to in proviso to clause 8 (i) such Memorandum may be filed with in one hundred and eighty days instead of ninety days
as provided in the Bill from the commencement of this Act.
Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 9
The Committee recommended that this Clause should also specifically include the ` tiny sector’ under the coverage of
promotional measures.
Further, the Committee was of the view that there was a need to encourage the women entrepreneurs in tiny, small and
medium enterprises. Therefore, the Clause 9(1) should have specific mention of women enterprises to underscore the
need for special incentives for women entrepreneurs.
The Committee acknowledged that competitiveness of Small and Medium Enterprises sector was severely constrained
by the outdated, inefficient technologies. Upgraded technologies were an imperative for these enterprises to withstand
the competition. Therefore, the Committee recommended that technology up-gradation must be reflected in Clause 9 (1)
for the promotional measures.
The Committee was also of the view that the growth of tiny and small sector has been stunted by the insufficient
infrastructural support and availability of critical inputs at reasonable prices. The Committee therefore felt that there
should have been specific mention of such measures to overcome these constraints in the Bill.  Accordingly, the
Committee recommended that Clause 9 should provide for the railways to earmark a definite percentage of its freight

176th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/176threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:46]
capacity for the transportation of raw material meant for tiny, small and medium enterprises as well as for the
transportation of the products of such units in wagon loads and small parcels.  Similar mention may be made in the
Clause 9 seeking the steel manufacturers and coal producers to reserve definite percentage of their production for the
tiny and small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) sector.
Subject to above changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 10
The Committee was of the view that credit facilities under RBI guidelines have existed for several years without much
of avail. The Committee also took cognizance of the views expressed by the State Governments and industry
associations on the inadequacy of bank credit at concessional rates to the tiny, small and medium enterprises despite
repeated RBI guidelines in this regard.  Implementation of RBI guidelines by banks has been major concern of the
Committee. While appreciating that the Bill recognized the need to clear such bottlenecks, the Committee recommended
to give greater force of law to the provisions of this Clause. The Committee accordingly suggested that term ‘ credit
facilities’ may be replaced with the phrase ‘ The policies and practices in respect of credit to the tiny’  
Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 11
The Committee recommended that Tiny enterprises may be included along with the small and medium enterprises
Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 12
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 13
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 14
The Committee was of the view that in order to facilitate that the Funds were utilized by the tiny, small and medium
enterprises all over the country, it was necessary that States too should establish similar funds with matching
contribution by Center and State governments. The Committee suggested that such provision should be made while
formulating Rules for this Clause under this Act.
Furthermore, the States should use these funds to finance R&D for the SME and Tiny enterprises.
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 15
The Committee recommends for inclusion of Tiny sector at appropriate places in the Clause.
Subject to the change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 16
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 17
The Committee felt that there was a need to expedite the payment due to tiny and small enterprises to enable them to
timely settle their liabilities with Banks without affecting their credit ratings. The Committee, therefore, recommended
that the small and tiny suppliers should get their payment within Forty –Five days instead of Seventy-five days from the
day of acceptance or deemed acceptance as mentioned in proviso to this Clause.
Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 18
The Committee was of the view that the rate of interest payable by the buyer on delayed payment should be high enough
to prevent delays in payment to tiny and small suppliers. The Committee, therefore, recommended that such interest rate
should be three times the bank rate instead of nine percent plus bank rate as prescribed in this Clause.
Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 19
The Committee was of the view that the recourse to recovery of amount by way of suit took longer time and involved
other procedural complexities.  Perhaps, this was the reason that Industrial Facilitation Council (IFCs) had to be
constituted to settle the dispute amongst the parties.  However, the Industrial Facilitation Council (IFC) did not have
power to execute its award.  The Committee, therefore, was the view that while recovery through civil suit remains an
option, the Industrial Facilitation Council (IFC) should be empowered with the powers to execute the awards, to provide
relief to the supplier.
The Committee, therefore, recommended that Industry Facilitation Councils should conferred with the similar powers as
vested with the Consumer Forum, to execute their awards.
 Subject to such change, the Clause was adopted.

Clause 20
The Bill provided for setting up of one or more Industry Facilitation Council by State Governments under Clause 22
specifying its jurisdiction. The Committee then considered the situation of inter-state disputes and recommended that
the Industrial Facilitation Council of the State where the supplier was located, should have the jurisdiction over such
inter-state cases. Such provision should be reflected specifically in the Clause.
The Committee was also of the view that the references made to Industrial Facilitation Council (IFCs) should be
decided within ninety days.
Subject to such changes, the Clause was adopted.
Clause 21
The Committee felt that filing appeal against any award made by an arbitrator like Industrial Facilitation Council   was a
right of the buyer that can not be infringed by such provisions as given in the Clause.  Further, the condition imposed on
buyer to deposit seventy five per cent of the amount due would critically affect the buyer without providing any relief to
supplier.  The Committee, therefore, recommended that such a condition might be removed from this Clause. The
Committee also noted that the Bill did not specify the Forum where such an appeal against the award could be filed. 
The Committee, accordingly, recommended that such appeal against the award of Industrial Facilitation Council could
be made in the High Court of that State and the clause may be amended accordingly.
Subject to such changes, the Clause adopted.
Clause 22
The Clause was adopted without any change.
Clause 23
The Committee suggested while constituting the IFCs the Tiny Sector should represented along with Small and Medium
Enterprises.
Subject to change the Clause was adopted.

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
Background
1.1       One of the declarations in the National Common Minimum Programme of the Government is that the Khadi and
Village Industries Commission (KVIC) will be revamped.
1.2.      Against the background of the steep decline in employment in the khadi sector and nearly stagnant sales of khadi
products over the past few years, it  became necessary to revamp the KVIC through organizational restructuring and
measures to introduce modern management practices, in order to make khadi and village industry products competitive in
the globalised economy while continuing to generate non-farm employment opportunities in the rural areas.
1.3       With these objectives, the Government dissolved the Commission in October 2004 and constituted a ten-member
Expert Committee in December 2004 to recommend suitable measures for its revamping, after reviewing the structure,
functioning and performance of the KVIC in the existing Act.  The Expert Committee submitted its report in April 2005.
1.4       After considering the recommendations of the Expert Committee, the Government   introduced the Khadi and
Village Industries Commission (Amendment) Bill, 2005 in Lok Sabha on 22.8.2005 to suitably amend the existing Khadi
and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956, so that the statutory provisions governing the organizational structure and
functions of the KVIC could be   made more professional and in keeping with the requirement of the present times.
1.5       Towards the objective  of making the membership of the KVIC more professional and broad-based, the Bill
proposes to include two more part-time members in the  Commission. One member would be an expert in the field of
marketing because improving the marketing of Khadi and Village Industry (KVI) products has been identified as one of
the most important requirements for speeding up the growth of the KVI sector.  Similarly, availability of credit is an
important requirement for improving the performance of the sector. Therefore, it has also been proposed in the Bill to
include the Chairman of the State Bank of India (or his nominee not below the rank of Deputy Managing Director of that
Bank) as a part-time member of the Commission. This is because the State Bank of India is not only the largest public
sector bank but also the highest lender to the working institutions and producing units in the khadi and village industry
sector.
1.6       In order to facilitate better coordination with the State Khadi and Village Industries Boards established by State
Governments, obtain regular feed-back on the problems being faced by the KVI sector in the six zones of the country and
suggest to the Commission measures to resolve difficulties after reviewing the implementation of the programmes at the
field level, provision for constitution of one Zonal Committee in each of the six geographical zones of the country has also
been provided in the Bill. The membership of the Zonal Committee includes the Chairmen of State KVI Boards in the
Zone.
1.7       In the existing KVIC Act, there is no provision for re-constitution of the Commission after its dissolution.
Therefore, to enable reconstitution of the Commission after its dissolution, suitable provision has also been proposed in the

1.8       (i)         In this Bill, it has also been proposed that the tenure of Chairman and Members of the Commission shall be
upto a continuous period of five years and that they shall hold office upto that period at the pleasure of the Government.
(ii)        Similarly, provision for regular meetings (at least twice a year) of the existing Khadi and Village Industries Board
(a central level consultative institution) has been made in the Bill.
(iii)       Provisions for clearer demarcation of the roles of the Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and Financial Adviser of
the Commission have also been proposed in the Bill.
1.9     The suggested changes will not adversely alter the basic objectives, powers and functions of the KVIC in the
existing KVIC Act.  In fact, it is expected and believed that with these proposed changes, the KVIC will become more
professional and relevant in the times to come and be better equipped in the discharge of its key role in facilitating
generation of sustainable and wide-spread non-farm employment in the rural areas of the country. 
1.10     The Bill aims at facilitating the promotion and development and enhancing the competitiveness of small and
medium enterprises and seeks to:-
(a)
                include two more part-time Members in the Khadi and Village Industries Commission;
 
(b)               confer voting rights upon the ex officio Members of the Commission;
 
(c)
                provide requirement of ten years of experience in appropriate fields for appointment as a member of the
Commission and also widen the field of expertise for appointment as a Member of the Commission;
 
(d)               make specific provisions for clear demarcation of functions and powers among the Commission, the Chief
Executive Officer and the Financial Adviser of the Commission;
 
(e)                provide for constitution of Zonal Committees, its functions and meetings;
 
(f)                 make specific provisions for undertaking certain functions by the Commission through specified agencies;
 
(g)                clarify that the Chairman and Members of the Commission shall hold office at the pleasure of the Central
Government which shall not exceed continuous period of five years as such in the Commission;
 
(h)                confer power upon the Central Government to re-establish the Commission after its dissolution; and
 
(i)                  make other provisions which are clarificatory or consequential in nature.

2.13          The proposed amendment in the Section 4 (2) of the Principal Act provides for either whole time or part-time
Members.  The Committee received the opinion that such differentiation between the Members should be done away with
and all the Members should be treated   as full-time Members.  The differentiation between the Members is at the root of
making other Members, excepting the Chairman ineffective and turns them into mere advisors, participating in the
activities of the KVIC on the days of meetings alone. 
 
2.14
          Taking cue from this provision, after the Amendment of 1987, Rules of KVIC (no.4) made all other Members,
excepting the Chairman as part time Members and the Chairman stopped sharing his responsibilities with the other
Members and thus began a downward trend in the KVIC in the field of performance, in spite of mounting administrative
costs.  The golden period of the KVIC from the point of view of growth, was between 1957-87, when all the Members
were entrusted with specific responsibilities of the KVIC, under the overall supervision and guidance of the Chairman.  
Hence all the Members should be made capable to share the responsibility of the Chairman of the KVIC.

3.0                   After   examining the provisions of the Khadi And Village Industries Commission (Amendment) Bill, 2005
and the consideration of suggestions thereto by the individual experts and organizations/institutions  and their implications
on the over- all working of the  Principal Act, the Committee took up the Clause-by-Clause consideration of the provisions
of the  Khadi and Village Industries Commission (Amendment) Bill, 2005, which are enumerated in the foregoing paras.   
 
CLAUSE – 2
 
3.1                   Clause-2 proposes Amendment in Section-2 of the Principal Act which deals with the definition of the
Village Industries.  Under the proposed amendment in Sub-Clause-(i) of Clause-(h) the Village Industry would be  defined
as  any Industries located in a rural area which produces any goods or renders any service with or without the use of poser
and in which the fixed capital investment per head of an artisan or a worker does not exceed one lakh rupees.  
 
3.1.1    The Committee is in agreement with the proposed Amendment in Sub-Clause-(i) of Clause-(h) of  in the  Section-2
of the Principal Act for enhancing the limit of the Village Industry for   fixed capital investment per head of an artisan or a
worker in general.   The Committee wonders as how the Village Industries continued to be defined with the fixed capital
of fifteen thousand which is a too meager amount for establishing even the Village Industries.  This Amendment must
have come much earlier.   
           
3.1.2    The Committee, however, feels that there  should be differential  criteria for defining the Village Industries for the
plain area and the hilly areas so far as the limit of the fixed capital investment per head of an artisan or a worker is
concerned.   That is so because the cost of establishment of Industry in the hilly areas is higher in comparison   to the plain
areas.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the proposed KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 must include provision for
the limit of the fixed capital investment per head of an artisan or a worker to the tune of rupees one lakh fifty thousand for
hilly areas. 
 
3.1.3.   The Committee takes note of the suggestion made by several stakeholders that the definition of “rural areas” as
given in Section 2 (ff) of the Principal Act needs to be revised in view of growing population.  The Committee is also of
the view that the definition of “rural areas” may be revised.  The Committee accordingly suggests that “rural areas”may
now be defined as  “the area comprised in any village, and includes the area comprised in any town, the population of
which does not exceed twenty thousand or such other figure as the Central Government may specify from time to time.” 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Section 2 (ff) of the Principal Act may accordingly be amended.
 
3.1.4    Subject to such changes , the Clause was adopted. 
 
CLAUSE – 3

Act. The Section 4 of the Principal Act stipulates KVIC as body corporate having perpetual succession with power to
acquire hold and dispose of property and to contract with KVIC assuming the juristic personality.   The proposed
amendment through insertion of new Clause (1A) after (a) after Sub-Section (1) in Section 4 of the Principal Act stipulates
that the exercise of all powers and discharge of all functions under this Act, including general superintendence, direction
and management of day-to-day affairs of the Commission, shall vest in the Commission.

corporate body with the team of experts in various segments of the Khadi and Village Industries.  The purpose of the
proposed amendment is to acquire professionalism in approach with functional autonomy.  The Committee is of the view
that the proposed amendment investing in the Commission the exercise of all the powers and discharge all the functions
including general superintendence, direction and the management of day-to-day affairs of the Commission may cause
apprehension of delay in the decision-making process.  Necessary precautions are required to be taken by the Government

CHAPTER-IV
 
GENERAL RECOMMENDATION/ OBSERVATION/CONCLUSION OF THE COMMITTEE ON THE AIM,
OBJECTIVES AND PROVISIONS OF THE BILL
 
            4.1       The Committee is of the view that the process of liberalization and globalization in the Indian economy
started since 1991 when the structural-adjustment gave fillip to the concept of corporatistion when the Companies in the
private sector and PSUs in the Government sector address the problem of management through having a body of
professional management.  The Committee wonders as to why the Government took almost 15 Years to adopt the concept

177th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/177threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:47]
in regard to functioning of the Khadi and Village Industries Commission.  The delay caused in adopting the KVIC to the
fast- changing economic and corporate environment crippled the growth and development of Khadi and Village Industries
in the Country and KVIC remained a mute spectator.
 
4.2              The Committee has been given to understand that the KVIC (Amendment)  Bill, 2005 is a step towards
corporatistion of the Commission.  But the real question arises to what extent ?  Is not the proposed amendment is a half –
way effort towards professionalisation of the Commission.  How  much time the Government would take for converting
the Commission into corporation.  The Government may take the plea that the Commission is dependent upon budgetary
support to provide subsidy to the Khadi Industries.  But how long the Government would be in position to provide subsidy
to the Khadi is a big question, which requires the immediate and in-depth attention of the Government. 
 
4.3
              The Committee, while giving due respect to the Khadi as national symbol during India’s struggle for Independence
and the importance being attached to Khadi by Father of the Nation, is of the view that sooner the Khadi Industries
become economically self-reliant, the better would be for its future business in the competitive environment and also for
the Government which is withdrawing itself from the business course.
 
4.4
              The Committee understands that the main objectives of the proposed KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 is to set into
place the professional team in the KVIC.  The Committee is, however, of the view that aiming at achieving the
professional standard in the working system through appointment of experts at top level is merely “ a window dressing”.
The Committee during the course of interactions with the various stake-holders including the representatives of State
Government received significant suggestions that total overhauling of Khadi and Village Industries Commission is
required to inject a new lease of life into the organizational structure to unleash   operational efficiency and functional
efficacy in the over all working system of the Khadi and Village Industries Sector.   The Committee is surprised to observe
that no provision has been made in the KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 for achieving professionalism in the middle and
lower level of management in the KVIC.  The Committee is of the considered view that in order to attain organizational
efficiency and professional proficiency KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 must have the provision for ushering
professionalism in all ranks and files of the overall umbrella under   KVIC. 
 
4.5
              The Committee is surprised to find that functions of Khadi and Village Industries Board has not been specified
either in the Principal Act or in its Rules except with the provision that it would assist the KVIC. The Committee is unable
to understand what sort of assistance is being imparted by KVI Board to the Commission in the absence of clear provisions
in the Principal Act.   Nor do the rules framed under the Act elaborate on this aspect.  The Committee desires that the
functions of the KVI Board should be clearly spelt out at least in the rules.
 
4.6
              In order to make the recovery proceedings effective, the officers of the KVIC at State level should be conferred
with the power of Revenue Recovery on the analogy of a similar empowerment of two Central Government Corporations
like ESI and EPF.  
 
4.7
              The Village Industries Programme also need identification of marketable products to undertake manufacturing of
the same, utilizing local raw material and workmen in its area-wise quality control common facilitation unit set up and run
under supervision and monitoring of technical and trained persons for supply of the indented items in given / contracted
time.  The successful marketing of Khadi and Village Industries Products in both i.e. domestic and foreign markets can
only be the real success key for revamping of Khadi and Village Industries Programme in the interest of the poor rural
beneficiaries. 
 
4.8
              One of the important factors envisaged for revamping of Khadi and Village Industries Programmes are to create
awareness, readiness and acceptability of the same by the targeted beneficiaries.  There is a pressing need for special
measures in this respect.  One such suitable method in the Committee’s opinion is to set up multi-disciplinary training
center at every State/district level to educate and train the local youth.
 
4.9
              The Committee received the suggestion that in order to usher National Khadi Revolution, the Government should
make it compulsory for the Government officials in various departments to wear khadi.  However, the Committee feels
that the State should not impose limitations/restrictions ‘on fashion’ and people of free India should be allowed the
‘freedom of choice’ so far as the fashion is concerned.  The Committee is of the view that if the khadi industries are to
grow, it has to grow on its own because of the ongoing liberlisation process and the prevalence of open and competitive
market.  However, the Khadi Institutions under the direction of the KVIC should make khadi more attractive to the

177th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/177threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:47]
consumer.  The Committee understands that it is through consensus, persuasion and appeals and not through coercion,
restriction and regulation, the Khadi revolution has to be ushered in the country. 
 
4.10
          The Committee has been given to understand that the proposed (Amendment) Bill, 2005 would not alter the
Working Equilibrium of KVIC  because the suggested  modifications will not adversely change the basic objectives,
powers and function of the KVIC as provided in existing Principal Act.  However, the Committee feels that the provisions
of the KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 based on the accepted recommendations of the Expert Committee should not get the
same fate as the recommendations made in the High Powered Committee and the Aurther Anderson Commission.

Report
 
1.      The Committee took up the issue pertaining to unlocking of surplus assets of the CPSEs to generate resources for their revival
and the status of ancillary units of such CPSEs. In the process of its examination the Committee took up the issue of HMT Ltd.  The
Committee interacted with the management of the HMT Ltd., representatives of Department of Heavy Industries, State Government
of Karnataka and those of the ancillary associations during its visit to Bangalore on 14
th November 2005 at Bengalore and on 21 st
February 2006 at Delhi once again heard the Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries and management of HMT Ltd.on the issue.
 
2.
      While considering the issue of disposal of surplus assets, the Committee took a look at  the mandate of the Board for
Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises advising the Government about the sources of funds in respect of unviable   CPSEs.
Such source of funds could also include the sale of surplus assets including land of the enterprise for the payment of all legitimate
dues and compensation to workers and other costs in case of their closure.
 
Revival of HMT Ltd.
 
3.
      The Committee noted that the HMT is the premier engineering conglomerate but over last few years its financial conditions
has been on decline. Though last year the Company’s performance in respect of production and sales performances have shown
growth of 19 % and 12% respectively, however the achievements still fall short of the annual growth targets. In 2004-05, the
HMT as a  group incurred a loss of Rs. 23.87 crore and this year proposes to earn a marginal profit of Rs. 0.15 crores only after
selling its Non-functional assets and waiver of interest by the Government in respect of HMT Bearings Ltd.
 
4.
      The Committee was informed that the Company has undertaken to re-align its product profile to the customer needs and
redesign its marketing strategy. The Company has also undertaken to consolidate its finances by recasting its debts and retiring
high cost borrowings, mobilizing internal resources including the disposal of non-functional assets and also by negotiating a one-
time settlement with Financial Institutions and Bond Holders. Further  the Committee noted that HMT had consolidated its
manufacturing facilities at Bangalore and Pinjore and closed the unviable units and divisions to reduce the cost.
 
5.
      The Committee was apprised that the Company and its subsidiaries had entered into technology collaborations with TVL, UK

178th Report of Committee On Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/178threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:57:48]
for the manufacturing of Trantors and Gudel System, Switzerland for supply and integration of automated systems.
 
6.      To address the long-terms issues and improve prospects, the six companies of HMT have sought an assistance of Rs. 1743.69
crores from the Central Government.  Of these two revival plans in respect of HMT Bearing Ltd. and Praga Tools Ltd. have been
approved and are under implementation whereas   the one for HMT Machine Tools has been approved by the BRPSE and was
being considered by the Committee of Secretaries og the Union Government.  The revival plans for HMT Ltd. and HMT Watches
have been submitted for BRPSE’s consideration. The Committee was also informed that the Cabinet Committee on Economic
Affairs had recommended merger of Praga Tools Ltd. with HMT Machine Tools to consolidate the resources and minimize the
costs so as to make the unit leader in manufacturing machine tools in the country.
 
7.
      The Committee was informed that the Revival Plans entailed fresh infusion of equity for capital expenditure, conversion of
Government loans into equity and waiver of interest on GOI loans as also the Government Guarantees for raising loan for
working capital.
 
Unlocking Of Assets of Company
 
8.
      The Committee was also informed by the Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries that the HMT like other CPSEs was
allocated land in its initial years by the State Government free of cost or at rather nominal rates.
 
9.
      In the meeting on the issue on 21st February 2006, the Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries stated that the Government
considered unlocking of assets of the CPSEs as a vital source of financing their revival.
 
10.
  The Committee was informed that in cases of HMT Machine Tools and HMT Watches, a subsidiary of HMT Rs. 470 crore
and Rs. 264 crores respectively would be realized by the disposal of surplus immovable properties. While in case of HMT Ltd.
Rs. 726 crores could be realized. The amount would be used towards servicing and repayment of GOI Guarnteed Bonds and
settlement of Bank borrowings of HMT Ltd. to the extent of Rs. 719.40 crores. The HMT Watches Ltd. will utilize these funds  
for liquidating existing high cost debts and settlement of Bank borrowings and also for the separation of 1000 employees. The
HMT Machine Tools will repay the Zero Coupon Preferential share capital of Rs. 443 crores to the Government. The Committee
was informed that the process of disposing of the surplus assets has been initiated to maximize the returns.
 
11.
  The Committee  is of the opinion that the CPSEs as commercial enterprises must be encouraged to generate their finances
through their internal sources. The Committee accordingly appreciates the initiatives being taken by the Company.
 
Ancillarisation
 
12.  The Committee has also undertaken the study to assess the impact of sickness among CPSEs on the industrialization of
adjoining region and more so over the ancillaries of respective CPSEs.
 
13.
  The Committee took cognizance of the Guidelines of the May 1978, issued by the then Bureau of Public Enterprises asking
all the CPSEs to boost ancillarisation. All the CPSEs were required to establish Plant Level Committees under their Chief
Executives with members from State Industries Department, SISI and representatives of ancillary associations. The focus of such
a guidelines was that the CPSEs and Ancillaries should share a relationship that was akin to Mother/Parent-Child.
 
14.
  The Plant Level Committees were the major organ of interface between the CPSE and its ancillaries. Non-core activities of a
CPSE were opened up for identified Ancillaries. Arrangements were such that half the product of an ancillary were off taken by
the parent CPSE. The pricing too ensured sufficient margin for the ancillaries.
 
15.
  However the system of Plant Level Committee was deleted from guidelines with the liberalisation of the economy where
private players and MNCs had greater flexibility to procure supplies either through imports or from the open market at a
competitive price. As a consequence the ancillaries restricted the choice of a CPSE to secure competitive prices for its supplies.
 
16.
  The Committee was also apprised of the steps taken by the Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO), which
conducts nation-wide Vendor Development Programmes and Sub-Contracting Exchanges, which have proved to be useful for the
vendors supplying to CPSEs and other Government Departments like Defence or Railways.
 
17.
  The Committee, however noted that the infirm financial conditions of the CPSEs adversely affected their ancillaries. Several
CPSEs particularly in the engineering sector lacked working capital as a result orders to ancillaries too dried down gradually.
There were also instances where CPSEs owed unsettled dues to its suppliers. The Committee observed that the sickness of a
CPSE had a cascading adverse affect over industrialization of its adjoining region.

allotted to entrepreneurs as ancillary units on license basis. 
 
20.  During its interaction on 14th November 2005 with the stakeholders of HMT, the representatives of the ancillary associations
sought the transfer of ownership of industrial sheds in HMT Industrial Estate, Jalhalli, Bangalore at the rates determined by an
independent evaluation done by the State Government agency, TECSOK. The Committee was also informed that the State
Government of Karnataka too had requested to transfer the industrial shed to the entrepreneurs at independent valuation rates by
TECSOK.
 
21.
  The Committee was informed by the representatives of the associations that other CPSEs like HAL, BHEL and ITI did
transfer the ownership to the ancillary entrepreneurs at concessional rates.
 
22.
  Having heard the representatives of the ancillary association in its meeting on 14 th November 2005 at Bangalore, the
Committee however advised the Department of Heavy Industries and the representatives of HMT to look into the request
earnestly and judiciously.
 
23.  In the last meeting of the Committee on the issue on 21 st February 2006, at New Delhi the Committee was informed by the
Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries and the CMD, HMT that the issue was considered at various for a and that the Board
of Directors of the Company directed the transfer of ownership to the ancillaries at the market rates. Further, the decisions of the
Board of Directors had been conveyed to entrepreneurs. It was also informed that HMT Ltd. had already sold five industrial
sheds to the highest bidders through a tender process including to an erstwhile licensee at the prevailing market rate during 2003-
05.
 
24.
  The Committee was informed by the HMT that though the ancillaries were asking the ownership of the sheds on the plea of
modernizing these Units, these units were essentially engaged in their own commercial activity and hardly supplement the needs
of HMT. The CMD of HMT further conveyed to the Committee that the Company had no intentions to dislodge these Units from
their present premises.
 
25.
  The Committee was informed by the CMD, HMT that in certain cases the CPSEs were granted perpetual lease of the land and
not the ownership. Furthermore in case of HMT, the land had been mortgaged to the Banks for the loans to garner capital for the
Company. The Committee was also apprised that the price that was being offered by the entrepreneurs for the sheds, was far less
than what the HMT expected to collect for its revival plan.
 
26.
  Upon the query regarding other CPSEs like ITI and HAL having offered land to their ancillaries at reasonable price, the
Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries, submitted that offers could differ case to case depending upon the resource
requirement of the concerned CPSE.
 
27.
  The Committee observes that since their inception the CPSEs had initiated a wave of industrialization in their adjoining
region. The CPSEs were direct mainstay for several small-scale ancillaries and suppliers and many more indirectly.   These Units
had thrived on the orders from CPSEs. The Committee is of the view that if the trend could continue this would have benefited
both parent company and the ancillary units.
 
28.
  But the ancillaries too have adversely been affected due to the sickness of the PSE and are at the verge of bankruptcy. They
have been forced by the circumstances to diversify their activities for which they require working capital which may be raised by
taking loans from the Banks and Financial Institutions who extend the loan if the shed or premises are owned by the ancillary
owners so that they can mortgage their sheds/premises. The Committee is of the opinion that since the ancillary owners are
diversifying under compulsion and in view of their long association with the PSE the onus of taking a lenient view in respect of
the survival of its ancillaries falls on the PSE itself. Since the revival of the PSE itself does not wholly depend on the sale of its
land and other assets, it can surely take a lenient view towards its ancillaries.
 
 
29.
  Considering the resource requirement of the HMT for its revival and the Committee’s consistent emphasis on need to
encourage the CPSEs to generate their own resources to assume full autonomy, also appreciating the long association of
ancillaries with their parent HMT Company and taking a view of their offer to purchase the sheds at the price ascertained by State
Government agency TECSOK as against the market price which is demanded by the HMT, the Committee recommends that the
CMD of the HMT, in exercise of the powers vested in him, on taking a lenient and favourable view on demand of the ancillary

1.8       The Purchase Preference Policy (PPP) was introduced in January, 1992 with the objective of enabling the CPSEs to
adjust in the new environment of competitiveness and efficiency created by the liberalization of economic and trade
policies. This policy has been reviewed and extended from time to time taking into account the threat of competition from
private sector and multinationals in securing orders as well as certain social and other obligations being observed by the
CPSEs which is not the case for the private sector/multinationals. However, on the considered advice of a Group of
Ministers (GOM) which examined in detail the various issues involved, it has been decided to extend the policy for a period
of three years with certain modifications and with a clear-cut sun-set clause that it will be terminated after 31.3.2008. In the
competitive and fast changing environment, the Government has recognized the need for enhancing the marketing and
technological efforts of CPSEs. Therefore, the decision making powers including those for formation of joint ventures,
diversification etc. are proposed to be enhanced.

3.1       The Committee feels that abolition of some of the divisions is unacceptable.  It observes that without constant
monitoring and consultations, the policy formulation will be reduced to a mere academic exercise.  The Committee

3.2            The role and functions of BPE were reviewed by a high powered Group of Secretaries towards the end of 1985.  As per the revised role
envisaged by the Group of Secretaries and accepted by the Government, BPE would function as a policy planning group for performing its basic role in
laying down guidelines in the fields of personnel policy and training, wage policy, performance indicators, work norms, etc, and as a nodal point for
collection and maintenance of information in respect of public enterprises.  The BPE was restructured in accordance with the recommendation of the
Group of Secretaries.  Certain functions of the BPE performed by the erstwhile Production Division, Construction Division and Information & Research
Division of BPE which were thought to have outlived their relevance or usefulness were shed and these Divisions were wound up. Since then, DPE had

PMA in 1989, CRR in 2001-02 and BRPSE in 2004. Guidelines are issued by DPE after consultation with Ministries/Departments dealing with CPSEs
As regards modification of BPE/DPE Guidelines, this is a continuous process and based on the recommendations of Vittal Committee and Nair
Committee, substantial reduction in DPE guidelines have taken place in a bid to facilitate CPSEs to work in a free environment. One of the major works

existing trends for which there is no arrangement is made in the mandate of Department of Public Enterprises. With the  absence of such a mandate and

Action Taken 
 
3.35     The action for revival/rehabilitation of sick/loss making Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) is taken by the
concerned administrative Ministries/Departments from time to time on case to case basis. Under the provisions of Sick
Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act,1985 (SICA), an industrial enterprise whose accumulated loss is equal to or
exceeded the networth during any Financial Year, is referred to the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction
(BIFR) for formulation of suitable revival/rehabilitation schemes. In case of other loss making CPSEs the concerned
administrative Ministries/Departments and CPSE take similar action. The performance of CPSEs is reviewed periodically
by the Ministries/Departments and action for improvement is initiated.  Further, a Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector
Enterprises (BRPSE) has been set up to examine the cases of revival/restructuring of sick and loss making CPSEs and make
recommendations accordingly. The concerned administrative Ministries/Departments have also been advised to take
appropriate timely measures.

3.38     The administrative Ministries/Departments are expected to prepare a comprehensive package for
revival/rehabilitation/closure of loss making PSEs after due consultations with all stakeholders. After constitution of
BRPSE, all the concerned administrative Ministries/Departments were requested to submit revival proposals in respect of

3.75       25.6, 25.7 & 25.8 Concept of independent directors is one of the basic pillars of Corporate Governance. In India,
Kumar Manglam Birla Committee (1999)   for the first time recommended that at least one-third of board should comprise
of independent directors and in case a company has an executive chairman at least half of board should comprise of 
independent directors.  Meanwhile Department of Company Affairs appointed Committee on Corporate Audit and
Governance (Naresh Chandra Committee 2002) which also recommended that “ not less than 50 per cent of the Board of
Directors of any listed   company, as well as unlisted public limited companies with a paid up share capital and free reserves
of Rs.10 crore and above, or turnover of Rs.50 crore and above, should consist of independent directors". Thereafter,
Department of Company Affairs issued a Concept Paper on Company Law 2004 which provided that "every public
company having paid up capital or turnover of such amounts may be prescribed shall have a minimum of seven directors out
of shich not less than three or such number  as near to fifty percent of the strength of the board, whichever is higher , shall
be independent director as defined in sub-section (45) of section 2 and possessing such attributes necessary for being
appointed as an independent director as may be as prescribed”.    Another committee (J.J. Irani Committee) established by
Department of Company Affairs recommended in May 2005 that “ a minimum of one third of the total number of directors
as independent directors should be adequate for a company having significant public interest, irrespective of whether the
Chairman is executive or non-executive.  In the first instance, this requirement should be extended to public listed
companies and companies accepting public deposits.”  Thus all committees have recommended to include independent
directors on the Board of Directors.  However, there are different views on the number of independent directors to be
included in Board.   While Securities and Exchange Board of India has mandated that 50 % of members of Board should be
independent if the Chairman is executive otherwise number of independent directors can be one third, Ministry of Company
Affairs has to firm up its views on this subject.

of CPSEs was again considered and it was decided  vide OM NO 18 (6)/91-GM dated 16 th March 1992 “the number of
Non-Official Part Time Directors on a Board should be atleast one-third of its actual strength”.  Government while
enhancing the autonomy and financial powers under the scheme of ‘Navratna’ and ‘Miniratna’ in 1997 ,  it was made
prerequisite to restructure the  Board of Directors by inducting at least one third of total number of directors as non-official
part time (independent) directors subject to minimum of four in case of Navratna and three in case of Miniratna, for exercise
of enhanced financial powers.   Pursuant to guidelines issued by SEBI,  it was advised by DPE vide its OM no 18(6)/2000-
GM dated 26
th November, 2001to reconstitute the Board of listed PSUs by inducting 50% of directors as independent in
case the Chairman is executive and in case of companies having non-executive chairman by inducting at least one third
number of directors as independent.

      apart from receiving director’s remuneration does not have any material pecuniary relationships or transactions with

3.78  Narayana Murthy Committee recommended that there shall be no nominee  directors.  Where an institution wishes
to appoint a director on the Board, such appointment should be made by the shareholders.  An institutional director, so
appointed shall have the same responsibilities and shall be subject to the same liabilities as any director.  Nominee of the
Government on public sector companies shall be similarly elected and shall be subject to the same responsibilities and
liabilities as other directors.   In a separate report on clause 49, it was stated that “An institutional director on the boards
of companies shall be considered as an independent director unless he does not satisfy the requirements of any of the
clauses (a) to (f)”.  Accordingly, as per revised clause 49 of listing agreement “nominee directors appointed by an
institution which has invested in or lent to  the company shall be deemed to be independent directors”.  Naresh Chandra
Committee recommended that Nominee Directors should neither be included in total number of directors nor should be
treated as independent directors.  J. J. Irani Committee took the view that such nominees represented specific interests
and could not, therefore, be correctly termed as independent.

                        The Committee also feels that in the CRR scheme, preference should be given to those junior level
functionaries to whom the VRS dues have still not been paid. Also the Committee would like to know about the
interim measures taken to provide sustenance to such VRS optees whose dues are still pending with the PSEs. (Para
11.6)
 
            The Committee recommends that DPE must take up the issue involved in the implementation of CRR Scheme with
respective PSEs and their Administrative Ministries to remove these constraints. The Committee would also like to know
the steps taken on the evaluation study conducted by V.V. Giri National Labour Institute, to overcome the above
constraints.
(Para 12.2)
 
                                The Committee would like to know the details of professional eligibility criterion for the non-official Members of the BRPSE and
the way they are selected.(Para 13.3)
 
                The Committee, however, expresses concern over delay in finalizing the revival of PSEs that has incurred heavy cost of such delay in terms of
depleting net worth and rising liabilities of PSEs. The Committee hopes that the delay in finalization of the revival of PSEs would be avoided.(Para 13.7)
 
            The Committee suggests that the Administrative Ministries/Departments should be given time limit to refer to the
complete proposal to BRPSE.(Para 13.8)
 
                                The Committee also notes that management development courses are the main benefit of DPE’s membership of ICPE, which has
been availed by only 76 executives in last three years with DPE paying an annual membership fee of US $ 75000. The Committee may be
apprised of the items included under this contribution. The Committee would also like the DPE to take a fresh look into the cost benefit ratio of
such membership and justify the same of next year’s Demands and inform the Committee accordingly. (Para 16.3)
 
                3.43          The Committee may also be apprised of the criteria and process for the selection of candidates for such courses.(Para 16.4)
            The Committee would like to know the nature of such support to PSEs in achieving the targets in MoU.  The
Committee observes that the number of PSEs earning favourable ratings is increasing while those getting  ‘Poor’ rating have
decreased.   Keeping this in view, the Committee has also observed that the number of PSEs entering the MoU has been
falling from 108 in 1999-2000 to 96 in 2003-04.  The Committee wonders, if the PSEs having poor ratings are being
excluded from the MOU system. If that is true, is it safe to construe that the Government’s support under MOU system is
practically not available to the loss making PSEs.  The Committee would like to know if there is a policy to exclude such
PSEs from signing the MOU.  If so, the Committee would like to know the rationale behind such policy.(Para 18.2)
 
                The Committee feels that the financial parameters in the MoU system still do not reflect the fact that the PSEs are still largely dependent on
bulk Government orders.  Most of the PSEs still do not have any significant presence in global export market despite being in the business for long. 
Most of the Excellent rated PSEs function in monopoly market environment.  The PSEs have not been able to secure the ‘Brand loyalty’ of customers,
wherever the sector has been opened up for private sector and this is reflected in the receding market share of such PSEs.  The Committee would like to

179th report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/179threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:58:48]
have DPE’s comment on its observations.(Para 20.4)
 
  Considering that the PSEs were envisaged as the pioneers in industrial technology, the Committee observes that
Technology and R&D have not been suitably factored in MoU ratings of the PSEs that are essentially Techno-commercial
entities. As such Technological upgradation and R&D should be an integral part of revival strategy of the PSEs.  It is
observed by the PSEs that most of the PSEs do not have an elaborate R&D set up.  The Committee wonders if PSEs have
owned any patent in recent years, which itself is a distinct commercial activity.  (Para 20.8)
 
The Committee recommends that technology upgradation and R&D must be given due weightage in MoU parameters in consultation with
expert bodies like DSIR.             (Para 20.9)
 
                Despite elaborate policy intentions to include persons of proven expertise in the Boards of PSEs, the Committee has observed that former
bureaucrats, serving representatives of autonomous organizations under government, representatives of subsidiary companies have been included in the
Boards as Independent Directors in addition to Functional and Official Part- time Directors. In several cases retired bureaucrats are reappointed as
Independent Directors. The Committee feels that such an arrangement does not fall in the spirit of the policy of appointing Independent Directors on the
Boards of Directors of the PSEs. The Committee also expresses reservation on the practice of renewing the tenures of existing Directors in some cases.
The Committee urges the department to ascertain that the implementation of the policy is in consonance with its true objectives and bring to the notice of
this Committee any dilution in the “Professionalisation” of Boards.(Para 21.5)
 
The Committee is of the opinion that there should be uniformity in the qualification, selection and mandate of Non-Functional Part-Time
Directors, as too many categories within the Board may affect its efficiency and autonomy. The Board must be defined in terms of its mandate and the
interest of the Company and not by the categories of its Directors. The Committee would like to have Government’s comments on the need for
uniformity in Part-Time Directors.(Para 24.3)
The Committee recommends that the government must impress upon the concerned Ministries to adhere to the time frame for the selection of
Directors and expedite the appointments of Directors.(Para 25.4)
 
            The Committee is constrained to observe that the information provided by the DPE was not only evasive but also
insufficient and incomplete.  The Committee observes that DPE  has not reacted  to the criteria of “Independent Directors”
as elaborated by the Naresh Chandra  Committee.  Similarly  the DPE  has not responded to the Narayan Murthy
Committee’s recommendation on “Nominee Directors”.(Para 25.6)
 
3.73     The Committee observes that these expert Committees were set up by the Government or the agencies under its
control. The Reports of these expert Committees are extremely relevant to the issue of Professionalisation of Boards as they
deal extensively the mandate, functional autonomy, obligations and the constitution of Boards of Diretors. Their findings
can be applied to enhance the autonomy and efficiency and draw greater degree of professional excellence to the Boards of
Directors. (Para 25.7)
 
3.74     The Committee recommends that the DPE should assess these reports more fruitfully instead of dismissing them for
administrative nuances and inform the Committee of its views and rationale thereof. (Para 25.8)
 
            Many PSEs particularly in Heavy Industry Sector have complained lack of orders from Government and PSEs as
major cause of their financial constraints. The Committee would like DPE to identify the Sectors that still rely heavily on
Government orders.”             (Para 27.5)
 
                                The Committee does not approve such an arrangement of allocating funds for the DPE under Iron & Steel Industry head.  This needs
to be corrected.  The Committee accordingly directs the DPE to take up the matter with appropriate Department to correct the same.(Para 5.2)
 
                                The Committee be apprised of the reasons on which is recommendation to extend the benefits of CRR scheme to family members
was refused by the Planning Commission. The Committee reiterates its recommendation as contained in its 150th Report in this respect, and
recommends a re-look into the issue as it will increase the family income of the VRS optees.(Para 11.7)
 
            The Committee feels that sufficient provisions should be made available to meet BRPSE’s requirements for
providing expert advise on techno-financial issues pertaining to revival of PSEs. The Committee, accordingly, recommends
the Government to provide sufficient funds for the smooth  functioning of the BRPSE.(Para 13.5)
 
                The Committee recommends that DPE must make efforts with concerned Departments and Institutions, to conduct similar EDPs in India, with
Indian Professional Institutions, for other ICPE members. Indian institutions must enter into huge global market of professional training and

179th report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/179threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:58:48]
consultancy.  Such programmes for other countries will enhance the academic and professional profile of our premier professional institutions. (Para
17.2)
 
                                The Committee notes with reservation that there was no specific programme for enhancing the skills of shop floor level techniques.
The Committee views it to be a stunted approach towards overall human development in PSEs. (Para 17.3)
 
                                The Committee, therefore, recommends that DPE must organize orientation and skill development programme for shop-floor level
technical functionaries as they are the end users of new material management and production techniques. The efficiency at shop-floor level
ultimately reflects in the corporate performance of the Company. The Committee recommends that CPSEs adhere to the principles of Total
Quality Management.(Para 17.4)
 
                                The Committee observed that distinct preference was given to serving officers from the Armed Forces in the Board level
appointments in the PSEs under the Ministry of Defence, on the plea that Armed forces were premier customers of these PSEs. The Committee
wonders, if such an arrangement reduces PSEs as a captive Company instead of an autonomous commercial entity. The Committee is of the
view that the products of these PSEs have a large civilian market too. The Committee feels that if the private sector is being involved in the
defence sector, why cannot the defence related PSEs harness potential in civilian and export market with their duel-use products and
technology.           (Para 21.8)
            The Committee feels that the minimum educational qualification should be raised to a Post Graduate
Degree/Diploma from a premier institution in a professional course, management, engineering, financial management or
HR  management. Also the size of corporate body should be specified for the CMD/MD being appointed as the Independent
Directors.(Para 26.2)
 
                The Committee feels that a Joint Secretary belongs to a generalized service, he may not have requisite and relevant expertise to become an
Independent Director in a PSE unless he has the experience of those many years in the field relevant to the functioning and corporate objectives of the
PSE.  The Committee recommends that this aspect should be specified in the eligibility criteria for Independent Directors.(Para 26.3)
4.24The Committee feels that the maximum age for Independent Directors too should be appropriately reduced to maintain
uniformity in the Board of Directors.(Para 26.4)
 
                The Committee seeks information on the action taken by the DPE and the Government on the outcome of these meetings.(Para 27.10)
 
                The Committee seeks DPE to apprise it on Revised Estimates and Supplementary Demands.(Para 27.11)
 
                The Committee directs the DPE to give its comments on the Committee’s queries, observations and recommendations contained in this Report.
(Para 27.12)

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having   been  authorized 
by the Committee, hereby present this  One hundred eightieth  Report on the  Action Taken  by the Government on the
Recommendations  contained in  the  169 th  Report of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry on Demands for Grants (2005-2006) in respect of Department of Heavy Industries.
 
2.         The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted  the Draft report at
its meeting held on the 22nd May, 2006.
 
NEW DELHI;
BAGRODIA 22nd May, 2006
 
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
Chairman
Department –related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry
 
REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Heavy Industry on the Recommendations
contained in the 169th Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry).
 
2.             Action Taken Notes have been received from the Department of Heavy Industry in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report.
These have been categorized as follows :-
 
Chapter -I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry.
 
Chapter -II- The recommendation/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue for now in view of the Government's replies.
 

180th report of Committee On Industry

Chapter -III- The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry
to review the reply or the replies of the Ministry are either not relevant to the question raised by the Committee. The Committee expresses its concern
over the non-implementations of recommendations contained in this Chapter and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect
of these recommendations. 
 
Chapter -IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been received. In respect of
recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim replies or matter has been forwarded to other agency/Department
whose reply is awaited or couched its language in vague terms like noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry
should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations categorised in this Chapter in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of
the recommendations of the Committee.
 
3.         A majority of replies have been put under Chapters III and IV, implying that the Department’s reply have fallen well
short of Committee’s estimates and the Committee would expect the Department to review its replies and furnish them
afresh. The Committee shall continue to pursue these issues and monitor the progress thereof.
 
4.         The Details of the ATR are being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
 
Observations of the Committee
 
1.1            The Committee recommends that both the R&D projects namely Coal Gasification Project and FCRI must be supported till they achieve
commercial viability.
(Para 28.3)
 
Action Taken
 
1.2       Both these projects are national R&D projects and are fully proposed to be supported through the grant from the
Government.
CHAPTER - II
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.1       The Committee apprehends that despite robust growth in capital goods sector, the PSEs find difficult to secure
orders and in several cases to execute the orders due to lack of working capital and other constraints.  The Committee,
accordingly, recommends that efforts should be made by the PSEs to utilize  current opportunities in the market.  As the
capital goods market is essentially technology-intensive, PSEs must undertake the technology upgradation to secure high-
end market.
(Para 6.4)
Action Taken 
 
2.2       While restructuring plans are being considered by BRPSE, all issues including technology upgradation etc. is being
addressed. Turnaround plans include business, organizational/financial restructuring so that the PSE are able to take up the
challenges arising out of liberalization of the economy. PSEs are being advised for considering necessary collaboration/tie-
up with world leaders and emphasis is being laid on continuous upgradation of related technologies including development
of new projects. Stress is also being laid on in-house R&D for improvement in performance and development of variants of
products etc.
 
Observations of the Committee
2.3            The Committee  recommends that the Government should decide the on linkage between BIFR and BRPSE at least, till such time a final
decision on BIFR is taken by the competent Court.(Para 9.3)
 
Action Taken
 
2.4       After the constitution of BRPSE in December, 2004, BIFR was informed that revival/restructuring is being
considered in case of sick/loss making PSEs. Accordingly, revival plans are being placed before BRPSE for seeking their
recommendations on the future of these enterprises.
After the revival plans are approved by the competent authority, BIFR shall be approached separately on a case-to-case
