basis.
Further Recommendation
2.5       Committee feels that DHI must avoid the multiplicity of approvals and delays caused due to protracted procedures.
  Observations of the Committee
2.6       The Committee  observes with concern that multiplicity of agencies even in deciding the revival may and has
resulted in different opinions, successive appeals and costly delays.  Even after deciding, the revival packages have failed in
several cases.  The Committee apprehends that in the process of analyzing the cases the BIFR has assessed the Techno-
Financial feasibilities of individual PSEs prepared by expert agencies.  Yet the appeals are filed in AAIFR and High
Courts/Supreme Court and now these may further will be referred to new BRPSE for appraisal before a final decision is
taken by the Cabinet.  The entire process is time consuming and costly.  The cost of delay has been immense in terms of
rising liabilities that have eaten up the net worth of the PSEs.  It may be an effort in duplication.(Para 9.4)
 
Action Taken
 
2.7       The process of revival is being expedited through the BRPSE. Out of 28 cases under the Department of Heavy
Industry,  in a short period of 8 months, 16 cases have already been considered by BRPSE. Recommendations have already
been given in case of 12 PSEs by BRPSE which are under process. In case of 3 PSEs Govt. have decided on revival of the
companies and such revival plans are already under implementation.  It is expected that remaining 12 PSEs shall also be
placed before BRPSE in the next 2-3 months time.
 
Further Recommendation
 
2.8       Committee would like to know if the BRPSEs recommendation on revival of individual PSEs are being
implemented in to as per the schedule recommended or in the piecemeal method. A piecemeal approach may affect the
efficiency of the investment. It  should be ensured that the survival of PSEs is sustainable after such a costly revival.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.9            The Committee recommends that the Department must take steps to expedite the decision and implementation for the PSEs’ sustained revival
once case is decided by the competent authority.(Para 9.5)
Action Taken
 
2.10     When a revival plan is approved by the Govt., necessary MOU is being signed between the Management and the
Government to ensure sustainable revival of the PSE. Reviews are proposed to be carried out on a regular basis to ensure
that the projected targets envisaged in the revival package are achieved.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.11          The Committee further recommends that the Government should inform the Committee of the revival packages approved by the Cabinet
before approaching the Parliament for Supplementary Demands.  The Department must also give a post-revival SWOT analysis of the PSEs and that
must reflect its Technological strengths and market viability.(Para 9.6)
Action Taken
2.12     So far Government have approved revival packages in case of the following 3 PSEs under the Department of Heavy
Industry :
 
(i)
                  Bridge & Roof Co Ltd.
(ii)                Hindustan Salts Ltd
(iii)               BBJ Construction Co.Ltd.
 
2.13     Revival plans in these companies are under implementation. Regular reviews shall be carried out on a regular basis
during the implementation period and upon full implementation of the package.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.14     The Committee recommends that the lump-sum expenditures should be sufficiently elaborated for Parliamentary
approval in future.(Para 12.10)
Action Taken

file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/180threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:59:49]
2.15     It is assured that DHI will follow the recommendations of the Committee and the lump sum expenditure will be
sufficiently elaborated.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.16          The Committee feels that the issue of payment of Guarantee Fee Subsidy needs to be re-examined in view of the fact that the PSEs which are
not able to even pay for Guarantee fee to the Government, how would they settle other liabilities.  The Committee would also like to know Department’s
comments, if it was necessary to give Guarantee Fee subsidy to same PSEs that utilized the facility even last year.  The government may also informed
about the purpose for which the resources were raised against such guarantee.(Para 20.4)
Action Taken
2.17     As  explained in reply to Para 19.3 that the guarantee fee subsidy is being provided to HEC, HMT and BSCL as
envisaged in their approved revival/restructuring plans for a fixed period. This guarantee fee subsidy will be provided to
these three PSEs for that fixed period as approved in their revival/restructuring plans. Govt. guarantee is being reviewed on
annual basis and extended on annual basis with the approval of Ministry of Finance. In the case of HEC, Govt. has given
guarantee to SBI for working capital facilities of Rs.253 crore to HEC. HMT had raised VRS Bonds for Rs.469 crore for the
separation of their excess manpower as per their turnaround plan for which Govt. has given Govt. guarantee and in the case
of BSCL, Govt. has given guarantee for Rs.55.50 crore for Cash credit limits for working capital from United Bank of India.
         
Observations of the Committee
 
2.18          The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the budgetary allocations do not sufficiently reflect the concern for technological
upgradation of PSEs and R&D which has direct bearing over the efficacy of the Companies keeping in view that PSEs were established as pioneers in
industrial technology.  The Committee feels that the Government should actively involve in the technological upgradation of PSEs and if necessary
extend the financial support.(Para 31.2)
Action Taken
2.19     When the revival plans are considered by the Department/BRPSE, overall packages developed included areas like
financial restructuring, modernization, manpower rationalization etc. apart from technology upgradation etc. Necessary
financial support as envisaged in the package is provided by the Government upon approval by the competent authority.
 
Further Recommendation
 
2.20     While the DHI appears to agree with Committee's view, Committee expects that DHI shall appreciate the criticality
of technology in heavy engineering market whose market is opening up for major global players.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.21          The Committee notes the diverse range of business in which subsidiaries of the BYNL are involved.  The Committee also notes despite
repeated recommendations by this Committee and other expert studies to merge the subsidiary companies into single entity; no initiative has been taken
in this respect.  The Committee would like to know the view of the Government in this respect.(Para 39.2)
Action Taken
2.22     The subsidiaries of BYNL Group of Companies are involved in diverse range of business activities ranging from
civil construction to manufacture of pumps/compressors or structural work. It may not be appropriate to merge these
subsidiaries into a single entity, as it may not result in better capacity utilization, nor  will it make more competitive/viable.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.23          The Committee recommends that Government must support the company’s resource and technology requirements to harness the potential of
non-conventional energy in the country.  The committee is of the view that the Government must help this sector in attaining the economies of scales. 
The non-conventional energy will be economically feasible for the community-based consumption in obscure villages and remote areas where the cost of
energy transmission is high.  The Non-conventional energy sources could be cost-effective supplementary source for energy needs of small habitats and
clusters. (Para 42.4)
Action Taken
 
2.24     The Department has been encouraging REIL to enhance their efforts in improving their presence in the area of non-
conventional energy sources including Solar Photo Voltaic etc. A proposal for establishment of a unit having manufacturing
facilities is under consideration.
Observations of the Committee

180th report of Committee On Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/180threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:59:49]
 
2.25          The Committee notes that DHI was unable to commit on firm and tangible long-term objectives in quantitative terms that could be a
benchmark against which the performance is assessed.  On most of the long-term issues Department’s reply has been elusive.  The Committee observes
that despite huge financial liabilities all the major decisions are still left to BRPSE.  Pending its recommendations being approved by the competent
authority, the Department is taking measures that are ad-hoc window-dressing of depleted worth of PSEs.  The Committee is of the opinion that scarce
resources cannot be lost endlessly amidst huge liabilities of PSEs.  A lasting solution has to be found urgently and accountability must be accordingly
fixed for which it is necessary to determine the benchmarks of performance.(Para 45.1)
Action Taken
 
2.26     The revival plans of the PSEs are prepared  in consultation with the Advisers and the PSEs. BRPSE makes
recommendations after thoroughly examining the proposals.  While the implementation is started  for revival of a PSE, a 
Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) is proposed to be entered / signed in each case between the Government and the
Management of the company to achieve pre-determined level of performance.  Regular reviews are also proposed to be
carried out to take care of any slippages or mid-course correction where  necessary.
 
Further Recommendation
 
2.27     The Committee accepts the reply of DHI but shall continue to monitor the progress and that the obligation of the
Government as a contracting party in MoU must be clearly defined. 
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.28          The Committee would like to suggest to the Government to consider the critical utility of any company before deciding on its sustainable and
comprehensive revival/restructuring instead of going only by their precarious financial condition.  The criticality will depend on long-term prospects of
the company in terms of technology spin-offs and self-reliance in mega-machinery in strategic areas.
Para 45.9)
Action Taken
 
2.29     All issues are taken into consideration while deciding on the viability/sustainability of the company including its
strategic importance. However, in the new regime of economic liberalization, the acid test of a company for survival is its
capability to compete in the globalised market and deliver as per the emerging requirements. None of the PSEs under the
Department of Heavy Industry are operating in the strategic areas where they would need to be run due to consideration of
self-reliance or criticality of the area in which they are operating.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.30          The Committee notes that the growth in exports is hindered due to non-availability of adequate supplier’s credit to buyers, higher rates of
interest and lower duration for which the credit is available.  The Committee recommends that the Government must take a favorable view of the
proposals made by the Department of Heavy Industry with regard to availability of adequate supplier’s credit to buyers, low rate of interest and longer
duration of credit to facilitate growth in export performance of the PSEs.(Para 5.5)
Action Taken
 
2.31     Based on the request received from PSEs on providing suppliers credit to buyers, the matter is taken up with the
concerned Ministries for appropriate financing of such overseas projects on a case-to-case basis.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.32          The Committee observes that while the aggregate growth in PSEs under DHI compares well with the capital goods growth, but this level of
growth is mainly contributed by one PSE namely Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL) which showed a growth of 15% during this period.  Most of the
PSEs have shown a negative growth mainly due to financial, marketing and technological constraints.(Para 6.3)
Action Taken
 
2.33     Major growth is seen in BHEL due to their order book position. PSEs operating in other sectors are suffering due to
poor order book, shortage of working capital, surplus manpower, obsolete machinery and technology etc. Consequently
many of these PSEs are making losses. As per the mandate under National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP),
restructuring/revival plans of such PSEs are being placed before BRPSE for improving their performance and achieve viable
turnaround.

180th report of Committee On Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/180threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:59:49]
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.34          The Committee notes that the expenditures are classified into two parallel categories Capital/Revenue expenditures and Plan/Non-Plan
expenditures.  These two parallel categories are curiously hybridized into four supposedly distinct categories of expenditure.  The Committee would like
to know the rational principles for such classified and sub-classifications, instead of description of expenditure under these categories.(Para 10.6)
Action Taken
2.35     As a general rule, the classification of transactions in Government Accounts, shall have closer reference to the
function, programme and activity of the Government and the object of the revenue or expenditure, rather than the
department in which the revenue or expenditure occurs. Rule 72 of General Financial Rules deals with the transactions in
Government Accounts and Rule 91 with the allocation between capital and revenue expenditure.
 
2.36          Plan Expenditure representing the expenditure on plan outlays approved for each scheme or organization by the Planning Commission and
indicating the extent to which such outlays are met out of budgetary provisions’ other expenditure which cannot be anticipated in advance, comes under
non-plan expenditure.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.37          The Committee desires to know that on what ground the Planning Commission’s approval was sought for certain Revenue and Capital
expenditures leaving remaining sizable Revenue and capital expenditures unapproved.  If any guideline is followed in this respect.  The Committee
would also like to be appraised on such a categorizastion in the Budget.  The Committee also desires to know if such segregation is scientific and does
not affect the efficiency of expenditure.  Further, the Committee would like to have a comment from the Department, if there is need to improve the
Budget scheme.
(Para 10.11)
Action Taken
 
2.38     While the proposals are submitted to Planning Commission by DHI, these are examined in Planning Commission
scheme-wise and necessary allocations are made keeping in view the priorities and resource constraints of the Govt.
Planning Commission specifies the total Govt. budgetary support for various plan schemes. However, subsequent
categorization of a particular scheme under revenue and capital is done as per GFR guidelines.
 
2.39          Significant Expenditure incurred with the  object of acquiring tangible assets of a permanent nature or enhancing the utility of existing assets,
shall broadly be defined as Capital Expenditure. Subsequent charges on maintenance, repair, upkeep and working expenses which are required to
maintain the assets in a running order as also all other expenses incurred for the day-to-day running of the organization, including establishment and
administrative expenses shall be classified as Revenue Expenditure. Capital and Revenue expenditure shall be shown separately in the Accounts (Rule
79 of GFRs).
Observations of the Committee
 
2.40          The Department has been closely associated with the promotion of Automobile R&D facility in the country.  However, a significant Grant in
Aid of Rs. 25 crores to R&D institution is still treated as a Non-Plan Revenue expenditure along with Secretariat expenditure and Interest subsidy.  The
Committee observes that the character of expenditure is too diverse to be kept under similar category.
(Para 14.2)
Action taken
 
Grants-in-Aid are kept under Revenue Expenditure.
 
2.41          Non-plan expenditure is a generic term, which is used to cover all expenditure of Government not included in the Plan. It includes both
developmental and non-developmental expenditure. Expenditure on maintaining the assets created in previous plans is also treated as Non-plan
expenditure. Similarly, expenditure on continuing services and activities at levels already reached in a Plan period is classified as Non-plan expenditure.
Therefore, the funds approved for promotion of Automobile R&D Facility are taken under Non-plan Revenue.
 
Observations of the Committee
 
2.42          The Committee observes with concern that every year during past few years the non-plan expenditure has been higher than plan expenditure.

Small Scale Industries on the move
1.1       The Committee understands that the Small Scale Industries is today on the move world wide, therefore, Small
Scale Industries in India should be given top priority by the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance in plan
allocation so that small scale units may get adequate space for maturing into medium enterprises to catch the global
trend.  The Ministry of SSI should provide the logistic support to the SSI sector to enable it to remain competitive in
market-led economy and generate additional employment opportunities.  The Ministry should assist the SSI sector in
accessing (or provide) proper and timely inputs like adequate credit from financial institutions/banks; funds for
technology up-gradation and modernization; adequate infrastructural facilities; modern testing facilities and quality
certification laboratories; modern management practices and skill up-gradation through suitable training facilities;
marketing assistance; and level playing field at par with the large industries sector.
(Para 1.4)
Action Taken/Comments

development and promotion of small scale sector in the form of infrastructure development, technology upgradation,
human resource development, better credit availability, market development etc.  The small scale sector has great
potential for growth in production, employment and exports.  In view of this, the observation of the Committee that the
small scale sector should receive top priority both by the Planning Commission and M/o Finance in allocation of funds
is very valid, so that the M/o SSI is able to strengthen and facilitate the SSIs to remain competitive.  The Planning
commission and M/o Finance shall be apprised of the concern of the committee, so that the allocation of funds for the

1.57     venture Capital Scheme was launched by SIDBI in October, 1992 and a separate VC fund with an initial corpus

rights to take up equity stake in the AMCs and Trustee companies (TCs).  Further, SIDBI also extends venture capital
assistance to SSI units directly and by way of subscription to the corpus of other Venture Capital Funds. SIDBI has also
extended assistance for setting up of two incubation centres at IIT, Kanpur and BIT, Mesra, Ranchi.

3.7       The Committee is of the view that the national policy and programmes/schemes should be suitable, and effective
for supporting the promotion and development of small scale industries.  The main emphasis should be on easy credit
availability, technological Upgradation and modernization, Infrastructural development, marketing support, etc. 
Moreover, for uniform and sustainable growth of small scale industries with an objective for greater employment
creation and equitable distribution of wealth all over the country, there is a need for a national policy for small
industries.  To address the needs in the changed economic scenario, the government must come out with a promotional
policy package at the earliest.  The findings of the Third Census can be used for policy formulation as follows:-
 
Liberalize credit policy to make institutional credit more accessible to SSI units, including the unregistered units.
Identify industries requiring technological up-gradation, which can be assisted either under the on-going
programmes/schemes or new appropriate schemes for the same.
Target sub-sectors, which have high employment potential, for assistance under different schemes.
Assistance for improving quality and productivity, especially of registered units which account for bulk of the output.
Identify high-tech industries, which can be promoted in the SSI sector.
Formulate schemes of assistance for the growing service sector (SSSBEs).
Evolve a system for regular collection of data through sample surveys at shorter intervals.
Evolve a mechanism for reaching the benefits of Government assistance to unregistered units.

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
1.0       Withdrawal of CVD exemption on raw materials for manufacture of blades for rotors of wind operated
electricity generators
1.1       The Committee directs the Government to look into the matter of withdrawal of CVD exemption on raw
materials for manufacture of blades for rotors of wind operated electricity generators and ensure that the industry is not
affected adversely
 
(Para 2.23 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
1.1.1    The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance has informed that the issue was examined in consultation with
Ministry of Non Conventional Energy Sources and CVD exemption on 15 specified raw materials for the manufacture
of rotor blades of wind operated energy generators has already been granted.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
1.2       Vocational institutes and recreational training
 
1.2.1    The Committee is of the view that the Department of Revenue should give kind consideration to exempt the
vocational institutes and recreational training institute including the institutes under philanthropic non-profit making
organizations from the Service Tax.  
(Para 2.45 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
 1.2.2   At present, service tax is levied on commercial training or coaching provided to any person by a commercial
training or coaching centers. Service tax is levied on the gross amount charged for rendering taxable service. No service
tax is leviable, if the taxable service is rendered without charging any amount from the recipient.
1.2.3    However, such commercial coaching or training provided by vocational training institutes and recreational
training institutes are presently exempt vide Notification No. 24/2004 - Service Tax, dated 10.9.2004.

182nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/182ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 13:00:50]
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
1.3       Early Harvest Scheme India-Thailand FTA
 
1.3.1    The Department of Revenue may re-consider the reduction of customs duties on inputs (up to 5%) required to
manufacture   products covered in Early Harvest Scheme India-Thailand FTA.(Para 3.19)
 
ACTION TAKEN
1.3.2    Vide notification No.27/2004-Cus dated 23.01.2004, concessional rate of duty has already been prescribed on a
number of inputs required for the manufacture of goods covered under the India-Thailand Early Harvesting Scheme.
 
RECOMMENDATION
1.4       Duty rates of 5% , 8% and 10%
1.4.1    The Committee desires that the Department of Revenue may facilitate the industries with its declared item wise
time frame for achieving duty rates of 5% , 8% and 10% as recommended by (FRBM)  task force headed by Dr. Vijay
Kelkar so that various segments of industries in general would accordingly chalk out their short term and long term
business strategy.                  (Para 3.22)
 
ACTION TAKEN
1.4.2    It is the declared policy of the Government to bring the customs duty structure closer to that of our East Asian
neighbours. In line with this policy, the peak rate of customs duty on non-agricultural goods (with a few exception) has
been reduced to 15%. Simultaneously, to further improve the competitiveness of domestic industry and to reduce costs,
customs duty on specified basic raw materials such as crude petroleum oil, specified chemicals, specified polymers,
primary iron and steel, etc., has been reduced to 5% or 10%.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.5       Continuation of 8% SED on car and aerated waters
 
1.5.1    While the Committee is in agreement with withdrawal of 8% SED on a number of items like tyre, tubes, flaps
and polyster, filament yarn and even air conditioner, however, the Committee would like to know the reasons for
continuation of 8% SED on car and aerated waters.  (Para 3.23 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
1.5.2    It is the intention of the Government to bring as many goods as possible to the Cenvat rate of 16%. With this end
in view, the 8% SED was withdrawn on tyres, polyester filament yarn and air-conditioners. Because of revenue
considerations, it was not possible to abolish the SED on all items. The Finance Minister in his Budget speech has
indicated that manufacturers of motorcars and aerated drinks would have to wait for some more time.
CHAPTER - II
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO
PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
2.0       Excise duty on synthetic and artificial staple fibers
 
2.1.1    The Committee, urges upon the Government that the excise duty on synthetic and artificial staple fibres under
Chapter Heading 55.03& 55.04 of Central Excise Tariff may be reduced to 8% in this Budget itself.
(Para 2.9 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
2.1.2    The issue was taken up with the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. They have informed that in 2004

182nd Report of Committee on Industry

budget, Government had rationalized the duty structure for textile sector.  So far as cotton is concerned, there are two
options. Under the first option, there is exemption right from the fibre to the garment stage.  For those units who want to
avail of credit of duty paid on inputs/capital goods and of service tax, an alternative option to pay duty at 4% was given.
So far as man-made and synthetic sector is concerned, there is a mandatory duty only at the first point
 i.e. fibre/filament
yarn stage. Beyond this stage, two options are available. Downstream manufacturers of spun yarn, fabrics, garment can
opt for full exemption. Under the other option, those who want to pay duty, 8% duty has been prescribed as against 16%
earlier. A lower duty of 8% on spun yarn and fabrics was proposed so that there was an incentive to the manufacturers
to opt for the Cenvat stream.   
 
2.1.3    Various stages in the manufacture of polyester fibres are as under:
Naphtha (16%)            Paraxylene  (16%)        DMT/PTA (16%)         Polyester Fibre (16%)
(Figures in brackets represent the rate of excise duty)
2.1.4    If excise duty on polyester fibre is reduced to 8%, the problem of inversion will shift tothe fibre manufacturers,
as in their case, the finished products will attract duty at 8%, while the raw materials would be paying 16%. Therefore,
if 8% rate has to be achieved on polyester fibre, excise duty has to be reduced down the line on all the raw materials
starting from Naphtha. This would involve a very substantial revenue loss.
2.1.5    It has been ascertained that some manufacturers of yarn are opting to pay duty and accumulating credit, hoping
to utilize the same later on or get a refund of the same in case of exports.   If a yarn manufacturer faces a problem of
excess credit by opting for the route of 8% rate, there is noting to prevent him to switch over to exemption route. If the
problem is one of excess credit, then the solution would lie in raising the optional excise duty to 16% as that would
obviate all problems of inversion. The suggestion to reduce the duty to 8% will also go against the policy of moving
towards a mean cenvat rate of 16%.  For a unit opting for the exemption route, with a single stage duty on a garment is
about 4% - 5% of the retail price of the garment, which cannot be considered as excessive.  Under the circumstances, it
is felt there is no case for reducing the mandatory duty of 16% on fibres.     
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
2.2.                  Duty differential of 5% between the finished product (PVC) and feedstock (VCM)
 
2.2.1    The Committee is an agreement with the argument of the representative of the industries that the present duty
differential of 5% between the finished product (PVC) and feedstock (VCM) is insufficient to cover even the variable
costs and is therefore not only detrimental to the growth of the industry but also threatening its very viability. Therefore,
The Committee desires that the Department of Revenue should reconsider to reduce the import duty on VCM to 0%
from the current level of 5% and roll back the import duty on finished product PVC resin to the earlier level of 15%.
(Para 2.18 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
2.2.2 Prior to 1.3.2005, Poly Vinyl Chloride (PVC) attracted customs duty of 15%, while Vinyl Chloride Monomer
(VCM) attracted duty of 10%. There was thus a duty differential of 5% between PVC and VCM.
 
2.2.3  Polymers are basic raw material and, in this year’s budget, customs duty on certain specified polymers including
PVC was reduced from 15% to 10%.  Simultaneously in order to maintain 5% duty differential between PVC and VCM,
duty on VCM was also reduced from 10% to 5%.  In a low customs duty regime, it would generally not be possible to
maintain a duty differential of more than 5% between feedstock and finished products.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
2.3       Excise duties exemption to SSI
 
2.3.1    The Committee pleads that even to the Department of Revenue the Kelkar Committee's recommendation on
confining the excise duties exemption to SSI to a limit of 40 lakh is not acceptable, and there is a valid reason for non
acceptance of the Kelker Committee's recommendations on the issue keeping in view the inflation rate and largely the
reasons on account of the need for giving adequate space to small enterprises to grow into medium enterprises as per the
declared policy of the Government.Therefore, there is the need for purposive and supportive tax structure   to give flip

182nd Report of Committee on Industry

to emerging SMEs.  The Committee understands that there is the strong reason for enhancing the excise duties
exemption to SSI from the current level to a reasonable level.
(Para 2.38 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
2.3.2    The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance has mentioned that the number of SSI units paying central
excise duty is about 37,000, which contribute only about 2.57% of the total revenue from central excise duties. SSI
exemption, thus, adversely affects the tax-GDP ratio. Excise duty being a tax at the manufacturing stage (the first stage),
exemption from it also leads to non-accounting of production, which in turn leads to non-payment of other taxes, such
as income tax, sales tax, etc. and generation of black money. Such exemption also leads to misuse of CENVAT credit
by large duty-paying units against duty-paid documents for materials supplied to the exempted SSI sector. It also results
in breaking of the CENVAT chain. State-level Value Added Tax (VAT) has been implemented from 1
st April 2005. 
Grant of more exemptions would adversely affect effective implementation of VAT. In view of the above-mentioned
facts, the Ministry of Finance has informed that it would not be possible to accede to the suggestion.
CHAPTER - III
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT OR THE COMMITTEE WANTS TO MAKE FURTHER
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.0       Level playing field to the domestic industry
 
3.1.1    The Committee understands that the tempest of globalisation would also gallop the Temple of Modern India
unless and until level playing field is provided to the domestic industry.  Therefore, the Committee is of the strong view
that the architect of Modern India should not forget to have the protected layer of extending certain tax
concessions/exemptions to protect against the onslaught of Faustian MNCs.  (Para 1.14 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.1.2    The General SSI Exemption Scheme provides full exemption from excise duty for first clearances of Rs.1 crore,
if no input tax credit is availed. On clearances beyond Rs.1 crore, the unit has to pay normal duty and take CENVAT
credit on inputs. The turnover eligibility limit for availing the benefit under the Scheme has been raised from Rs.3 crore
to Rs.4 crore in the Budget 2005-06.
 
3.1.3    Further, the Income Tax Act provides a variety of fiscal incentives for promoting the industrial sector and
facilitating exports, which are also available to the small-scale industries. The Act provides for a 100% deduction of
export profits of 100% Export Oriented Units (EOUs) engaged in the manufacture or production of any article, thing or
computer software under section 10B and of units engaged in the export of wood-based handicrafts under Section
10BA, upto assessment year 2009-10. In addition, a 10-year tax benefit is provided under Section 10A of the Act to
units in Special Economic Zones (SEZs).
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.1.4    The Committee notes that the Government is extending a variety of fiscal incentives for promoting the Small
Scale Industries, however, this Committee feels that the Advisory Committee, constituted under the Chairmanship of
Member (Central Excise), Central Board of Excise and Custom (CBEC) to  advise the Government on the extent of
abatement for both excise and Service Tex, should also examine the issue of the requisite period for which such fiscal
incentive is required to promote the SSI  units. The said Advisory committee may also examine the issue of extending
the central fiscal incentives to SSI units engaged in the SSI activities to the select region of the country in such a way
that it  must ensure the balanced industrial distribution and development and prevent the shifting of the industries from
one region to another due to aberration  in the tax-incentives.
 

182nd Report of Committee on Industry

3.1,5    The Committee observes that  since the Medium enterprises are being emerging out of the SSI units and they are
on the move towards the consolidation stage, therefore, the Advisory Committee may also consider the issue of
examining  as to whether the emerging MEs require central fiscal incentives for the rapid promotion and proliferation
and catching up the global pace of growth.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.2       Advisory Committee on the extent of abatement of excise duty and Service Tax
 
3.2.1    The Committee welcomes the move for setting up of Advisory Committee to advise the Government on the
extent of abatement of excise duty and Service Tax.  However, the Committee desires that the Advisory Committee
must have the representatives from various sections of economy including various segments of industry as well as
Federations/ Associations from Industries so that any conclusion could be drawn only after consultation and mutual
understanding in the general interest of the industry. (Para 2.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.2.2    Advisory Committee to advise the Government on the extent of abatement for both excise duty and service tax
has been constituted under the chairmanship of Member (Central Excise), Central Board of Excise and Customs
(CBEC). Member (Service Tax), CBEC, Additional Chief Advisor (Cost), Department of Expenditure, and Joint
Secretary (Tax Research Unit) are the members of the Committee. It has also been provided for the Committee to co-opt
any other officials of Government of India and invite experts and concerned representatives of trade and industry as
special invitees depending upon the need.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.2.3    The Committee recommends that Advisory Committee (to  advise the Government on the extent of abatement
for both excise duty and service tax) should have stake-holders as Members than merely associating them  as Special 
Invitees, that  too,  depending upon the need as felt by the Government. It would provide much more opportunity in
addressing their grievances and make the them feel of a participation in the decision-making process. It is being
observed that need is much  more felt on the part of  the stake-holders then the regulator. Moreover, the Committee feels
that the Government apparatus has to play not only the role of regulator but also that of a facilitator, therefore,
encouraging the stake-holders to participate in the decision-making process on equal footing would provide the example
of good governance. 
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.3       Electronic Consumer Products
 
3.3.1    The Committee understands that the market of consumer electronics is rapidly growing.  The electronic
components are the input products and back bone of electronic consumer products.  Even then no growth is coming in
the manufacture of electronic components because it cannot compete with the rapidly growing grey market due to
highest rate of excise duty @ 16%. The Committee, therefore, feels that the excise duty may be reduce to 8% for all
locally manufactured electronics products and inputs.(Para 2.11 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
Manufacturers of electronic goods can avail of CENVAT credit of excise duty paid on electronic
components/inputs/consumables. The actual impact of excise duties on electronic goods is less than 16%.
 
The revenue implication of reduction of excise duty/CVD on electronic components from 16% to 8% will be substantial
(over Rs.1000 crore approximately).
 
3.3.4    Reduction in excise duty from 16% to 8% would go against the stated policy of the Government that, as far as
possible, manufactured items should attract the mean CENVAT rate of 16%.   

182nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/182ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 13:00:50]
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.3.5    The Committee impresses upon the Government to review the Policy which has been referred to  in their replies
so as to favourably  accommodate the electronic consumer products.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.4       Import duty on the raw materials
 
3.4.1    The Committee wishes to point out an accepted policy of the Government that the import duty on the raw
materials has got to be lower than the duty on the finished products. Even in the world-class plants like Reliance, IPCL,
GAIL, Haldia, Finolex etc. the duty differential between the raw material and the end product is maintained.     
                                                                                                                    
(Para 2.14  )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.4.2    The policy of the Government, in general, has been to obviate any inverted customs duty.  However, it may not
be feasible to remove the inverted duty structure in all cases, on account of various reasons such as the output of one
industry being the input of another industry, etc.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.4.3    The Committee understands the need for obviating the inverted customs duty in order to maintain the differential
duty-structure on the raw-materials and the finished products. The Committee is in agreement with the reply of the
Government that the output of one Industry may be the input of another industry therefore, it may not be possible to
remove the duty-structure in all cases. However, the Committee is of the view that tax-structure can not be on the
random basis, it has to be based on certain reasons and principles that  distinctly identifying products are the finished
products and from those which can be used still as raw - material. Such identification and its classification has to  be on
rational basis to avoid the double-taxation and to maintain the accepted general principle of taxable that the import duty
on the raw-material has got to be lower then the duty structure on the finished products. The committee’s concern is
that  the end-users should  get the solace from the rational duty structure.  and Government would also not be under any
revenue loss from the intermediate user of products which still remains as the raw materials.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.5       Policies of the Government at least at par with the Large Scale Sector
 
3.5.1    In accordance with the announced policies of the Government at least at par with the Large Scale Sector, which
are at present, being rather penalized:-
 
Allow the import of DOP (HS Code 29173920 & 29173200) DBP (HS Code 19173910 & 29173100) only from the
Exporters who qualify the Indian norms of S.S.I.Units.
AND/OR
Restore fair competition by subjecting DOP and DBP to a higher rate of customs duty in cases where the exporters do
not qualify as SSI units as per Indian Regulations. Such imports may be subjected to duty at the bound rate of 40%.  It is
submitted that such a course of action will be compatible with the WTO Article III on national treatment.
 
Provide a 10% duty differential between raw material to end products. The custom duty on its  Raw Material (HS
Code), Octanol/2 Ethyl Hexannol (29051600&29051620, Butanol (Iso/Normal?mixed) 29051300& 29051400, Iso
Nonanol/Other (29051900), Phthalic Anhydride (29173500)
(Para  2.15)
 

182nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/182ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 13:00:50]
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.3.2    The Committee was apprised fo the following action taken by the government:-
 
Customs duty on DOP and DBP is 15%.  Duty on their raw material is 15%. Thus, there is no anomaly in the duty
structure.
Providing differentiated duty structure depending on the status of exporter would complicate the duty structure and be
administratively difficult to implement.
With a peak customs duty of 15%, it may not always be possible to provide a duty differential of 10% between raw
materials and final products, in all cases. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.5.3    The Committee desires that SSI units should be given preferential treatment so far the duty structure is
concerned in order to promote them in the international market. Particularly, such preferential treatment may be allowed
where there remains the scope for maintaining the DOP and DBP to higher rate upto bound rate of 40% which is also
compatible to the WTO-provision. The Committee further desires that the duty differential between raw-material to end 
products has to be maintained for the sake of regulating the market-mechanics and restoration of fair competition.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.6       Paint & Coating Industry
 
3.6.1    The Committee understands the problems being faced by the industry and therefore, is in agreement that the
exemption limit be reasonably raised and the restoration of concessional rate of 60% duty with the CENVAT up to
Rs.1.00 crore,  as such fiscal measures would help  in reducing the cost of SSI products and  imbibe competitive
resilience in the units engaged in Paint & Coating Industry.  (Para 2.42 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.6.2    Prior to 1
st April 2005,there were two separate schemes of excise duty exemption for SSI units:
Scheme I - This scheme provided full exemption from excise duty for first clearances of Rs.1 crore, if no input tax credit
is availed.   On clearances beyond Rs. 1 crore, unit was to pay normal duty.  (Notification no. 8/2003- Central Excise
dated 1st March 2003).
Scheme II - This option provided a concessional rate of excise duty of 60% of normal rate, for first clearances of Rs.1
crore, if input tax credit is availed. On clearances beyond Rs. 1 crore, unit was to pay normal duty.  (Notification no.
9/2003 - Central Excise dated 1st March 2003.)
3.6.3    In the context of excise duty exemption for SSI, the clearance limit of Rs.1 crore is referred to as ‘exemption
limit’.  In both the above schemes, exemption/concession was available only if total value of clearances of a unit in the
preceding financial year did not exceed Rs. 3 crore. This clearance limit of Rs.3 crore during the previous year is
referred to as ‘eligibility limit’
3.6.4    Before the presentation of this year’s budget, representations/recommendations were received from trade and
industry, Ministry of Small Scale Industries and VIPs seeking changes in the SSI excise duty exemption scheme, which
inter alia suggested:
Increase in exemption limit for SSI from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2 crore.
Increase in eligibility limit for SSI from Rs. 3 crore to 5 crore.
3.6.5    A number of Committees have looked into the scheme of exemption for the SSI units, and suggested
modifications.
3.6.6    Shome Committee on ‘ Tax Policy and Tax Administration for the Tenth Plan’ had noted that the Scheme II,
which provided for a concessional rate of 60% of normal rate with Cenvat credit, did result in a kind of subsidy due to
accumulation of credit and gave a higher benefit than the other scheme. In this background, the Committee had

be taken to establish a SSI-friendly tax regime.  These include:
 
3.7.1    Extension of General SSI Excise Exemption to SSI units manufacturing branded goods in urban areas, as
available in rural areas;                                                                                        (Para  2.50)
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.7.2    The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance, which has informed that to check misuse of SSI

FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.7.3    The Committee is of the view that SSI units manufacturing branded goods in Urban areas cannot be debarred

units from availing the Central Excise exemption. Dividing the rural and urban areas for extending SSI exemption to
SSI units would amount to differential treatment and unreasonable classification, therefore, the Committee recommends
that General SSI Excise Exemptin to SSI Units manufacturing branded goods must be `general’ and not on illogical
classification of rural or urban areas, therefore, the same be also extended to urban areas as now being extended to the
rural areas.

3.7.4    Increase in the excise exemption to new as well as existing SSI units in rural as well as urban areas;

ACTION TAKEN
 
3.7.5    Ministry of Finance has mentioned that the number of SSI units paying central excise duty is about 37,000,
which contribute only about 2.57% of the total revenue from central excise duties.  SSI exemption, thus, adversely
affects the tax-GDP ratio. Excise duty being a tax at the manufacturing stage (the first stage), exemption from it also
leads to non-accounting of production, which in turn leads to non-payment of other taxes, such as income tax, sales tax,
etc. and generation of black money. Such exemption also leads to misuse of CENVAT credit by large duty-paying units
against duty-paid documents for materials supplied to the exempted SSI sector. It also results in breaking of the
CENVAT chain. State-level Value Added Tax (VAT) has been implemented from 1
st April 2005. Grant of more
exemptions would adversely affect effective implementation of VAT. In view of the above-mentioned facts, Ministry of
Finance has informed that it would not be possible to accede to these suggestions.

RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.8       Lowering the customs and increasing the excise duty
 
3.8.1    The Committee views that current regime of lowering the customs and increasing the excise duty on items like
steel will have serious implications for the PSEs in capital goods sector. The Committee cautions the Government that
such a Duty regime would result in an uneven competition with PSEs facing serious handicap against cheaper imports
and MNCs. If the Government is serious about reviving the PSEs, it must help them regain their standing in domestic
market instead of imposing a duty regime that perpetuates the disadvantage against cheap imports. It is the
responsibility of the Government to seek redressal, if necessary, against such an uneven competition under the WTO
provisions.(Para  3.3)
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.8.2    The Committee was apprised of the following action taken by the government:-
 
The general rate of customs duty on capital goods is 15%, which is the peak rate of customs duty for non-agricultural
goods.
Customs duty on specified capital goods such as specified project imports, specified capital goods required in the
infrastructure and IT/Electronics/Telecom sectors and textile machinery not having a strong domestic angle has been
kept below 15% so as to reduce investment costs and facilitate technology upgradation/modernization.
Metals such as alloy steel, aluminum and copper, major inputs for capital goods, attract 10% customs duty. As regards
specified textile machinery attracts customs duty @ 5%, import of their parts is allowed at 5%, so as to provide level
playing field to the domestic manufacturers of such machines.
Increase in excise duty on steel should not result in increase in costs, since credit of the same would be available.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION

Recommendation
 
1.4       Utilisation of funds under the PMRY scheme
 
1.4.1    The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI and Ministry of Finance should ensure the optimum
utilization of funds under the PMRY Scheme by basing the release/utilization of funds under the Scheme on
performance/achievement of target by the State/UTs.  The funds released to State/UTs should be epent during the same
year.
(Para. 10.2)
Action Taken
 
1.4.2    The Ministry has revised the quarterly schedule for achievement of activities of sponsoring, sanction and
disbursement for 2005-06.  It is expected that with strict adherence to the schedule by the implementing agencies, target
of sanction and disbursement will be achieved by 31.03.2006.  This will also ensure utilization of the funds released
within a financial year.    
 
Recommendation
1.5       Changing the mindset of bankers
 
1.5.1    The Committee desires that public sector banks must yield to the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India
in regard to disbursement of loans on the PMRY.  The managers at the top level should also direct the branch managers
to adopt client-friendly approach and create such atmosphere that the general opinion about the mindset of the bankers
should itself change.  It is possible through making PMRY more popular among the unemployed youth.  The Committee
commends the role of RBI for suitable intervention from time to time whereby the RBI issued guidelines for
consumer/client-friendly working of banks.  As the banking sector is being empowered with functional autonomy, the
onus/lies on the public sector banks and its administrative Ministry to implement the guidelines of RBI in the best
interest of the industries its  objective to serve the nation and not use this functional discretion for denying the
prospective entrepreneurs in harnessing the opportunity for contributing to economic growth and industrial
development. (Para 13.2)
Recommendation
 
1.6       Coordinating and monitoring the working of PMRY
 
1.6.1    The Committee further desires that the financial institutions, respective State Governments and the Ministry of
ARI should coordinate and monitor the working of PMRY in such a way as to enable the process of sponsoring,
sanctioning and disbursement of applications by the States and banks by avoiding the stoppage/delay of disbursement in
PMRY on flimsy grounds and for quick disposal of application on the part of DICs and forwarding the same to the
banks.  Adequate mechanism may be adopted for timely communication of targets to the banks for necessary action on
their part; coverage of SC/STs/OBCs under the scheme as per the norms stipulated by the Government of India;
effective orientation programmes conducted by DIC for the target groups at block/taluka level to
enlighten/popularization of PMRY and giving accordance to the provision of PMRY for advancing loans in the ratio of
50%; 30% and 20% in respect of industry, service and business sector. (Para. 13.3)
 
Action Taken
 
1.6.2    In the review meeting of PMRY held on 16.09.2005 under the chairmanship of Secretary (SSI&ARI),
Government of India, representatives of State Governments, financial institutions, etc., deliberated on improving the
implementation of the Yojana.  Various decisions taken in this meeting to improve the implementation of scheme
include: timely reporting of monthly progress report by the implementing agencies, adherence to the revised quarterly
schedule, convergence of PMRY with other schemes of the Ministry of ARI and Ministry of SSI, regular furnishing of
information by banks on the number of cases rejected by them to the District Industries Centres (DICs) concerned so
that fresh cases could be sponsored in time, etc. States/UTs have also been requested to constitute Task Force
Committees at block level/mandal level.  The recommendations of this meeting have been forwarded to the Reserve

Bank of India, Department of Banking; Ministry of Finance and all State/UTs for initiating necessary action for better
implementation of PMRY.
 
Recommendation
 
1.7       Problems being faced by khadi industries
 
1.7.1    The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should take up the issue of requirement of working capital and
budgetary support with the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission for modernization and renovation of sales
outlets, alongwith the strategy and time frame to execute the same. Adequate steps must also be taken for modernisation
of charkhas and looms, for which a separate fund and scheme i.e. modernization of traditional industries has been made.
(Para 17.1)
Action Taken
 
1.7.2    The recommendation of the Committee is noted.  While making annual budgetary plan proposal for 2006-07 to
the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of ARI has already included allocations necessitated
by the following requirements of implementing NCMP declarations for revamping of KVIC:
 
Replacement of charkhas and Looms that have outlived their utility and scheme to convert khadi fabric into readymade
garments, thus adding value.
Modernisation of sales outlets.
Strengthening of Confederation for Promotion of Khadi and Village Industries CPKVI by providing corpus fund.
Introduction of new scheme for external market development assurance scheme in line with MDA scheme of
Department of Commerce.
Scheme for upgradation of existing training institutes of KVIC/KVIBs and institutions affiliated to KVIC/KVIBs
 
1.7.3    Further, in pursuance of the announcement of Finance Minister in his Budget speech of July 2004 regarding
establishment of a fund for regeneration of traditional industries like coir, handloom handicrafts, sericulture, leather,
pottery and other cottage industries, the Government has approved a scheme titled the "Scheme of Fund for
Regeneration of Traditional Industries” (SFURTI), for the integrated development of traditional clusters of khadi, coir
and village industries, including leather and pottery. It is proposed to take up development of hundred clusters (25
khadi, 50 village industries and 25 coir) over the next five years (beginning 2005-06) at a total cost of Rs. 97.25 crore.
The scheme envisages integrated development of clusters of khadi, coir and traditional village industries and has the
components of replacement of charkhas and looms for increasing the productivity of khadi spinners and weavers, setting
up of common facility centers for various post loom facilities like dyeing, printing, readymade garment manufacturing,
product testing laboratory, etc., and for processing and manufacture of village industry items, development of new
products and designs in khadi and village industries sector, market promotion assistance, capacity building measures
like training, exposure visits, etc.  A provision of Rs. 8.65 crore has been made for this scheme during 2005-06.
 
Recommendation
 
1.8       The Committee feels that conversion of outstanding balance i.e. to the tune of Rs. 238.02 crore which was lying
as outstanding balance with khadi implementing agencies under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) into working capital
would solve the problem of requirement of working capital to a certain extent.                   (Para 17.2.)
Action Taken
 
1.8.1    The Ministry appreciates the recommendation of the Committee. As on 31-01-2005, Rs. 238.02 crore was lying
as outstanding balance under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) loan. The Government has now approved the conversion
of outstanding balance under CBC scheme into working capital and for this purpose KVIC has executed necessary
documents and forwarded the same to the lead bank in the consortium - State Bank of India.

1.9.1    The Committee is of the view that the Government must give the utmost attention to the Village Industries by
undertaking serious study of SWOT analysis and outlining the "Key Areas for Massive Action" as India being a country
of villages and undergoing industrial development must tap the opportunities and bank upon its strength and remove the
weaknesses and threats for rapid and ensured rural industrialization and development. Special/specific strategic
programme should be sketched out for developing and consolidating village industries in Bihar, Jharkhand and West
Bengal, basing the strategy on the availability of local raw material and providing adequate working capital and
budgetary support.
 
(Para 19.1)
 
Action Taken
 
1.9.2    Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) each year as detailed in reply to the Para. No. 5.13 above is in line with the
intention of the Government to give utmost attention to the village industries and to ensure  rural industrialisation and
development in all parts of the country including Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal.
 
Recommendation
 
1.10     Employment generation under village industries
 
1.10.1  The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry of ARI that KVIC is adopting a strategy to generate large-
scale employment in rural sector by channelising institutional finance. A Working Group constituted by Planning
Commission for the Tenth Five Year Plan has recommended employment target of 89.57 lakh (15 lakh under khadi and
74.57 lakh under V.I.) by the terminal year of the Tenth Five Year Plan.  For this purpose, the Planning Commission has
allocated Rs. 2080 crore to KVIC. Under its REGP scheme, it is proposed to generate 25 lakh employment by the
terminal year of Tenth Five Year Plan. The Committee is of the considered view that an all out efforts should be made
for achieving the target set by the Planning Commission. The Committee wishes to point out that while combating the
problem of unemployment and especially setting the target (that should be determined/fixed time frame) proper and
adequate attention must be paid to population growth rate and the prevalence of level of poverty so that the problem of
unemployment, poverty and population explosion may be solved in a time bound frame with a holistic approach.       
(Para 20.8)
 
Action Taken
 
1.10.2  The Ministry as well as the KVIC is making all out efforts to ensure that employment generation targets are
met.  In fact the Working Group had recommended that the total employment generated (not additional employment)
would reach 89.57 lakh by the terminal year of 10
th Five Year Plan, from the level of 62.64 lakh at the end of the
terminal year of 9th Five Year Plan.  By the end of 2004-05 i.e. 3rd year of 10th Five Year Plan, the employment
generation was to the extent of 76.77 lakh in KVI sector. The target is to reach 82.20 lakh employment generation by
the end of 2005-06 and 88.70 lakh by the end of 2006-07.  In fact during the period 2004-05, as against the target of
generating 5.25 lakh additional job opportunities under REGP, 5.30 lakh additional job opportunities were created. It is
expected that the KVIC would be able to meet the employment generation targets under village industries during the
period 2005-06 and also that of entire10
th Plan period.

1.11.1  The Committee understands that the Government Departments/Ministries functions with specific mandate,
however, there is the need for comprehensive and coordinated emphasis for tackling the intrinsic problems of the
national economy. The Committee desires the problem of national economy should be tackled through comprehensive
and intergraded planning and having coordination and collaboration among Government Departments/Ministries for

2.5       NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION
 
The Committee takes stock of the fact that NPRI which was announced in the budget 1990-2000 with the objective of
setting up of hundred rural industrial clusters in the country every year for boosting rural economy by creating more
employment avenues and to arrest the migration of the rural artisans to  town/cities.  The irony of the programme was
that no separate fund was made available to implement the programme and it was conceived that since the various
Ministries/Departments are having their own programme in the “coveted areas and their co-ordination and synergistic
harnessing would be significant/harness the objectives of the programmes.  The result that comes out is that the

expectation regarding the success of the programme felled apart, and that was bound to happen with the programme
without financial support. (Para 42.6)
 
Action Taken
 
2.5.1    The Committee observes that the co-ordination and synergetic approach so conceived among various
Government Ministries/ Departments to make NPRI a success could not succeed the test of the time and the
administrative (Ministry of ARI) which was supposed to implement the NPRI spent no time in screwing the
bureaucratic skill for advocating the countless reasons for “unsatisfactory performance of NPRI i.e. meager financial
assistance of Rs. 5 lakh per cluster for wide intervention, fill in gap arrangements, non-availability of credit linked
subsidy component and also the inadequate synergy with the Ministries/Departments with their own scheme in this
area.  When this Committee recommended for comprehensive over hauling and synchronization of all schemes and
programmes for employment generation and poverty alleviation, the Ministry of ARI who beautifully referred the
allocation of transaction of business among various Government’s Ministries/Departments with a stress that sufficient
co-ordination and synergy exists among various Government’s Ministries/Departments.  The Committee wonders as
how the same Ministry of ARI is now wanting out the lack of co-ordination and synergy as the reason for unsatisfactory
performance of NPRI.  This Committee is of the view that logic and argument of the Ministry of ARI is of selective
nature. (Para 42.7)
 
2.6       Regarding NPRI, the Committee in its Report on Demands for Grants(2004-05)  had observed that NPRI has the
potential for actual rural industrialization and consolidation of rural economy and had recommended that the
Government should undertake concrete measures to combat the problems in achieving the objectives, targets,  credit
flow, implementation and monitoring mechanism and "Key Concern Areas "  of NPRI. But of no avail. Sensing the slow
but sure death knell of the NPRI, the Ministry of ARI has now decided to abandon the so acclaimed programme (NPRI)
and the Ministry comes out with re-christened programme, coincidently, the name of the programme is SFURTI,
Scheme of Funds for Re-generation of Traditional Industries. NPRI had made a slow start, thereof, it seems that the
name of the new programme is carefully drafted as SFURTI, obviously to instill the hope among those who are having
their heart in the efficient working of the Government machinery.                                            (Para 42.8)
 
2.7       The Committee is awfully shocked to observe the pathetic working of the programmes/schemes and the
monitoring mechanism as maintained within the Governmental structure which is being imparted to make the
programme a success. The Committee is of the considered view that re-christening of scheme is not the guarantee to
make the new scheme a success unless and until the scheme is backed by adequate financial fund and willing
administrative backup to deliver in the system.   The Committee has no objection with launching of new programme
like SFURTI or with whatever names it comes in future but the Committee strongly feels that NPRI has cherished
national goal and appropriate objectives and had no inherent weaknesses/problems as such except the lack of allocation
for a separate fund, the Committee therefore, reiterates that NPRI must continue in order to achieve those
goals/objectives and a separate fund must be allocated to NPRI. (Para 42.9)
 
Action Taken
 
2.7.1    The Ministry has reviewed the programmes under its purview.  The Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of
Traditional Industries (SFURTI) is much more comprehensive scheme for integrated development of clusters in ARI
sector.  The scheme would be taken up in selected clusters of traditional industries in various parts of the country. 
Under SFURTI, it is proposed to develop 100 clusters (25 clusters for khadi, 50 clusters for village industries and 25
clusters for coir industry) over a period of five years commencing 2005-06.  The Scheme would cover an estimated
50,000 beneficiary families. The objective of SFURTI is to establish a regenerated, holistic, sustainable and replicable
model of integrated cluster-based development of traditional industries. This will primarily mean:-
more competitive traditional industries with more market-driven, productive, profitable and sustained employment for
the participants;
strengthened local socio-economic governance system of the industry clusters, with the active participation by the  local
stakeholders that can help to continue undertake development initiatives by themselves; and
building up innovated and traditional skills, improved technologies, advanced processes, market intelligence and new
models of public-private partnerships, so as to gradually replicate similar models of cluster-based regenerated traditional

3.9.3    The Committee  impresses upon the Government to prepare an action plan to  promote inter-sectoral co-
operation and assistance among rural development, poverty alleviation programmes, food processing sector and other
such programmes/schemes with the Agro & Rural sector in order to give greater thrust and coordinated efforts and
synergistic approach towards implementation of rural infrastructural development projects, employment Generation and
Rural industrialization and Development and poverty alleviation.
 
Recommendation
 
3.10     NATIONAL POLICY FOR AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
 
3.10.1  The Committee feels that the Ministry of ARI should give serious thought for formulation of National Policy for
Agro and Rural Industries for the growth of rural industries, instead of rejecting the suggestion on the first instance. 
Had the every thing been right with the existing policy measures, India’s Agro and  Rural Industries would have been in
a better position, contributing the national economy and particularly consolidating the rural economy.  The Committee
understands that the Ministry through a dynamic process of policy amendments and positioning is consistently
addressing policy initiatives in response to the changed economic scenario and its challenges, however, the colossal
problem of India is also persisting and that too consistently.  Therefore, it is desirable that the Ministry of ARI should
act and not react on the recommendation of the Committee without giving a proper thought to the ideas behind the
recommendations. (Para. 53.2)
Action Taken
 
3.10.2  Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries appreciates the recommendations of the Committee.   As declared in the
National Common Minimum Programme, the Government dissolved the KVIC and constituted a ten-Member Expert
Committee to review the existing structure, functioning and performance, etc., of the KVIC and recommend suitable
measures for its revamping
 
3.10.3  Based on the recommendation of the Expert Committee, the KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 was introduced in
the Lok Sabha in August 2005 and referred to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee (DRPSC) on
Industry for examination and report.  Further necessary action is being taken on the Bill in the light of the
recommendations of the DRPSC.  The Expert Committee also made recommendations relating to programmes and
policies of the KVIC.  These are being examined and a proposal relating to new schemes and also revising the existing
schemes in the KVI sector is under active consideration of the Government. These include (i) scheme for making the
khadi industry more productive and competitive by improving the production infrastructure available with the khadi
institutions, in a phased manner and generating sustainable additional employment for khadi artisans, (ii) scheme for
facilitating graduation ofsuccessful PMRY enterprises in rural areas and small towns with population up to 20,000 to
higher levels of investment, operation and employment generationwith assistance under the REGP, (iii) schemes for

strengthening domestic and international efforts in the KVI sector, (iv)  scheme for upgradation of infrastructure,
equipments and other facilities available in the training institutions of KVIC/State/UTs KVIBs and those of institutions
(v)  re-designing of relevant training courses for providing long-term vocational training for skill development and
entrepreneurial capacity to first generation entrepreneurs, etc.
 
3.10.4  Further, in order to bring further improvements to  review the design and implementation practices of the Prime
Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY), Government has set up a Group under the chairmanship of Adviser (VSE),
Planning Commission, Government of India to examine all relevant issues and make recommendations in this regard.
Based on the recommendations of the Group, suitable modifications in the PMRY scheme would be made to make it
more effective creating employment opportunities for the educated unemployed youth in the country.
 
3.10.5  The Government has recently launched the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries
(SFURTI)) under which 100 traditional industry clusters (of khadi, village industry and coir) would be taken up for
comprehensive development over 5 years.  The KVIC and the Coir Board are the nodal agencies for the scheme, which
will be the first comprehensive initiative for regeneration of the khadi and village industries sector, based on the cluster
development methodology.
 
3.10.6  It is expected that the above policy initiatives will lead to further growth of agro and rural industries in the
country and contribute substantially to the national economy.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.10.7  The Committee is of the view that the   amendment  of  KVIC Bill , modification in PMRY, NPRI, REGP,
formulation of SFURTI etc are only the sectoral policy formulations or mere modifications, while the  formulation of
National Policy needs greater vision, setting targets, making objectives with wider perspective. The Committee strongly
feels the need for comprehensive policy for the Agro and  Rural industries.
 
Recommendation
 
3.11     CO-ORDINATED AND CONCERTED EFFORTS TO TACKLE THE PROBLEM OF
UNEMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION
 
3.11.1  The Committee refers to the concern expressed by Finance Minister in the General Budget 2005-06 and the need
to tackle the twin problem of unemployment and poverty with focused and co-ordinated approach.  The Committee
appreciates the approach of the Finance Minister as stated in the General Budget 2005-06 which is in consonance with
the recommendation of the Committee given in its Report on Demands for Grants (2004-05).  The Committee’s
observation in that report reads as under:
 
3.11.2  “The Committee is pleased to note that the Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector and
especially the Agro and Rural Industries.  The Committee, however, desires that the Government should come out with
pragmatic planning for Agro and Rural Industries keeping in view the twin objectives of employment generation and
poverty alleviation.  The Committee wishes to highlight that the Agro and Rural Industries has the potential of
employment generation and since large chunk of Indian population dwells in rural areas under the abject poverty
therefore, holistic and comprehensive planning for rural sector and its effective implementation is the need of the hour.”
 
(Para. 31.4 of Report No. 152)
Action Taken
 
3.11.3  The recommendations of the Committee are noted.  The Ministry of ARI will continue to give thrust to the
REGP and PMRY through higher budgetary support as these programmes are important for creating self-employment
opportunities in the rural areas of the country which in turn would help to tackle the problems of poverty.
 
3.11.4  The Committee in its 124
th Report on Demands for Grants 2003-04 had recommended as under:-

"The Committee is of the opinion that Government should fix the target under PMRY keeping in mind the stark reality
of population growth rate, quantum of poverty and absolute number of unemployment (disguised unemployment as well
as seasonal employment).  Need of the hour is formulation of Integrated and Total Planning after having objective
assessment of empirical fact and figures.  The rate of employment generations must be twice/thrice than the population
growth rate so that the problem of unemployment gets out rooted in a time bound manner.  The Committee would be
pleased to observe that the planning is done for exploring employment generation at the geo-metrical rate and
population growth be limited at the arithmetical rate.  Though at the first instance the suggestion may seem illusive but
to change the fate of India it has to be done and Government must strive in this direction.  This is possible only through
co-ordinate and total Planning and when the problems of Population, Poverty and unemployment are studied and
visualized in a holistic manner and policy-maker has to go beyond the cocoon of department/ministries of the
Government. "
(Para 7.6.3 of 124
th  Report )
           
3.11.5  The Planning Commission had set up a Special Group on Targeting 10 million jobs per year over the 10
th Plan
period under the chairmanship of Dr. S.P. Gupta, Member, Planning Commission. This report of the Special Group
which was published in May 2002 has taken into account the present unemployment scenario in the country and has
chalked out an Action Plan for all the sectors of the government for generating adequate work opportunities for the
growing labour force in the country. The recommendations of this report have been incorporated in the 10
th Plan
document and form the basis for fixing up targets under all the schemes for all Ministries for creation of job
opportunities. Based on the recommendation of the Special Group, the Ministry of ARI has set targets for REGP,
PMRY and the Coir sector.
 
3.11.6  What the Finance Minister is pronouncing in the General Budget (2005-06), the Committee has been observing
and making recommendations since its report on Demands for Grants (2003-04). The Committee therefore, expects that
the two wings of the Government should not act in water-tight compartmentalisation manner. The problem of
unemployment and poverty are intrinsically related to each other therefore, focused and co-ordinate approach is
required, then and only then  India’s Developing  Economy can be converted into a developed one at  a rapid  track and
within stipulated time-frame.
 
(Paras 57.2, 57.3 and 57.4)
Action Taken
 
3.11.7  The recommendations of the Committee are noted.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.11.8  The Committee  observes that the   Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector and especially
the Agro and Rural Industries. The Government is also appreciating the need to tackle the twin problem of
unemployment and poverty with focused and co-ordinated approach.  The Committee welcomed the observation and
approach of the Government as this is a positive  thinking on the part of the Government.  But where the apparatus of
the  Government  is failing is the mode of implementation of its positive thinking i.e. converting its thought into action.
The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the ministry to take appropriate steps in this regard.

GOVERNMENT 
  
Recommendation 
  
1.0       Cost reduction of coir products 
  
1.1       The Committee takes note of the basic characteristics and problem of coir industries and the 
action taken or be envisaged to be taken by the  Coir Board and the Ministry of ARI. The Committee is 
of the view  that with massive efforts and implementation of financial assistance  scheme to encourage 
setting up of new units would result into higher utilisation of husk from the present level of thirty seven 
percent. The  Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI and Coir Board to undertake cost 
management programme in the coir manufacturing units with the assistance of Research Institute like 
Entrepreneurship Development Institute of India, Ahmedabad and others.  Due impetus may also be 
given to cluster development activities and consortium approach to reduce the cost of production. 
(Para. 4.2) 
1.1.1    The Committee understands that Coir Industries is a labour intensive industry and major 
components of the labour force are the women. Therefore, promotion and furtherance of coir industries 
would lead to empowerment of women besides enhancing  the economic prosperity of the States. Action 
Plan may be chalked out for enhancing the economy of scale so that cost of production may come down 
and avenues of employment generation may further be explored. 
(Para. 4.5) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2    Observations of the Committee on financial assistance, cost reduction, women empowerment , 
economies of scale, etc., serve as guidelines to the Ministry of ARI and Coir Board  for formulation of 
future schemes and policies for development of the  coir industry. The Coir Board has been trying to 
involve financial  institutions  in funding the  coir industry. The Board has been arranging meetings of 
lead bank officers, State Industries Department officials and entrepreneurs in all coir producing States  
to facilitate  flow of adequate funds to the coir sector. As 80% of the work force in the coir industry 
consists women, they will benefit the most from future developments. Cost reduction by encouraging 
economies of scale  is feasible through cluster based development. This is one of the objectives of the 
SFURTI ( Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries).  
  
Recommendations

y as export oriented industry

natural products like Chinese Grass Mats, Rubber, Sisal and coir products being exported by Sri Lanka, 
Taiwan, Philippines etc. Synthetic products manufactured using improved technology and supported by 
publicity also pose great threat to the coir exports.  The Coir  geo-textiles  are  facing competition from 
Sri Lanka and  synthetic geo-textiles materials which dominate the market. Therefore, the Committee 
feels that the Government should provide assistance by reimbursing  a portion of the expenditure 
incurred on brand based publicity  abroad projecting the eco-friendly nature of the coir geo-textiles to 
meet this competition.  
( Para. 5.8)
