1.2.2    To promote the export of coir products, including geotextiles, the Government extends assistance 
under the scheme of Export Market Promotion for various activities like participation in exhibitions, 
conduct of market study, sponsoring delegations, release of product specific advertisements in foreign 
trade magazines, etc. 
Recommendation  
1.3       Marketing Strategy 
1.3.1    The Committee is of the view that steps being contemplated by the Coir Board to promote the 
marketing and sales of coir products in the domestic market  which inter-alia include intensification of 
promotional measures like publicity through print and electronic media;  increased  participation in trade 
fairs and exhibitions; organisation of Buyer Seller Meets  in potential regions;  organisastion of special 
sales campaign and festival discount offer to promote sales;  organising collective participation of 
manufactures in selected trade fairs and exhibitions;  popularization of new products like coir geo-
textiles, garden articles, coir pith based  products through awareness creation programmes etc would go 
a long way in the promotion and furtherance of the Coir Industries in India and would inject competitive 
resilience to face the global competition wherein China is becoming a great threat to the India’s 
monopoly in  the Coir Industries.  (Para. 7.2) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2    Participation in trade fairs, exhibitions buyer-seller meets, etc.,  is organised by   the Board  both 
within the country and abroad for popularisation of coir products. Almost all coir products and their 
applications are displayed at these exhibitions. Coir Board participated in 61 domestic exhibitions  
during 2004-2005.        Participation in the specialised  international exhibition is another scheme 
implemented by the Coir Board to expand the export market for coir products. During 2004-2005,  the 
Board participated in  four different specialised exhibitions at New Delhi. 
1.3.3    The Board also participated in  4 exhibitions abroad, alongwith the exporters, during  2004-2005. 
One of these exhibitions  was the Domotex International Trade Fair, Hannover, Germany. From coir 
sector ,22 exporters participated in the fair on their own and 5 exporters attended the fair by availing of 
government assistance through the Coir Board. The Coir Board also participated  in the product 
promotion programme coinciding with the Formex  Fair at Stockholm,  Sweden by arranging an 
attractive display of coir products and literature on coir.  
1.3.4    Catalogue shows are also a useful way of exposing the innovative products which generate new 
trade leads, enrich existing trade and also help establish fresh business contacts. Coir Board participated 
in six catalogue shows during 2004-2005 in countries like Algeria, Germany, Greece, Mangolia, South 
Africa and Vietnam.  The Board also released advertisements  projecting the bio-degradable, 
environment friendly aspects and  varied end use applications of Indian coir products in nine foreign 
magazines during 2004-2005.

1.4.1    The Committee is of the  opinion  that in the liberalized and globalisation market structure since 
the consumer is the king, all marketing and sales strategy should be based on the plank of the actual 
need and taste of the consumer therefore, the marketing should be conducted accordingly and efforts

3.3.1    The Coir Board may concentrate on capturing new markets as well as expansion of existing

may participate in exhibitions de pending upon the markets and targeti ng specified regions. Coir Board 
may also organisse exhibitions like India International Coir Fair  and Coir India. 
(Para. 23.3)

3.3.2    Important international fairs and exhibitions offer opportunities for dissemination of information 
about the end uses of coir products and display of new coir products. The entrepreneurs participating in 
the exhibitions are also able to canvass business and establish new contacts. it  also helps to assess 
market preferences and requirements as well. In additi on to foreign fairs, the Bo ard also participates in 
important exhibitions, catalogue s hows and product promoti on programmes held in India. The  Coir 
Board prioritizes and selects only exhibitions both within and outside the country which are capable of  
conveying our message to the intended target group/ region.

well-as make efforts to expand the ex isting market so that the market share of the Coir products is

Recommendation  
  
4.0       Restructuring the coir industry 
  
4.1       The Committee understands that the Low productivity of traditional technology, age old looms 
and equipments, slow phase of mode rnisation , absence of systematic collection of raw materials, lack 
of adequate  credit  availability, low le vel of capacity building, inadequa te infrastructural facilities, 
limited marketing skills , lack of  working capital are the bane of  this industry.  The Committee 
therefore, feels that it is necessary  to put in place an integrated a nd complimentary set of measures to 
encourage and support coir industry so that they  become more productiv e and competitive and 
development and expenditure take place in a  sustainable manner. 
(Para. 14.2) 
Action Taken 
  
4.1.1    The Coir Board has been attempting to a ddress these problems thr ough its Plan schemes and 
programmes. In addition, schemes ha ve been approved for clusters ba sed development of coir industry. 
Recently, under the Industrial Infras tructure Upgradation Sc heme  of the Minist ry of Commerce and 
Industry, Government has approved and launched Alappuzha Coir Clus ter Development Project at a 
total cost of Rs. 56.8 crore -75% (42.6 crore) by way of  grant under the IIUS a nd the balance by way of 
equity and stakeholders contribut ions This scheme includes improve ment of husk coll ection, extension 
of defibreing units, modernisation of spinning sector , establishmen t of common facili ty centre and 
common effluent treatment pl ant, etc. Similar cluster -based development schemes for self -employment 
generation through village le vel units will be repli cated in coir producing States like Tamil Nadu, 
Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa  , Lakshadweep, etc., with fundi ng support under II US and SGSY  
The States like Tamil Nadu and Karnataka have already formulated propos als for assistance under 
Industrial Infrastructure  Upgradation Scheme (IIUS). 
  
4.1.2    For regeneration of tradi tional industries like coir , khadi and village industries the Central 
Government has also approved the “ Scheme of Fund for Regenerati on of Traditional Industries 
( SFURTI)”.   
Recommendations 
4.2       Modernization Fund 
  
4.2.1    The Committee is of the strong opinion that  a modernisation fund may be created for extending 
one time financial assistance to the exporter s for modernisation of pr oduction, importing necessary 
machinery and equipments including packaging and labeling machineries and also for setting up of R& 
D facilities. This would enhance production and quality and  would act as a means to meet 
competition.    (Para. 16.2)           
Action Taken 
  
4.2.2    Recommendations of the Committee have been noted and follow up action would be taken 
during the formulation of the 11th Plan.  
  
Recommendation 
  
4.3       Measures Required for Promotion and Proliferation of the Coir Industry 
  
4.3.1    The Committee understands the need for e nhancing the harnessing of  coconut husk for coir 
production from existing level of thirty seven percent. With a view to mobilize  husk available in plenty 
in coconut producing states and to increase the percenta ge of utilization of coc onut husk, the collection

mechanism will have to be streamlined with the active partic ipation of NGOs Se lf Help Groups 
( SHGs) etc. through introduction of an appropriate scheme. It would pave wa y for level utilization 
reaching 50% thereby facilitating pr oduction unhindered and to increase  output of coir fibre in the 
country. 
(Para. 24.1.2) 
  
Action Taken 
  
4.3.2    Coir Board has prepared a Millennium De velopment Mission document, for development of 
coir industry in India. The Mi ssion document envisages a total fina ncial outlay of Rs . 3000 crore to

Five Year Plan. Under this programme, State -wise Action Plans have to be prepared, based on the 
development need of the coir producing districts of the State concerned. The document envisages an 
increase in export performance by 25%  each year so as to achieve a total export worth Rs. 1000 crore 
by 2008-2009 . The Mission envisages generation of add itional employment to half a million workers 
over five years. Appropriate schemes can be formulated to enhance husk collection under the Mission. 
  
4.3.3    Under the Industrial Infrastructure Upgradat ion Scheme (IIUS) of th e Ministry Commerce and 
Industry, the Government of India has approved the project titled “Development of Coir 
Clusters in the Alleppe y District of Kerala ” with an outlay of Rs.56.8 crore with Central 
grant of 75 per cent of the total outlay, i.e., Rs.42.6 crore.  T he husk collection  
mechanism is slated to be one of the main action  points of  the scheme.

(Para. 24.1.4)

Recommendation 
  
1.1       Defining SME Sector 
1.1.1    The Committee observes that World over, policies are being  devised to meet the requirement of 
small and medium enterprises (SME).  In India too, adequate steps are required to initiate policies for 
Medium Enterprises in order to give the SSI units to grow into Medium Enterprises. The Committee is 
of the view that Government should, at the earliest, delineate and draw the demarcation line between 
SEs and MEs by providing suitable definition and the mechanism for institutional arrangement, along 
with the classification of incentive and the exemption required for units of  the Small scale Industries 
and the medium enterprises for their growth and development.  
( Para 1.3.2) 
Action Taken

1.1.2    Action in this regard  has already been initiated.  The Small & Medium Enterprises Development 
(SMED) Bill, 2005 has  proposed to define  small and medium enterprises (both in manufacturing and 
service sectors) and the Parliamentary Standing Committee has further recommended, inter alia,  
inclusion of definition  of micro (tiny) enterprises, as well. The recommendations of the Standing 
Committee are under active consideration of the Government. 
Recommendation  
1.2       Technology management for SMEs 
1.2.1    The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that schemes for technology up-gradation 
for SMEs should be made more functional and accessible to the existing entrepreneurs as well as the 
first generation entrepreneurs.  Due budgetary provisions should be made for R & D so that outcome of 
the research work should assist the entrepreneurs in cutting the cost of production as well as enhancing 
the value engineering of SMEs product through product development and product diversification.  The 
Committee recommends that public private partnership approach may be focused by the Government for 
infusion of latest technology in the SMEs sector. 
(Para  1.6.7) 
Action Taken  
  
1.2.2    The Ministry of SSI operates two schemes for technology upgradation of SSI units.  These are: 
(a) Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) and  (b) Small Industry Cluster Development 
Programme (SICDP). While the former provides  15%  capital  subsidy (subject to a maximum loan 
amount of Rs. 1 crore)  to the  SSIs,  including tiny units,  on institutional loan availed of by them, the 
SICDP aims at  holistic  development of clusters as a whole,  including technology upgradation. The 
SICDP  is implemented  in a cluster in which active participation of the local associations is ensured.  
The members of the association are made aware of  the outcome of the programme  from time to time 
through seminars, workshops, etc. Technicalinstitutions, CSIR laboratories and other Research and 
Development institutions are involved in the  research activities for product development and product  
diversification of the SSI units in the cluster. The  Department of Scientific and Industrial Research 
(DSIR) is implementing  schemes which promote and facilitate R & D activities taken up by the 
industry. The  Ministry of SSI remains in close contact with these institutions and the  DSIR and utilises 
their services for implementing the SICDP. 
  
1.2.3    The concept of public private partnership  is made use of while implementing the SICDP.  The 
participation of the associations concerned is ensured and so is their financial commitment. Common 
Facility Centers,  raw material banks,  processing centers of raw materials, etc.,  are set up in the cluster 
under the scheme.  The small enterprises associations make contributions to the cost of land & building 
and plant and machinery needed for the common facility centers, etc.   Moreover, the running of these 
centres on self sustainable basis is entirely the responsibility of the associations concerned.

Recommendation  
1.4       Handloom Sector 
1.4.1    The Committee observes that large number of handloom weavers remain outside the fold of the 
cooperative, and the cooperative structures are being increasingly weekend due to financial and other 
mismanagement.  Therefore, the Committee feels that the Office of the Development Commissioner for 
Handlooms should give impetus to cluster based approach to the development of the handloom sector.  
The cluster scheme would provide and promote small and medium enterprises in the handloom sector in 
the ambit of development initiatives of the Central Government. (Para   2.5.8) 
Action Taken  
1.4.1    In the budget  of 2005–06, Government has already announced an outlay of Rs. 40  crore for the 
development of 20 clusters in the country.  Accordingly, a scheme under the name of “Integrated 
Handloom Cluster Development Scheme” is under formulation by the Ministry of Textiles.  The 
proposed scheme envisages a comprehensive package of assistance to the selected handloom clusters in 
the country,  involving holistic and total intervention by the Central Government. 
Recommendations

Following Steps should be taken to promote and develop its exclusiveness for the global market:-  
training modules may be developed for weavers engaged in the production of low value added items, 
with the objective of upgrading their skills to enable them to find alternate employment in the textile or 
other allied sector;  
Comprehensive welfare measures will continue to be implemented in close cooperation with the State 
Governments, for better working environment and the social security of the weavers;  
Effective support systems in research and development, design inputs, skill upgradation and market

Revamping of Weavers Service Centres will be revamped in consonance with the contemporary trends,

Recommendation  
  
1.8       Adequate and timely supply of coal to Small Scale Industries 
  
1.8.1    The Committee takes note of the fact that Indian Small Scale Industries suffer from inadequate 
supply of coal to the SSI units. As per the extant policy, the supply of coal to the SSI units falls under 
the non-core sector.  As a result, there has been huge mismatch between the demand and supply of coal 
to SSI sector.  As many of the SSI units require timely and adequate supply of coal for running the units, 
non-availability of coal has adversely affected to growth of SSI sector. 
(Para   5.7.1) 
Action Taken  
  
1.8.2    The Government has given approval for sale of 10 million tones of coal through electronic 
auction on the Internet for the year 2005-06 on trial basis.  In this e-auction,  non-core consumers, 
irrespective of linkage  and sponsorships as well as traders,  can participate and bid for the quantity  as 
per requirement from the preferred sources.  This would be in addition to the quantity sold to non-core 
consumers during 2004-05 which is also offered to no-core valid linked consumers based on the 
Maximum Permissible Quantity (MPQ) at the weighted average e-auction price of  the preceding 
month.  Hence the valid non-core linked consumers need not participate in the e-auction to receive coal 
at the weighted average e-auction price of preceding month. The non-core sector consumers would 
continue to receive coal on the basis of past linkages and sponsorships and MPQ,  subject to furnishing 
of the desired documents by the consumers arising out of the re-verification exercise being conducted by 
the State  authorities.

institutional finance and development of the units is restricted by non-availability of finance at the time 
of need. In order to encourage broad basing of the ownership of SSI enterprises, provisional for some 
additional facilities for units going in for company formation could be considered. The SSI units going 
in for company formation should be provided some additional facilities like incentives to form 
cooperatives, concession to create infrastructure, increase in investment limit etc. 
(Para    1.6.8) 
Action Taken  
  
3.5.1    For smoother and enhanced  delivery of credit to this sector is concerned,  both the Reserve Bank

doubling the flow of credit to the small enterprises in the next five years.  Apart from the efforts to get 
the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005 passed, the Government has also been 
working on  including small enterprises within the ambit of a Limited Liability Partnership Act.  These 
enactments,  when passed,  will help more small enterprises to get organised as companies or limited 
liability partnerships and improve their capability to access institutional credit.

Ministry to liase with the concerned Ministry & Department.

3.14     Leather Products 
  
3.14.1  The Committee is of the view that the Indian leather industry has not been able to make its 
presence felt in the international market mainly because of technological obsolescence and is losing to 
China in cost leadership. Major leather goods manufacturers are also shifting their production centres to 
south Asian countries posing stiff competition to Indian goods. Another problem for Indian 
manufacturers is that almost the entire range of machines for making quality leather goods are imported 
making them costly for small entrepreneurs. The availability of chemical inputs used in leather

3.20     SWOT –analysis of Jute Industry  
  
3.201   The Committee is of the view that  conscious efforts may be made for assessing the SWOT 
analysis of Jute Industry in India and harvesting,  marketing and diversification of Jute and Jute products 
should be carried out with the mission as per details given below: 
  
Creation of strong marketing network for better market linkage of raw jute; 
Providing market information to jute growers in order to enable them to take a decision regarding sale o
f 
their produce at market driven price; 
Implementation of Technology Transfer programmes for better and quicker retting of raw jute for 
ensuring improvement in fibre quality; 
Development of cost effective community retting facilities; 
Transfer of Technology as discovered after R & D efforts by IJIRA to jute industry and growers. 
  
(Para   3.2.1) 
Action Taken  
  
3.20.2  A synoptic  SWOT analysis of Jute Industry in India is as follows: 
  
Strength:           Jute as a natural fibre has some inherent advantages like silky luster, high tensile 
strength,  considerable heat resistance and long staple length ,  qualities that cannot be matched by 
synthetic fibres.  Jute is easily available in abundant quantity at a comparatively reasonable price.  
Moreover, jute can easily be blended with other natural and man made fibres.  Being a natural renewable 
source, it helps in the maintenance of the environment and ecological  balance.  It is a natural and 
annually renewable fibre,  is bio-degradable,  non-toxic and environment friendly and offers excellent 
scope as a raw material for different textile and other diversified products. 
  
Weakness:  There is widespread sickness  in the jute industry.  Out of 78 jute mills,  38 are sick and 
most of them have been referred to the BIFR.  19 jute mills have been lying close for varied periods. A 
combination of factors such as instability in supply of quality raw jute of uniform specifications,  high 
labour cost, demand erosion due to competition from .synthetics,  obsolescence of machinery,  
uneconomical management practices, etc.  has resulted in the widespread sickness. 
             
Opportunity:  The jute sector has lot of potential for creation of employment opportunities in the 
agricultural,  organised & decentralised industrial sectors and rural & urban areas,  particularly for 
women and the disadvantaged.  There is also tremendous potential for increasing export earnings of the 
country   thus  contributing to the overall  economic growth of the  country and preparing it  to compete 
with confidence for an increasing  share of the global market in geotextiles,  composites and jute 
diversified products (JDPs). 
  
Threats:   The perceived threat to the jute industry is primarily from alternative packaging material like 
plastics, card board, etc., and from synthetic fibres.  Technological obsolescence and high labour cost 
are also some of the inhibiting factors affecting the health of the jute industry. 
  
3.20.3  On the basis of the deliberations held and the recommendations arrived at the two-day National 
Conference held in November 2004 at Kolkata, the National Jute  Policy  2005 was framed.  The 
recommendations of the Committee as mentioned above find a mention in the Policy document.

Associations should also be the member of the Standing Advisory Committee.

private sector as a matter of reserved mines for SSI sector and it should be made mandatory to any big 
private mine owner whoever gets coal mine from Government of India to ensure that priority must  be 
fixed for SSI units. 
Government should consolidate the Small Scale Industries in the country by       implementing    the 
Action Plan to enable the sector to provide employment   generation opportunities to millions of youths

Action Taken  
3.23.2  As regards allocation of captive mining block to SSI units is concerned,  as per the existing legal 
framework governing coal mining, companies in the private sector engaged in iron and steel production,  
power generation and cement production can do mining of coal for captive use in their respective end-
use projects. The SSI units engaged in any of the aforesaid approved end-uses can apply for any of the 
unallocated coal blocks identified for captive mining.  If the requirement of SSI units is small in 
quantity,  a number of SSI units could form consortium and apply for coal blocks for joint operation and

Government.  Further, SSI units with small requirements could apply for small and isolated reserves,

coal  mined  from such reserve in their plants and in the local areas.  This is as per provisions of section

            4.8.1    The Committee express its concern that it is because of the inadequate credit flow to SSI 
sector, the mortality rate is increasing year after year and sickness of SSI units is posing a matter of great 
concern.  Moreover, after the deregulation of interest rates regime from 18-20% in 1997-98, the lending 
rates have come down to around 9-12% at present.  As per extant guidelines the banks are required to fix 
their own prime lending rates (PLRs) and the maximum band over the PLR.  The existing guidelines for 
banks for lending SSI is plus/minus 2% on PLR which translates into a range of 8.25% to 12%.  While 
interest rates for Large Scale Industries are negotiable and are generally at sub-PLR.  Limiting to the

clusters for transpirations of raw-materials and finished SSI and ARI  products of Small quantity at 
sustainable fright charge. (Para 3.26.2) 
Credit flow  to SSI sector   
  
            The Committee is pleased to find that the Government has recently announced the Policy

package for stepping up the credit to Small and Medium Enterprises and the Committee takes note of

to SMEs provided the intended actionS therein are implemented in letter and spirit  by all those

Credit Flow to Medium Enterprises 
 
            The Committee understands that the Government comes out with Annual Monetary & Credit 
Policy each year and accordingly RBI issues guidelines to banks & implement the stated objective in the 
policy, however the Committee desires that the financial institution must go beyond the formation of 
Policy and issuance of guidelines and circulars.  Banks should ensure that their policy & guidelines are

            The Committee takes note of the recommendations of the Ganguly Committee on flow of credit 
to SSI Sector, as accepted by RBI and commended to the banks for implementations. The Committee

and what have been their financial strength. , enough to provide capital to SMEs.

            The Committee  held meetings   with the representatives  of SSI Associations and nationalized 
banks  on 7th Febuary, 2006 and 7th March, 2006 and noted with  concern  the  declining Net Bank 
Credit Flow to the SSI to the point of 9.8 percent  of the Net Bank Credit which  poses a serious threat to 
the survival to the SSI sector, therefore, all comprehensive and correctives measures are  therefore, 
required to enhance the Credit Flow to the SSI, if the target of 12 percent growth rate is to be achieved

Recommendation
 
1.4       Utilisation of funds under the PMRY scheme
 
1.4.1    The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI and Ministry of Finance should ensure the optimum
utilization of funds under the PMRY Scheme by basing the release/utilization of funds under the Scheme on
performance/achievement of target by the State/UTs.  The funds released to State/UTs should be epent during the same
year.
(Para. 10.2)
Action Taken
 
1.4.2    The Ministry has revised the quarterly schedule for achievement of activities of sponsoring, sanction and
disbursement for 2005-06.  It is expected that with strict adherence to the schedule by the implementing agencies, target
of sanction and disbursement will be achieved by 31.03.2006.  This will also ensure utilization of the funds released
within a financial year.    
 
Recommendation
1.5       Changing the mindset of bankers
 
1.5.1    The Committee desires that public sector banks must yield to the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India
in regard to disbursement of loans on the PMRY.  The managers at the top level should also direct the branch managers
to adopt client-friendly approach and create such atmosphere that the general opinion about the mindset of the bankers
should itself change.  It is possible through making PMRY more popular among the unemployed youth.  The Committee
commends the role of RBI for suitable intervention from time to time whereby the RBI issued guidelines for
consumer/client-friendly working of banks.  As the banking sector is being empowered with functional autonomy, the
onus/lies on the public sector banks and its administrative Ministry to implement the guidelines of RBI in the best
interest of the industries its  objective to serve the nation and not use this functional discretion for denying the
prospective entrepreneurs in harnessing the opportunity for contributing to economic growth and industrial
development. (Para 13.2)
Recommendation
 
1.6       Coordinating and monitoring the working of PMRY
 
1.6.1    The Committee further desires that the financial institutions, respective State Governments and the Ministry of
ARI should coordinate and monitor the working of PMRY in such a way as to enable the process of sponsoring,
sanctioning and disbursement of applications by the States and banks by avoiding the stoppage/delay of disbursement in
PMRY on flimsy grounds and for quick disposal of application on the part of DICs and forwarding the same to the
banks.  Adequate mechanism may be adopted for timely communication of targets to the banks for necessary action on
their part; coverage of SC/STs/OBCs under the scheme as per the norms stipulated by the Government of India;
effective orientation programmes conducted by DIC for the target groups at block/taluka level to
enlighten/popularization of PMRY and giving accordance to the provision of PMRY for advancing loans in the ratio of
50%; 30% and 20% in respect of industry, service and business sector. (Para. 13.3)
 
Action Taken
 
1.6.2    In the review meeting of PMRY held on 16.09.2005 under the chairmanship of Secretary (SSI&ARI),
Government of India, representatives of State Governments, financial institutions, etc., deliberated on improving the
implementation of the Yojana.  Various decisions taken in this meeting to improve the implementation of scheme
include: timely reporting of monthly progress report by the implementing agencies, adherence to the revised quarterly
schedule, convergence of PMRY with other schemes of the Ministry of ARI and Ministry of SSI, regular furnishing of
information by banks on the number of cases rejected by them to the District Industries Centres (DICs) concerned so
that fresh cases could be sponsored in time, etc. States/UTs have also been requested to constitute Task Force
Committees at block level/mandal level.  The recommendations of this meeting have been forwarded to the Reserve

2.5       NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION
 
The Committee takes stock of the fact that NPRI which was announced in the budget 1990-2000 with the objective of
setting up of hundred rural industrial clusters in the country every year for boosting rural economy by creating more
employment avenues and to arrest the migration of the rural artisans to  town/cities.  The irony of the programme was
that no separate fund was made available to implement the programme and it was conceived that since the various
Ministries/Departments are having their own programme in the “coveted areas and their co-ordination and synergistic
harnessing would be significant/harness the objectives of the programmes.  The result that comes out is that the

183rd Report of Committee on Industry

expectation regarding the success of the programme felled apart, and that was bound to happen with the programme
without financial support. (Para 42.6)
 
Action Taken
 
2.5.1    The Committee observes that the co-ordination and synergetic approach so conceived among various
Government Ministries/ Departments to make NPRI a success could not succeed the test of the time and the
administrative (Ministry of ARI) which was supposed to implement the NPRI spent no time in screwing the
bureaucratic skill for advocating the countless reasons for “unsatisfactory performance of NPRI i.e. meager financial
assistance of Rs. 5 lakh per cluster for wide intervention, fill in gap arrangements, non-availability of credit linked
subsidy component and also the inadequate synergy with the Ministries/Departments with their own scheme in this
area.  When this Committee recommended for comprehensive over hauling and synchronization of all schemes and
programmes for employment generation and poverty alleviation, the Ministry of ARI who beautifully referred the
allocation of transaction of business among various Government’s Ministries/Departments with a stress that sufficient
co-ordination and synergy exists among various Government’s Ministries/Departments.  The Committee wonders as
how the same Ministry of ARI is now wanting out the lack of co-ordination and synergy as the reason for unsatisfactory
performance of NPRI.  This Committee is of the view that logic and argument of the Ministry of ARI is of selective
nature. (Para 42.7)
 
2.6       Regarding NPRI, the Committee in its Report on Demands for Grants(2004-05)  had observed that NPRI has the
potential for actual rural industrialization and consolidation of rural economy and had recommended that the
Government should undertake concrete measures to combat the problems in achieving the objectives, targets,  credit
flow, implementation and monitoring mechanism and "Key Concern Areas "  of NPRI. But of no avail. Sensing the slow
but sure death knell of the NPRI, the Ministry of ARI has now decided to abandon the so acclaimed programme (NPRI)
and the Ministry comes out with re-christened programme, coincidently, the name of the programme is SFURTI,
Scheme of Funds for Re-generation of Traditional Industries. NPRI had made a slow start, thereof, it seems that the
name of the new programme is carefully drafted as SFURTI, obviously to instill the hope among those who are having
their heart in the efficient working of the Government machinery.                                            (Para 42.8)
 
2.7       The Committee is awfully shocked to observe the pathetic working of the programmes/schemes and the
monitoring mechanism as maintained within the Governmental structure which is being imparted to make the
programme a success. The Committee is of the considered view that re-christening of scheme is not the guarantee to
make the new scheme a success unless and until the scheme is backed by adequate financial fund and willing
administrative backup to deliver in the system.   The Committee has no objection with launching of new programme
like SFURTI or with whatever names it comes in future but the Committee strongly feels that NPRI has cherished
national goal and appropriate objectives and had no inherent weaknesses/problems as such except the lack of allocation
for a separate fund, the Committee therefore, reiterates that NPRI must continue in order to achieve those
goals/objectives and a separate fund must be allocated to NPRI. (Para 42.9)
 
Action Taken
 
2.7.1    The Ministry has reviewed the programmes under its purview.  The Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of
Traditional Industries (SFURTI) is much more comprehensive scheme for integrated development of clusters in ARI
sector.  The scheme would be taken up in selected clusters of traditional industries in various parts of the country. 
Under SFURTI, it is proposed to develop 100 clusters (25 clusters for khadi, 50 clusters for village industries and 25
clusters for coir industry) over a period of five years commencing 2005-06.  The Scheme would cover an estimated
50,000 beneficiary families. The objective of SFURTI is to establish a regenerated, holistic, sustainable and replicable
model of integrated cluster-based development of traditional industries. This will primarily mean:-
more competitive traditional industries with more market-driven, productive, profitable and sustained employment for
the participants;
strengthened local socio-economic governance system of the industry clusters, with the active participation by the  local
stakeholders that can help to continue undertake development initiatives by themselves; and
building up innovated and traditional skills, improved technologies, advanced processes, market intelligence and new
models of public-private partnerships, so as to gradually replicate similar models of cluster-based regenerated traditional

any State share.  The various components of the scheme include replacement of charkhas and looms for increasing the
productivity of khadi and weavers, Common Facility Centres (CFC) for readymade warp units for supply of ready-to-
use warps for weaving, post-loom facilities, viz., dyeing and printing, setting up composite ready made garment
manufacturing facilities to convert fabrics into ready-to-wear khadi products, product testing laboratory to enforce
quality standards,service and maintenance, processing and manufacture of village industry items like testing
equipment/laboratory to enforce quality standards specially for processed food items, service and maintenance and other
common infrastructure, etc., Product Development & Design Intervention for fabric designing for upholstery, new
designs for high fashion garments, fabric development, embroidery in silk items, use of natural dyes, development of
new products specially for items like hand bags, shoes, new designs for pottery items; improved/new design for
packaging, specially for herbal and cosmetics, confectionery items, etc., Market Promotion Assistance for activities such
as organization of and participation in domestic/international exhibitions, participation in buyer-seller meets, renovation
and upgradation of marketing outlets, computerisation of sales outlets, bar-coding, etc., Capacity Building Measures for
undertaking following activities like exposure visits to other clusters and institutions (outside) to understand the self-
help actions, new products, technology, need based training within the clusters (related to global trade issues, skill
development, self-help, credit and other need based issues, support for establishment of cluster level networks (industry
associations) in the form of basic office infrastructure, including books, other need based support as emerge from the
diagnostic study, handholding support by NGOs/institutions of repute who would act as implementing agencies,
appointment of cluster development agents, who would work in the cluster for entire period of five years of cluster
development and technical support and guidance from reputed national level institutes having expertise in cluster
development such as Entrepreneurship Development Institute, Ahmedabad, NISIET, Hyderabad, IIE, Guwahati,
NIESBUD, Noida (UP).  While formulating the scheme of SFURTI, the Ministry of Finance and also the Planning
Commission had advised that “Schemes with overlapping objectives and coverage should be proposed for merger with

comprehensive scope of SFURTI and the advise of Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission, it was decided to

MATCHING OF ALLOCATION AND RELEASES FOR THE VILLAGE INDUSTRIES
 
            The Committee understands that unutilized allocation has to be surrendered as  there is no way out  to keep the

unutilized allocation in any other account or making expenses  in other Head unless the permission of do so is expressly
sought.  But surrendering of unutilized allocation can not be made the usual and regular practice just to ensure that funds
are used within the financial year itself.  If the allocation remained unutilized it cannot be said to be “used as such”
under any accounting practice.  Rather, the practice would cast apprehensions on the effective implementation of
scheme and the efficacy of the Ministry of ARI.  The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to ensure the utilization of
allocation within the respective financial year. This will not only ensure timely implementation of the projects/ schemes
but will also set up model accounting practice. (Para 3.5.3)
 
ACTION PLAN TO PROMOTE THE KHADI IN INTERNATIONAL MARKET
 
            The Committee notes that KVIC is extending cash  incentives to the registered exporting institutions and

reimbursement of 90% of to and fro  fare to Khadi institution/entrepreneurs  particularly in the international fair.

            The Committee wishes to know as to what extent the participation of Khadi institutions/entrepreneurs in the
international exhibition/fair and the cash incentives of 5% on FOB helped the  export promotion. (Para 3.6.5)
STOCK INVENTORIES
 
            The Committee is of the considered view that the lasting solution has to be found out to the continuing problem
of stock inventories in order to clear the stock inventories in Khadi Sector, the Committee , therefore,  reiterates its

th Report desiring the Government to act promptly for chalking  out
action plan to dispose off  the same in a time bound manner.
(Para 3.7.2)
 
STRENGTHENING OF CO-OPERATIVISATION SCHEME
 
            The Committee is of the considered view that the strengthening of Co-operativisation Scheme for coir industries
would  lead to  promotion of coir industries not only  in coir traditional zones like Kerala and Karnataka  but would
result into proliferation of the coir industries in the  non-traditional zones as well.   The Committee therefore, desires
that the Ministry and the State Governments  of both ,traditional and non- traditional State coordinate and promote co-
operative activity in the coir industry so that this centrally sponsored scheme becomes instrumental in coir  production.  
(Para 3.8.3)
 
STRATEGY TO PROMOTE INTER-SECTORAL CO-OPERATION AND ASSISTANCE
 
            The Committee  impresses  upon the Government to prepare an action plan to  promote inter-sectoral co-
operation and assistance among rural development, poverty alleviation programmes, food processing sector and other
such programmes/schemes with the Agro & Rural sector in order to give greater thrust and coordinated efforts and
synergistic approach towards implementation of rural infrastructural development projects, employment Generation and
Rural industrialization and Development and poverty alleviation. (Para 3.9.3)
 
NATIONAL POLICY FOR AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
            The Committee is of the view that the   amendment of   KVIC Bill , modification in PMRY, NPRI, REGP,
formulation of SFURTI etc are only the sectoral policy formulations or mere modifications, while the  formulation of
National Policy needs greater vision, setting targets, making objectives with wider perspective. The Committee strongly
feels the need for comprehensive policy for the Agro and  Rural industries.
(Para 3.10.7)
CO-ORDINATED AND CONCERTED EFFORTS TO TACKLE THE PROBLEM OF UNEMPLOYMENT
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION
 
            The Committee  observes that the   Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector and especially
the Agro and Rural Industries. So  far so good. The Government is also appreciating the need to tackle the twin problem

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
1.0       Recommendation
 
1.1       Lack of ancillarisation of  industries in the Small and Medium sectors
 
1.1.1    No major efforts have been made to put the state on the industrial development track, and therefore there is the
lack of ancillarisation of  industries in the Small and Medium sectors.  Besides the general problems like lack of
infrastructural development and marketing assistance and shortage of timely and adequate credit flow etc, the state has
also been the victim of natural calamities like super cyclone in 1999 which have actually devastated the Small Scale
Industrial set up and thus arrested the industrial growth and promotion and proliferation of small and medium
enterprises in the state.
(Para 1.1.5)
 
Action Taken
 
1.1.2    The Government has recently announced a  ‘Policy Package for Stepping up Credit to Small and Medium
Enterprises (SMEs)’.  The measures in the Policy Package to increase the quantum of credit to SMEs (including Small
Scale Industries – SSIs) include:
Public sector banks to fix their own targets for funding SMEs in order to achieve a minimum 20 per cent year-on-year
growth in credit to the SME sector.
Public sector banks to follow a transparent rating system with cost of credit linked to the credit rating of the enterprise.
Commercial banks to make concerted efforts to provide credit cover on an average to at least 5 new tiny, small and
medium enterprises at each of their semi-urban / urban branches per year.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to issue detailed guidelines relating to debt restructuring mechanism so as to ensure
restructuring of all eligible small and medium enterprises.
Introduction of a one-time settlement scheme to apply to small scale Non-Performing Asset (NPA) accounts in the
books of the banks as on March 31, 2004.

Taking the existing RBI guidelines as indicative minimum, banks to formulate a comprehensive and more liberal policy
relating to advances to the SME sector.
Special dispensation under the Credit Guarantee Scheme for all (a) loans upto Rs.2 lakh, (b) eligible women
entrepreneurs and (c) eligible borrowers located in the North Eastern region (including Sikkim) and Jammu and
Kashmir.
Banks to adopt cluster based approach for SME financing.
The RBI to constitute empowered committees with the Regional Director of RBI as the Chairman to review the progress
in SME financing and rehabilitation of sick small and medium enterprises.
Boards of banks to review the progress in achieving the self-set targets as also rehabilitation and restructuring of SME
accounts on a quarterly basis.
 
1.1.3    The RBI has issued circulars to the banks dated 19
th August, 2005 and 25th August, 2005 advising them to
implement the measures announced in the Policy Package. Further, as per the announcement made by the Governor,
RBI in the Annual Policy Statement for 2005-06, the RBI has formulated a scheme for strategic alliance between
branches of banks and SIDBI located in the clusters, viz., Scheme for Small Enterprises Financial Centres (SEFCs).
This scheme is important in the context of expanding the outreach of banks and improving credit flow to the Small
Scale Industries (SSI) sector. The SIDBI has operationalised the Small & Medium Enterprises (SME) Fund w.e.f. April
1, 2004.  The major initiatives taken by SIDBI towards SME Fund implementation are as under:
 
To make available, funds to the SME sector at competitive rates and thereby encourage availment under the Fund, the
interest rate for direct lending by SIDBI under the SME Fund has been fixed at a competitive rate 2% below PLR,
which currently works out to 9.5% p.a.
Apart from direct lending by SIDBI, the SME Fund is being deployed through other intermediaries so as to enhance the
credit flow.  For this purpose, funds are being made available to all Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding RRBs &
Cooperative Banks) at a rate of 6.25% p.a. to 7.25% p.a. and to SFCs/ SIDCs/ TFIDCs at 7.5% p.a. to 8% p.a.
During the financial year ended March 31, 2005, sanctions and disbursement under SME Fund amounted to around Rs.
2,730 crore and Rs. 1,830 crore respectively.
 
1.1.4    As far as Industrial Infrastructural Development is concerned, three IID Centres have been sanctioned in the
State of Orissa under the scheme of IID.  One IID Centre was sanctioned in the year 1996 in Distt. Rayagada and Distt.
Jagatsinghpur.  The implementation of IID Centre in Distt. Rayagada, which falls in the backward KBK (Koraput,
Bolangir & Kalahandi) region of the state has been slow due to poor response from entrepreneurs.  In order to publicise
the IID Centre at Rayagada, the IDCO has planned to organize an “Investors Meet” in the month of July,2005. 
Regarding IID Centre at Paradeep., Distt.Jagatsinghpur, the implementing agency, IDCO is not in a position to
implement the project because of the land dispute and Court Case with Paradeep Port Trust.  IDCO has informed that
case is likely to be decided by the Hon’ble High Court soon.
 
Recommendation
1.2       Key Areas for effective action
           
1.2.1    The Committee further recommends that following key areas must be selected for effective action:-
 
Strengthening the functional aspects of State Level Inter-Institutional Committee(SLIIC) and promotional agencies;
 
Financial restructuring of Orissa State Financial co-operation by seriously considering the proposal of adjustment of
interest payment to the tune of Rs.160.33 crore against principle liabilities besides wavering of the interest;
 
Extension of income tax and central excise exemption for setting up of SMEs in economically backward districts like
Bolangir, Koraput and Kalahandi on NER, Uttranchal and Himachal Pradesh line;
 
Special liberal package to super cyclone effected SSI units like rehabilitation package and one time settlement(OTS).
(Para 1.1.7)

1.2.2    The RBI has advised their Regional Offices to play a proactive role in timely holding of State Level Inter-
institutional Committee (SLIIC) meetings in coordinating with different Government agencies.
 
1.2.3    As a pro-active measure to strengthen the SFCs, SIDBI has offered a restructuring package to the SFCs and
entered into a Memorandum of Understanding with them.  The package, inter-alia, covers reduced rate of interest on the
existing outstanding portfolio and future disbursements on prompt payment of dues.  The package also offers
moratorium on repayment of principal dues by one year.  OSFC after due approval of the State Government had
selected UTI Bank Ltd., as Consultant to make a diagnostic study and suggest a restructuring plan and programme to
make the Corporation a viable organization on a sustainable basis.  After getting a positive indication about possibility
of infusion of fresh equity by the State Government in OSFC, SIDBI may consider the matter for restructuring package
envisaging above measures/ facilities, subject to fulfillment of conditions as may be prescribed by the Bank.
 
1.2.4Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue has informed that section 80-IB (5) of the Income-tax Act provides
for substantial income-tax concessions for industrial undertakings set up in backward districts during the period
1.4.1994 to 31.3.2004.  Undertakings set up in Category-A backward districts are entitled to a 100% deduction of profits
for a period of 5 years followed by 25% (30% in the case of companies) for the next 5 years.  In the case of units set up
in Category-B districts, the deduction available is 100% for 3 years and 25% (30% in the case of companies) for the
next 5 years.  These concessions are available to small and medium enterprises as well, which are located in these
districts. Such concessions are also available in the backward districts of Orissa so classified viz., Kalahandi, Bolangir,
etc. Excise exemption is already available on clearance of rupees one crore to Small Scale Industries having total annual
turnover not exceeding Rs. 4 crore. Area based exemptions create economic distortions affecting economic viability of
units located in non-exempted areas and result in shifting of industry from non-exempted areas to exempted areas.  Such
exemptions also lead to shrinkage of Tax base and adversely affect buoyancy in revenue collection, apart from breaking
the CENVAT chain.  Such region specific exemptions are difficult to administer and are prone to misuse and
consequent loss of revenue. Durability of such investments beyond the exemption period is also doubtful. Further both
Shome and Kelkar Committees have recommended discontinuance of area-based incentives to the backward districts
and states since they result in distortions and have an adverse effect on the industrial development of contiguous states. 
In view of the above, the Ministry of Finance has opined that it would not be desirable to extend area-based exemptions.
 
1.2.5    The SIDBI had extended relaxations and launched ‘Relief Refinance Scheme for Cyclone Affected Units’ in the
year 1999. Accordingly, Prime Lending Institutions were made eligible for refinance on liberal terms in respect of their
fresh loans extended to cyclone affected SSI units in the notified areas.  Further, a higher moratorium of two years was
provided under the Scheme to the affected units. As per the ‘Policy Package for Stepping up Credit to Small and
Medium Enterprises’ announced by the Government, the RBI circulated to all the public sector banks on 3

by encouraging SMEs in the sun rise Small Scale Industries and thus explore avenues for employment generation by

1.11     Challenges of globalization and liberalization
 
1.11.1  The Committee desires that the Government should take measures for preparing SSI Sector to meet the
challenges of globalization and liberalization under the WTO regime.  However, the basic concern of the Committee is
the protection and promotion of domestic SSI sector under the prevailing global market economy.  Therefore, the
continuous and concrete efforts should be made by the Government to protect the domestic Small Scale Industries from
the on-slaught of adverse impact of globalization and liberalization through appropriate tariff adjustment, anti dumping
measures and other safeguards.  Simultaneously the process of strengthening SSI Sector and acquiring the requisite
competitive  resilience should be enhanced on the ground level.  The Committee is in agreement with the views of SSI
associations/ federations that the Ministry of SSI should make efforts for Streamlining and strengthening the Anti-
dumping mechanism.
 
Conversion of Quantitative restriction(QRs) into rationalized  tariff regime for providing protection to the domestic
SSIs;
 
Implementation of VAT and safeguard duties to protect domestic producers in consonance with WTO provision; and
 
Expeditious disposal cases are anti-dumping actions thereto, in view of almost all SSI products under open general
license(OGL) list.
(Para 2.11.1)
Action Taken

1.11.2  The Government is fully aware of the WTO environment and has taken appropriate measures for preparing the

Government has put in place several measures to help small enterprises to become globally competitive.  These include

fee up to Rs.15,000 for adopting bar coding of products, etc.  The government has also put in place appropriate trade
defence mechanisms, such as import licensing, safeguards against surge in imports and anti-dumping measures to
provide protection to domestic industries, including small and cottage industries. 
 
Conversion of Quantitative restriction(QRs) into rationalized tariff regime for providing protection to the
domestic SSIs:
 
1.11.3  Under the WTO regime all Quantitative Restrictions(QRs)  have been abolished except 430 QRs maintained on
account of public morality, safety & health etc.  The current average  tariff is 15% for non-agriculture products  These
tariffs are considered as higher tariffs amongst the tariffs  applied by the various Member States in the WTO regime. 
 
1.11.4  Regarding rationalized tariff regime for providing protection to the domestic SSIs, it is stated that during annual
exercise for formulation of budget proposals concerning customs/excise for submission to the Ministry of Finance, EA
Division of this office consults all concerned Technical Divisions as well as SSI Associations, etc. On the basis of
proposals so  received, suitable budget proposals are formulated and sent to Ministry of Finance for their consideration
so as to protect the interests of domestic industries.  The budget proposals do include suggestions for increase/decrease
in custom duties including rationalization of the rates so as to protect the interests of domestic industries. 
 
1.11.5  Ministry of Commerce & Industry consults this office while formulating Bi-lateral/Regional Trade Agreements. 
Here also, this office makes   appropriate recommendations to the Department of Commerce after consulting the
concerned Technical Divisions. While making recommendations, factors like reservation of an item for exclusive
manufacture in the SSI sector,  its production base in terms of  number of units manufacturing the item, our competitive
strengths, potential for employment generation & exports, etc.are  taken into consideration.
 
1.11.6  In general, the Ministry of Commerce & Industry is the nodal Ministry for  monitoring trade flows including that
falling under the SSI sector.  That Ministry keeps a watch on the applied tariffs on various products.  Necessary
adjustment in the tariff rates is done as per the requirements of the situation in the domestic/world market, as and when
needed. 
 
Implementation of VAT and safeguard duties to protect domestic producers in consonance with WTO provision:
 
1.11.7  “Value Added Tax (VAT) intends to replace the States’ sales tax. VAT is a simple transparent and modern tax
system which has been adopted by more than 130 countries around the world.  It is a multi-stage tax with input tax
credit  which eliminates cascading of tax (tax on tax).  Consequently, there is no price escalation due to tax on tax. 
Moreover, because of the availability of input tax credit on tax paid on earlier stages of production, the cost of
production is expected to be lower under the VAT system vis-à-vis the earlier Sales Tax system.  Therefore,
implementation of the value Added Tax(VAT) system  is not likely to adversely  affect the interest of small and cottage
industries.
           
1.11.8  Regarding  imports, the Government has put in place appropriate trade-defence mechanisms, such as import
licensing, safeguards against surge in imports and anti-dumping measures, to provide protection to the domestic
industries, including small and cottage industries. The Director General of Safeguards has taken action in respect of  18
products for investigations.  And safeguard duty in respect of 10  cases have been  imposed.

Action Taken
 
1.12.2  Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides a single unified Act governing the rules pertaining to retrenchment and
lay-offs.  The Act also protects the vested rights of provisions relating to lay-off and retrenchments of workmen. 
Chapter VA of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides provisions relating to lay-off and retrenchment  of workman.
Lay off compensation is required to be paid by the employer to the workman laid off  in the industrial establishment
employing less than 50 workmen.  This Chapter also contains provisions that an industrial establishment employing on
an average more than 50 workmen is required to give 60 days notice before affecting closure.  The provisions of
retrenchment compensation equivalent to 15 days wages for every completed year of service by the workman and
principal of last come first go in case of retrenchment.
 
1.12.3  Under Chapter V B of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, prior permission is required by the industrial
establishments i.e. factory, mines and plantations wherein 100 or more workmen are employed before effecting lay-off,
retrenchment or closure.

ORISSA
Recommendation
 
3.0       A paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty
 
3.1       The Committee observes that Orissa demonstrates a paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty as the state,
despite having mineral and marine resources, has been bereft of sustainable industrial growth and economic
development.  The Committee finds that the cherished Charter of the Planning Commission which was “ to combine a
rapid rise in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing
production and offering opportunities to all for employment in the service of the community”, has not seen the light of

187th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/187threport.htm[04-07-2016 13:00:54]
the day in the state.  The state has been devoid of planned development giving rise to the economically backward district
like Bolangir, Koraput and above all the Kalahandi.
(Para 1.1.4)
Action Taken
 
3.1.1    The Parliamentary Standing Committee has observed that no major efforts have been made to put the State of
Orissa on the industrial development track and there has been lack of infrastructural development.  The state has been
devoid of development giving rise to the economically backward districts like Koraput, Bolangir & Kalahandi.
 
3.1.2    As far as Industrial Infrastructural Development is concerned, three Integrated Infrastructure Development (IID)
Centres have been sanctioned by SIDO under the Ministry of SSI in the State of Orissa under the scheme of IID.  One
IID Centre was sanctioned in the year 1996 in Distt. Rayagada and Distt. Jagatsinghpur.  The implementation of IID
Centre in Distt. Rayagada, which falls in the backward KBK (Koraput, Bolangir & Kalahandi) region of the State has
been slow due to poor response from entrepreneurs.  In order to publicise the IID Centre at Rayagada, the IDCO has
planned to organize an “Investors Meet” in the month of July,2005.  Regarding IID Centre at Paradeep.,
Distt.Jagatsinghpur, the implementing agency, IDCO is not in a position to implement the project because of the land
dispute and Court Case with Paradeep Port Trust.  IDCO has informed that case is likely to be decided by the Hon’ble
High Court soon.Apart from this, the Small Industries Service Institute, Cuttack has been directed to get in touch with
the Industries Department or the corporation concerned  of the State and advise them to set up IID Centres at
appropriate locations.
Further  Recommendation
 
3.1.3    The Committee, keeping in view the  prevailing economic standard  in Orissa and more specifically  the
backward  district  like  Koraput, Bolangir, and Kalahandi, reiterates  its view point that  Orissa is yet to be put  on
Industrial development track by  harnessing  the available raw material in each district  under integrated economic
planning  systems , if the vision as spelt out in the cherished  charter of planning commission  “to   combine a rapid rise
in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing production
and offering opportunities to all for employment in the service of the community”,  is to be realized .
 
3.1.4    As  regard the   existence  of three Industrial  Infrastructure Development (IID) sanctioned  by the SIDO  is
concerned , the Committee is of the view that where structural existence is not  going  to have any  meaning unless the
same has bearing  on the functional aspects and that too  empirically  result -oriented .  Therefore the Committee 
recommends that  the Ministry of SSI must  encourage the upcoming  SMEs  by the younger entrepreneurs through to
Seminar Investment Meet  and Conference to establish  small and medium enterprises in the state.  
 
Recommendation
 
3.2       Timely and adequate credit flow
 
3.2.1    The committee, therefore, is of the view that the financial institutions should come forward for providing timely
and adequate credit flow to the entrepreneurs for accelerated industrial growth and promotion of SMEs in the state.  The
Committee recommends that concerted efforts must be undertaken for popularization of venture capital, factoring
services and other financial linked schemes like CGYTSI, CLCSS,NEF and SME Fund of SIDBI.
(Para 1.1.6)
Action Taken
 
3.2.2    he Government and RBI/ SIDBI have initiated various measures with a view to improving the flow of credit to
the SSI sector. The SIDBI has been popularizing all the Government schemes in the State of Orissa particularly, Credit
Guarantee Scheme, CLCSS, NEF, TUFS and SME fund through meetings, seminars and press/ media.  Six active
industry associations viz., Utkal Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Confederation of Indian Industry, Orissa
Assembly of Small & Medium Enterprise, Orissa Small Scale Industries Association, Orissa Industries Federation,
Orissa Young Entrepreneurs Association are regularly informed about the details of the schemes and progress through
meetings and seminars.  About 40 project consultants and the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India,
Bhubaneshwar Chapter have been apprised of the schemes.  Besides, the potential entrepreneurs are made aware of the

schemes through EDPs supported by SIDBI and conducted by various organizations including SISI.  All DICs have
been apprised of the schemes directly and indirectly through the Director of Industries, Orissa.
 
3.2.3    Venture Capital Scheme was launched by SIDBI in October, 1992 and a separate VC fund with an initial corpus
of Rs. 10 crore was set up for the purpose. Further allocations to the corpus have been made on an annual basis from the
profits of the SIDBI. The fund was initially utilized for direct VC assistance to SSI units. Over the years, the focus
changed and in order to enlarge the reach for extending VC assistance to small scale units, SIDBI assumed the role of
“Fund of funds” by contributing to the corpus of National/Regional VC Funds for extending assistance to SSI units. So
far, SIDBI has committed an aggregate contribution of Rs. 450.82 crore to 14 All India Funds, 9 Regional Funds, 1
International Fund and Asset Management Companies/ Trustee Companies (AMC/TCs) of 5 VCFs.
 
3.2.4    The venture capital strategy of SIDBI has been to create a 3-tier venture capital structure viz., at the Regional,
National and International levels so as to effectively integrate and enhance the opportunities for the SMEs. Besides, in
order to keep a close watch on the functioning of the Asset Management Companies (AMCs), SIDBI started retaining
rights to take up equity stake in the AMCs and Trustee Companies (TCs). Further, SIDBI also extends venture capital
assistance to SSI units directly and by way of subscription to the corpus of other Venture Capital Funds. SIDBI has also
extended assistance for setting up of two incubation centres at IIT, Kanpur and BITS, Mesra, Ranchi.
 
3.2.5    In September, 1999, SIDBI created SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd. (SVCL) and SIDBI Trustee Company Ltd.
(STCL), as wholly owned subsidiaries of SIDBI primarily to be the Investment Manager and Trustee of the National
Venture Fund for Software and IT Industry (NFSIT) respectively. SVCL currently manages the Rs.100 crore NSFIT,
which has contributions from SIDBI (Rs.50 crore), Ministry of Communications and Information Technology,
Government of India (Rs.30 crore) and IDBI (Rs.20 crore). The entire fund corpus has been drawn by SVCL from the
contributors. SVCL works actively with its investee companies in implementing systems, MIS and corporate

3.2.5    In October, 2004, SIDBI launched a Rs. 500 crore venture capital fund for SMEs viz., SME Growth Fund (SGF)

technology, infrastructure related to services such as health care, logistics and distributions, etc. It is an 8-year close-
ended Venture Capital Fund.  As on 31
st March, 2005, over and above Rs. 100 crore from SIDBI, SGF has received
commitments for an aggregate amount of Rs. 400 crore from various banks, with which the fund has received
commitment for entire target corpus.  The Fund has started its operations and approved three investments aggregating
Rs. 26 crore in alternative fuels, pharmaceuticals and services company.  An amount of Rs. 10.50 crore has also been
disbursed in two of these companies. 
 
3.2.7    The Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries (CGTSI) has been taking steps to popularize the Credit
Guarantee Scheme by adopting a multi-level strategy. The SSI Associations as well as Branch Managers of Member

about the Scheme. In order to further popularize the scheme, a Workshop for the officials of SISIs and Commissionerate
/Directorate of Industries identified as Nodal Officers was conducted for familiarizing them with the features of Credit

Small and Medium Enterprises’ announced by the Government envisages special dispensation under the Credit
Guarantee Scheme for all (a) loans upto Rs. 2 lakh, (b) eligible women entrepreneurs and (c) eligible borrowers located
in the North Eastern region (including Sikkim) and Jammu and Kashmir.
           
Further  Recommendation
 
3.2.8    The action taken notes as furnished  by  the Ministry of SSI  shows the mirror –image of the  concerted efforts

level of the Member Banks/ Lending Institutions (MLIs) and encourage them to extend more collateral-free credit

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
A paradoxical picture of poverty amidst plenty
 
            The Committee, keeping in view the  prevailing economic standard  in Orissa and more specifically  the
backward  districts  like  Koraput, Bolangir, and Kalahandi, reiterates  its view point that  Orissa is yet to be put  on
Industrial development track by  harnessing  the available raw material in each district  under integrated economic
planning  systems , if the vision as spelt out in the cherished  charter of planning commission  “to   combine a rapid rise
in the Standard of living of the people by efficient exploitation of the resources of the country, increasing production
and offering opportunities to all for employment in the service of the community”,  is to be realized . (Para 3.1.3)
 
Industrial  Infrastructure Development (IID)
 
            As  regard the   existence  of three Industrial  Infrastructure Development (IID) sanctioned  by the SIDO  is
concerned , the Committee is of the view that where structural existence is not  going  to have any  meaning unless the
same has bearing  on the functional aspects and that too  empirically  result -oriented .  Therefore the Committee 
recommends that  the Ministry of SSI must  encourage the upcoming  SMEs  by the younger entrepreneurs through to
Seminar Investment Meet  and Conference to establish  small and medium enterprises in the state. (Para 3.1.4)
Timely and adequate credit flow
 
            The action taken notes as furnished  by  the Ministry of SSI  shows the mirror –image of the  concerted efforts
being undertaken by the  financial institutions for providing timely and adequate credit to the  entrepreneurs for  
accelerated  industrial growth and promotion of SMEs in the State of Orissa, however, the Committee feels  that all
existing institutional arrangements  and financial  facilities  as seems to being extended  to SMEs in general has yet   to
have visible  bearing on State’s  economy, as  the State  remains  deprived of planned development.  Such situation 
prevails  probably because we have elaborate institutional arrangement and large number of  schemes  on paper  but on
the ground realities the  situation/circumstances  remain entirely different.  Need  is to take  action  on  the  ground level

Promotion of Industrial Development through Cluster approach

Inviting  IIID scheme

Strive on the Part of each state to catch up with the globle pace to promote SMEs

leading economies of the world and  each Government  in world  is giving special impetus to the growth and

            The Committee is of the view that each State should make SWOT analysis of the prevailing SMEs in the state

in regard to progress made in implementation of  Industrial Policy   and its impact on the emergence of SMEs in the
state. (Para 3.14.10)
Formulation of district wise development strategy
 
            In regard to the Committee’s recommendation for formulation of district wise development strategy in each state
for promotion and proliferation of SSI units. The Committee does not merely mean the district-wise target under various
schemes for industrial development sponsored by State and Central Government  or the district-credit plan but chalking
out plan for massive action to boost the SMEs as per the distribution of raw material and opportunity for marketing
facilities and infrastructure.  For this, the Small Industries Service Institutes (SISIs) in the state has really to play pro-
active role in making awareness among the entrepreneurs of the first generation to undertake the SME activities. (Para
3.14.11)
 
Policy Package for stepping up credit to small and medium enterprises 
           
            While the Committee understands the merits of Policy Package for stepping up credit to small and medium
enterprises  but at the same time the Committee feels that  the policy has to be  implemented in letter  and spirit.  (Para
3.14.12)
 
Promotion and proliferation of  SMEs 
 
            The Committee is of the considered view that the Government should take up the issue of promotion and
proliferation of  SMEs  on the priority basis in economically  backward regions like Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and
Orissa  in order to tackle twin problems of unemployment and stark poverty prevailing in these states.   The impact of 
the various training programmes,  Market Development  Assistance schemes, credit facilities and the integrated
infrastructural development scheme  would be felt in real terms only when people of  the states  dwells in peace and
prosperity.
(Para 3.15.10)
 
Marketing assistance and export promotion
 
            The Committee finds that the action taken notes as furnished by the  Ministry of SSI merely enumerates policy
and programmes in operation but the ATN does not mention anything about chalking out action plan in the
economically backward regions for boosting SMEs  in the states.  The Ministry may categorically comment on the
committee’suggestion.(Para 3.16.6)

technological up-gradation in SSI sector.  The progress so far in the States of Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa,
Jharkhand, Maharashtra and Gujarat, as. (Para 3.17.1)

Inclusion of new product/sub- sectors and  improved technologies, sensitisation activities
 
The Committee notes  the comments of the Ministry  that the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme could not take off
in some states like Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa and Jharkhand since the general level of industrial activity
in the product groups/sub- sectors approved under the scheme is low for these States.   The Committee is in agreement 
with the view of the Ministry of SSI  that with the inclusion of new product/sub- sectors and  improved technologies,
sensitisation activities undertaken to popularise the scheme among various stakeholders in these States and general
improvement in the business environment would lead to improvement in the working of the credit linked capital subsidy
scheme but question arises by when in how.  The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the Government should come
out with growth promoting scheme having the potential of opening   venues for new opportunities.  Such schemes must
have effective implementing agencies at the field level.(Para 3.17.3)
Implementation of  the credit linked capital subsidy scheme
 
The Committee is of the view that the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) and the National Bank for
Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) should play pro-active and effective role in implementing the credit
linked capital subsidy scheme (CLCSS) for ensuring its success in the states of  Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh,
Orissa, Jharkhand, Maharashtra and Gujarat where the scheme has to be implemented for producing positive results. 
The Committee would like to know  the response of the SIDBI, NABARD and SISIs  in regard to the suggestion of

            The Committee would like to know the overall  impact of the efforts undertaken by the Ministry of Small Scale

Export Potential of SSI products
 
            The  Committee feels that  the process and product development is the essential  link in any business, be  it
