56.0     Credit Policy Package as announced by the Finance Minister on  10
th August  2005
 
56.1     The Committee was informed that a ‘Policy Package for Stepping up of Credit to Small and Medium Enterprises’ was placed before
the Parliament on August 10, 2005. Public Sector Banks will be advised to fix their own targets for funding SMEs in order to achieve a
minimum 20% year-on-year growth in credit to the SME sector.  The objective is to double the flow of credit from Rs.67,600 crore in 2004-
05 to Rs.1,35,000 crore to the SME sector by 2009-10, i.e. within a period of five years.  Public Sector Banks will be advised to follow a
transparent rating system with cost of credit being linked to the credit rating of the enterprise. The commercial banks (including regional rural
banks) with over 67,000 branches will make concerted efforts to provide credit cover on an average to at least 5 new tiny, small and medium
enterprises at each of their semi urban/ urban branches per year. Reserve Bank will issue detailed guidelines relating to debt restructuring
mechanism so as to ensure restructuring of debt of all eligible small and medium enterprises at terms which are not less favourable than the
Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) mechanism in the banking sector. A one-time settlement scheme to apply to small scale NPA accounts
in the books of the banks as on March 31, 2004 will be introduced.  The scheme will be in force up to March 31, 2006. In order to reduce the
cost of guarantee to the weaker segments of the borrowers, particularly tiny units, the CGTSI will be advised to reduce the one time guarantee
fee from 2.5% to 1.5% for all (i) loans up to Rs.2 lakh, (ii) eligible women entrepreneurs, and (iii) eligible borrowers located in the North
Eastern region (including Sikkim) and Jammu and Kashmir. Further, public sector banks will be encouraged to absorb the annual service fee
in excess of  0.25% in respect of guarantee for all (i) loans up to Rs.2 lakh, (ii) eligible women entrepreneurs, and (iii) eligible borrowers
located in the North Eastern region (including Sikkim) and Jammu and Kashmir. To broaden the financing options for infrastructure
development in clusters through public private partnership, SIDBI will formulate a scheme in consultation with the stakeholders. SIDBI has
already initiated the process of establishing Small Enterprises Financial Centres in select clusters.  Risk profile of each cluster would be
studied by a professional credit rating agency and such risk profile reports would be made available to commercial banks.  Each lead bank of
a district will consider adoption of at least one cluster. At the Regional Offices, the Reserve Bank will constitute empowered committees with
the Regional Director of the Reserve Bank as the Chairman to review the progress in SME financing and rehabilitation of sick small (SSI) and
medium units and to coordinate with other banks/ financial institutions and the State Governments in removing bottlenecks, if any, to ensure
smooth flow of credit to the sector.  The said regional level committees may decide on the need to have similar committees at cluster/district
levels.  Banks will ensure specialized SME branches in identified clusters/ centres with preponderance of small enterprises to enable the
entrepreneurs to have easy access to bank credit and to equip bank personnel to develop the requisite expertise.  The existing specialized   SSI
branches will be redesignated as SME branches. Boards of banks will be advised to review the progress in achieving the self-set targets as
also rehabilitation and restructuring of SME accounts on a quarterly basis to ensure that the required emphasis is given to this sector.  For
wider dissemination and easy accessibility, the policy guidelines formulated by Boards of banks as well as instructions/ guidelines issued by
Reserve Bank will be displayed on the respective websites of the Public Sector Banks as well as the website of SIDBI. The banks would also
be advised to prominently display all the facilities/schemes offered by them to the small entrepreneurs at each of their branches.

private sector banks/foreign banks/ RRBs respectively, advising them to implement the measures announced in the Policy Package. In line
with the Policy Package, the RBI has also circulated the guidelines on One-Time Settlement (OTS) Scheme for SME accounts to all the

57.0     Measures for SMEs friendly tax regime
 
57.1     In order to promote the small enterprises sector, certain fiscal measures need to be taken to establish a SSI-friendly tax regime.  These
include: Extension of General SSI Excise Exemption to SSI units manufacturing branded goods in urban areas, as available in rural areas;
Increase in the excise exemption from Rs.1 crore to Rs.1.25 crore to new as well as existing SSI units in rural as well as urban areas;  Lower
custom duties on import of raw material (basic raw material and intermediate goods) and higher duties on finished products;  Incentives to
facilitate exports by the small enterprises;  In order to induce small enterprises sector to undertake technology upgradation, excise and
customs duty relief / concession be provided to small enterprises on purchase of plant and machinery for technology upgradation;  Incentives
for ancillarisation so as to establish better linkages between the large and small enterprises
 
57.2     The Committee was given an understanding that the various taxes which affect the working of small scale units are excise duties,
customs duties, income tax, service tax, sales tax  (central sales tax as well as state level sales tax), octroi, stamp duties, local and municipal
taxes, etc. Some of the incentives/ exemptions which have helped in the growth of the SSI sector are (i) General SSI Excise Exemption
Scheme, (ii) Excise exemption on branded goods manufactured by SSI units located in rural areas, (iii) Tax holiday under the Income Tax Act
for new as well as existing small enterprises in the States of Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttaranchal and the North-eastern States, etc.
 
57.3     The prevailing pattern of tax structure for small enterprises sector, including the announcements made by the Finance Minister in the
Budget Speech relates to the  promotion of SSI sector. General SSI Excise Exemption upto Rs. 100 lakh on the first clearances of specified
goods during the year, for SSI units. Units availing of this exemption are not entitled to take CENVAT credit on the inputs or utilize the
CENVAT credit on capital goods. Clearances beyond Rs. 100 lakh are chargeable to duty at normal rate. Only those units whose aggregate
value of clearances in the preceding financial year has not exceeded Rs.400 lakh are eligible for the exemption. Excise exemption on branded
goods manufactured by SSI units located in rural areas.Tax holiday under the Income Tax Act for new and existing enterprises including SSI
enterprises in the States of Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttaranchal and North Eastern States and also the enterprises which go for substantial
expansion, i.e., increase in investment in Plant and Machinery by at least 50% of their book value.  Small service providers having gross
annual turnover less than Rs. 4 lakh have been exempted from the purview of service tax.Service tax on business auxiliary service has been
exempted for persons producing/ processing goods, from the inputs received from a manufacturer and sending the resultant product to the
same manufacturer for further manufacture of final products, which are cleared on payment of excise duty. An Advisory Committee set up to
advise the Government on the extent of abatement for excise duty and service tax. Peak rate of customs duty for non-agricultural products
reduced from 15% to 12.5%.
57.4     The Committee has been apprised that the announcements made by the Union Finance Minister in his Budget Speech 2006-07 would
have a positive impact on the SSI sector:  (a) recognize SMEs in the services sector, and treat the small scale enterprises in the services sector
on par with the small scale enterprises in the manufacture sector; (b) Raise the corpus of the Credit Guarantee Fund to Rs.2500 crore in five
years; (c) Advise Credit Guarantee Trust for Small Industries (CGTSI) to reduce the one time guarantee fee from 2.5 per cent to 1.5 per cent
for all loans; (d) Extend insurance cover to approximately 30,000 borrowers, identified as chief promoters, under the CGTSI. The sum assured
would be Rs.200,000 per beneficiary and the premium will be paid by CGTSI; and (e) The National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council
(NMCC) has finalized a five-year National Manufacturing Competitiveness Programme. Ten schemes have been drawn up including schemes
for promotion of ICT, mini tool rooms, design clinics and marketing support for SMEs. Implementation will be in the PPP model. 
 
57.5     The Committee, while taking note of the fiscal concessions being extended by the Government  to  facilitate  the sector in growing and
providing large scale employment. The Committee, however, is of the view that  to give a boost to the growth of the small enterprises sector
to generate employment at faster rate, the under-metioned tax-related measures may further be taken :
 
The General SSI Excise Exemption limit may be enhanced from Rs. 100 lakh to Rs. 125 lakh on the first clearance  of SSI units.
Increasing the SSI Turnover Eligibility Limit from Rs. 4 crore to Rs. 5 crore, for Availing of General SSI Excise Exemption benefit.
Restoration of option to pay Excise Duty at the rate of 60% along with CENVAT credit.
To allow excise exemption to SSI units manufacturing branded goods in urban areas, as available to the units set up in the rural areas.
Capital Gains Exemption to sick SSI units selling off Fixed Assets to repay their Bank Loans.
Exemption from Service Tax to SSI Units providing Business Auxiliary Services.
The limit of 15 days for payment of excise duty should be increased to 45 days for micro and tiny small enterprises.
SSI units having annual turn over up to Rs. 10 lakh be exempted from levy of service tax.

58.0     Impact of WTO provisions on various sectors of Small Scale Industries
 
58.1     The Committee was informed that Government is constantly assessing and monitoring the impact of the removal of Quantitative
Restrictions (QRs) and Globalisation on the growth and development of Small Scale Industries (SSIs) in the country.  Though removal of QRs
have exposed the SSIs to a greater competition, yet the SSI sector has continued to grow. However, even after the removal of QRs, protection
to the industries is available in the form of raising custom duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards
measures in case of surge in imports, etc.
 
58.2     Removal of QRs does not automatically remove all the protection available to the domestic producers.  India can regulate imports
through adjustments in tariff within the bound rates.  Apart from tariff, action under anti-dumping and safeguard measures can be taken to
provide protection to the domestic producers.  For initiating anti-dumping action and imposition of safeguard duty separate Directorates are
already working under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry   and the Ministry of Finance respectively. 
 
58.3     As on  31
st January, 2006 final anti-dumping duty has been imposed on 176 items, preliminary duty has been imposed on 02 items and
09 cases are under investigation.  DGAD has imposed final duties on dry batteries and sports goods after initiating suo moto investigations.
The Director General of Safeguards has taken up action in respect of 18 products for investigations.  So far, safeguard duties in respect of 10
cases have been imposed.  The Government is also in the process of amending   the provisions of Foreign Trade (Development and
Regulation) Act 1992 so that safeguard action in the form of QRs could be applied if there are sudden and massive imports. Government can
also specify standards, impose Sanitary and phyto-sanitary( SPS )measures and other conditions for reasons of public, plant & animal health,
security and public morality on goods entering India.
 
58.4     The Government has put in place several measures to help small enterprises become globally competitive.  These include special focus
on areas such as technology upgradation, infrastructure assistance through the cluster approach, timely availability of credit, adoption of
modern management practices, use of electronic infrastructure and other IT applications, marketing and timely information dissemination,
including sensitization of small industries to the emerging challenges of trade liberalization. 
 
58.5     The Committee is in agreement with the Government policy in the post QRs phase , to provide protection to the industries in the form
of raising custom duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of surge in imports which
would protect the domestic industries from the on- slaught of MNCs.  
Raising equity participation from the existing 24% to 49%  (FDI) in SSI sector

Ministry of Commerce & Industry, who do not have any such proposal at present.   However, the Steering Committee on FDI in various
Sectors, set up by the Planning Commission in August 2002, recommended enhancement of equity participation to 49% in SSI Sector, which
was discussed with the stakeholders.  Based on the discussions with the Stakeholders and others concerned, the following views were
communicated to the Department of IPP:
 
“ The Ministry has no objection to the enhancement of equity participation / FDI limit from 24% to 49% in the case of SSI items where
investment limit has been enhanced to Rs.5 crore.  FDI in this respect could perhaps be routed through the FIPB Type agency with

59.0     Country’s  Model of SSI Sector Stand today vis-a-vis model of SSI sectors
 
59.1     Our country  has been consistently following the policy of promotion and Development of Small Scale Industry Sector since
independence, in view of its higher employment potential, locational flexibility, low capital requirement and capacity to utilize local resources
and skills. Presently, an industrial undertaking in which the investment in fixed assets in plant & machinery (whether held on ownership terms
or on lease, or by hire-purchase) does not exceed  rupees one crore enjoys the status of Small Scale Industry.,  The model of SSI sector in the
country  includes inter-alia Tiny Enterprises, with investment in plant & machinery not exceeding 25 lacs and Small Scale Service And
Business (Industry Related) Enterprises with investment in fixed assets , excluding land & building, upto rupees 10 lacs .

61.       Recognizing SMEs in the service sector
61.1     In the recent years the services sector has emerged as a significant contributor  to the economy displaying a high rate of growth and
possibility of generation of employment for  millions of workers.  Therefore, it has become necessary, as is the practice worldwide, to address
the concerns of both the small scale industries and services together and recognize them as “small enterprises”.  As stated above, at present,
small scale industries have been dealt in the Industries (Development & Regulations) Act, [I(D&R)Act], 1951 in two sections.  However, this
Act also does not define “Medium Industries”.  Thus, neither “small enterprises” nor “medium enterprises” have been defined in any statutes.
 On the other hand, the worldwide practice today is to view “Small and Medium Enterprises” (SME) as a composite sector. Recognising this
fact, the Government has  drafted the Small and Medium Enterprises Development (SMED) Bill, 2005 which has been introduced in Lok
Sabha on 12 May 2005.  SMED Bill, 2005, inter alia, contains the definition of small enterprises and medium enterprises in clause 7. 
Detailed criteria for defining manufacturing sector and the services sector in both the categories i.e. small enterprises and medium enterprises
have been provided in this clause.  Treating the small scale enterprises in the services sector at par with small scale enterprises in the
manufacturing sector will facilitate fast growth of the services sector in India thereby improving the employment scenario and the GDP of our
country.  This would also enable the Government to plan and implement schemes/programmes for promoting the growth of the services
sector.
 
61.2     The Committee welcomes the announcement of the Finance Minister in the Budget  (2006-07) and treating the small scale enterprises
in the services sector on par with the small scale enterprises in the manufacturing sector. The Committee would like to know the   impact  and
implication of recognizing SMEs in the service sector.

informal sector as a result of forward and backward linkages in productive activities  . (Para : 41.24.1)
 
Investments in Public Enterprises
 
The Committee recommends that NSIC must be  guided by the Principle of Management by Objectives (MBO) . The Committee feels that in
order to ensure smooth credit flow to small enterprises, NSIC should  enter  into strategic alliances with commercial banks to facilitate long
term / working capital financing of the small enterprises across the country.

(Para : 42.5)
            The Committee feels that NSIC must be  able to implement the strategy of "Focused Sectoral Approach" i.e. up-grading identified
sectors in terms of the projects, business applications of the new technologies, quality control, packaging marketing and linking to the global
markets in order to meet the twin challenges of growth and competition of SMEs with human face. (Para : 42.11)
Tiny and Micro Enterprises
 
            The Committee is of the view that concrete  steps may be taken to strengthen and streamline the tiny sector and in order to give tiny
sector an organized outlook. The Committee finds that Small Scale Industries (SSIs) including tiny units in the country  have enough
competitive strength to withstand the impact of free imports and intense global competition.  Government should launch awareness
programme  of the WTO provision and international  environment for preparing the small scale sector including tiny sector to meet the
challenges of globalization. Government should  constantly monitor  the impact of the removal of QRs and WTO Agreements on the economy
including the SSIs in the country. The committee is aware that the removal of QRs have exposed the SSIs to a greater competition, yet the SSI
sector including tiny sector  is bound to grow.(Para : 43.3)
Mechanism of institutional arrangement
 
            The Committee is in agreement with  the the Finance Minister who has recognized  the  small scale industries as the engine of 
growth.  The committee is also of the view that  finance  to SSI must be treated as financing to  SME in order to give the SSI units to grow
into Medium Enterprises, therefore, recommends that concerted efforts step must be undertaken to meet the requirement of Small and
Medium Enterprises (SME). Adequate steps must be taken to promote and proliferate the  Medium Enterprises. And due incentive and
exemption be granted required for each the Small scale industries and the Medium enterprises. (Para : 44.5)
Institutional support in rehabilitation of Sick SSI units
 
                        The Committee is however, of the view that all for effective  rehabilitation of Sick SSI units and promotion of SSI Sectors  all
the Regional Offices of RBI should ensure that meetings of State Level Inter-Institutional Committee SLIICs are convened at regular
periodical intervals and the meetings are attended by the senior officials of banks/financial institutions so as to serve the desired objective.
The representatives of the local SSI Associations should also be invited to the meetings of SLIIC, which should play a major role in
rehabilitation of sick units. SLIICs should address the  issues regarding delay in carrying out viability studies and initiating nursing
programmes of viable units as also progress in revival of units, which have been placed under the nursing programme. Further, the issues
relating to the progress made in implementation of the revised guidelines issued by the RBI based on the recommendations of Kohli Working
Group must  be addressed  to ensure that the banks strictly follow these guidelines for detection of sickness at an early stage and take remedial
measures for speedy rehabilitation of sick SSI units identified as potentially viable. (Para : 45.2)
 
Sunrise industries in the SMEs sector
 
            The Committee desires that  suitable  steps may be  taken  to identify / address the problems being faced by the sunrise industries and
enhance the prospects of  the sunrise industries in the SMEs sector e.g. Information Technology (IT), Biotechnology (BT) Pharmaceuticals
and Nanotechnologies along with IT enabled services . The Committee desires that  suitable  steps must be  undertaken to reinforce
appropriate policy regime to promote sunrise SMEs industries which have the potential to be the winners of tomorrow.  The Committee
directs the Government that the issue such as IPR protection and management of rapid up-scaling of operations should be taken up on priority
basis.(Para : 46.6)
 Working of SME Development Fund
            The Committee understands that SME Development Fund promoted by SIDBI/banks with a corpus of Rs.500 crore aims at  funding 
export oriented and high technology SME. The Committee advises the Ministry of SSI to examine whether   there is the need to enhance the
said corpus fund to proliferate the SMEs, and if yes,  the strategy/ mechanism to support SMEs in knowledge-  based industries such as
Pharma, Bio-tech. and I.T. to this fund. The Committee would like to know the progress made in this regard during 2005-06 and the  steps
which may further be taken during the year 2006-07 contributing to  the accredited cluster which  can play catalytic role in the advancement
of SME sector.
(Para : 47.2)
Credit rating system for SSI unit or group of SSI units during the year 2006-07"
 
            The Committee welcomes  the  Credit Rating Agency for SMEs namely, SME Rating Agency of India Ltd. (SMERA) which  aims at
providing affordable, credible and independent ratings to the SMEs, and thus  would help enhancing their credibility and standing.(Para :
48.3)
Towards Technology upgradation
            The Committee understands that the technology upgradation of SSI  units is the most urgent requirement to do business in a
competitiveness environment". In this regard, the Committee welcomes the announcement of the  Finance Minister in his Budget Speech
(2006-07) that the “new thrust is towards up-scaling the size and technological upgradation”, therefore, the committee desire that the ministry
of SSI should undertake  the  to achieve the intention of Finance Minister in line with the recommendation of the Committee.(Para : 49.2)
Linkages between large and small enterprises   
 
            The Committee is of the view that the concrete  steps may be undertaken  to accelerate and strengthen the partnership approach to
develop linkages between large and small enterprises. Steps may also be taken for revitalization and regeneration of existing organization and

revamping  of existing organization and revamping of the mechanism for technological up gradation. The committee would like to know the
Status of R&D in technology up gradation further steps required for designing and Outcome of efforts towards cost-reduction in consequent to
the technological up gradation and steps being taken towards avoidance of waste and non-value adding activities. (Para : 50.3)
The Policy of Reservation
 
            The Committee notes the stand of the Government that  the Policy of Reservation discourages investment competition & Technology
up-gradation in the small sector. The Committee also takes note that  dereservation of 180 items, as announced in the Budget (2006-07)
would  help the small scale sector to meet the demand for technological upgradation, encourage research and development and make the
sector competitive to face the domestic and global competition. The committee would like to be apprised of the overall impact of the
dereservation of reserved items.(Para : 51.2)
Anti-dumping mechanism 
 
            The Committee would like to know the views  on the following issues along with progress made in regard to: -
 
Working of renewed provision in Indo-Nepal Treaty in Trade Transit in checking influx of chinese goods en-route Nepal during the years
2006-07;
Conversion of Quantitative restriction (QRs) into rationalised tariff regime for providing protection to the domestic SSIs;
Rationalisation of countervailing duties and safeguard duties to protect domestic producers in consonance  with WTO provision; and
Expeditious disposal of dumping cases are anti-dumping actions thereto, in view of almost all SSI products under open general license (OGL)
list.(Para : 52.2)
 
Working Group on rehabilitation of Sick units
 
            The Committee views that banks should carry  out specialized studies to ascertain the reasons for sickness so that suitable
rehabilitation measures can be drawn up for sick SSIs units. (Para : 53.3)
Sickness in SSI sector
 
            The Committee takes note of the information  from the RBI data on sickness in SSI sector, that  the number of sick units amongst SSI
has declined marginally from 1,38,811 in 2004 to 1,38,041 in 2005, however, the Committee observes that very little has been achieved in
regard to rehabilitations process , therefore, concrete steps are required to be taken.
(Para : 53.7)
Implementation Status of A.S. Ganguly's  recommendations in regard to credit flow to SSI sector by pubic sector Banks
            The Committee desires that the Government should implement the A.S. Ganguly's  recommendations in regard to credit flow to SSI
sector by pubic sector Banks to facilitate additional capacity generation, expansion of existing units and improving the capacity  utilization, 
diversification of products  and to enhance competitiveness of SSI sectors. 
 
(Para : 54.3)
Popularizing the  venture capital funding to SSI units
            The Committee is of the view that to encourage Venture Capital funding to SSI units, the banks must be  guided  by the RBI that
investment in venture capital will be eligible for inclusion in priority sector lending.(Para : 55.4.3)
Credit Policy Package as announced by the Finance Minister on  10
th August  2005
 
            The Committee welcomes the announcement of the Government for ‘Policy Package for stepping up of Credit to Small and Medium
Enterprises’ whereby the  Public Sector Banks have been advised to fix their own targets for funding SMEs in order to achieve a minimum
20% year-on-year growth in credit to the SME sector. The Committee notes that under policy package although   objective is to double the
flow of credit from Rs.67,600 crore in 2004-05 to Rs.1,35,000 crore to the SME sector by 2009-10, i.e. within a period of five years, the
committee feels that the Government needs to  do more in this regard to ensure the adequate credit to the SME sector. (Para : 56.3)
Measures for SMEs friendly tax regime
 
            The Committee, while taking note of the fiscal concessions being extended by the Government  to  facilitate  the sector in growing and
providing large scale employment. The Committee, however, is of the view that  to give a boost to the growth of the small enterprises sector
to generate employment at faster rate, the under-metioned tax-related measures may further be taken :
The General SSI Excise Exemption limit may be enhanced from Rs. 100 lakh to Rs. 125 lakh on the first clearance  of SSI units.
Increasing the SSI Turnover Eligibility Limit from Rs. 4 crore to Rs. 5 crore, for Availing of General SSI Excise Exemption benefit.
Restoration of option to pay Excise Duty at the rate of 60% along with CENVAT credit.
To allow excise exemption to SSI units manufacturing branded goods in urban areas, as available to the units set up in the rural areas.
Capital Gains Exemption to sick SSI units selling off Fixed Assets to repay their Bank Loans.
Exemption from Service Tax to SSI Units providing Business Auxiliary Services.
The limit of 15 days for payment of excise duty should be increased to 45 days for micro and tiny small enterprises.
SSI units having annual turn over up to Rs. 10 lakh be exempted from levy of service tax.(Para : 57.5)
Impact of WTO provisions on various sectors of Small Scale Industries
 
            The Committee is in agreement with the Government policy in the post QRs phase , to provide protection to the industries in the form

of raising custom duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of surge in imports which
would protect the domestic industries from the on- slaught of MNCs.  
Raising equity participation from the existing 24% to 49%  (FDI) in SSI sector (Para : 58.5)
 
Raising equity participation from the existing 24% to 49%  (FDI) in SSI sector
 
            The Committee desires that  the Government may consider the  proposal for raising equity participation from the existing 24% to 49% 
(FDI) in SSI sector for better technology transfer and further  FDI can be encouraged for sizeable investments towards larger returns give for
space to grow SEs out MEs.(Para : 58.10)
 
Country’s  Model of SSI Sector Stand today vis-a-vis model of SSI sectors
 
 
            The Committee is of the view that in the context of globalisation there is a growing trend to boost the SME sector, therefore,   country
should not lag behind in boosting the SMEs. There is the urgent need to provide adequate space for SSIs to grow into Medium enterprises.
Country  should   recognize the lower end of the industrial and enterprise segment of the economy as consisting of the SME sector as one
distinct entity requiring almost similar policy interventions. 
(Para : 59.3)
Policies for SME
 
            The Committee is of the view that there is the need for undertaking the initiatives like Small & Medium Enterprises Fund of SIDBI,
strengthening the institutional back up to be able to suggest, formulate, coordinate and ensure implementation of policies and programmes for
small and medium enterprise (SME) Sector. There is the need to  provide sensitization programmes in respect of the fast changing economic
scenario and ensure dissemination of information, cluster oriented Infrastructural development, trade specific measures, market assistance and
simplification of rules and regulations. Such   concrete initiatives must intends  for promotion and development of the SME Sector,  Service
enterprises, fast growing trades like IT, pharma, biotechnology, etc., needs special attention.  (Para : 60.2)
 
Recognizing SMEs in the service sector
 
            The Committee welcomes the announcement of the Finance Minister in the Budget  (2006-07) and treating the small scale enterprises
in the services sector on par with the small scale enterprises in the manufacturing sector. The Committee would like to know the   impact  and
implication of recognizing SMEs in the service sector. (Para : 61.2)
 
Promotion of  SMEs during the financial year 2006-07
 
            The Committee would like to know as to what steps are being envisaged to promote SMEs during the financial year 2006-07 in regard
to strengthening credit delivery system and support services agencies; net percentage of credit to Small Scale Industries  vis-a-vis the large
Scale Industriesand  the details of NPAs of SSI sector in comparison to large Scale Industries for last five years; Progress made in regard to
Restructuirng of State Financial Corporations (SFCs);  Steps revised to be taken for securtisation  of debt to enhance flow of additional credit
for SSI sector; Reinforcing Technology Bank for SME up gradation to facilitate technology transfer project evaluation, risks management
etc.;  Modalities of re-orienting the role of Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) for extending credit flow to rural Small Scale Industries; 
Programme for introducing and encouraging Laghu Udyog Credit Cards during the year 2005-06 ; Status and financial assistance extended to
Self Help Groups and Initiative for the promotion of Micro - Finance .(Para : 62.1 )

PREFACE
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Ninetieth Report on the Demand for
Grants (2006-2007) pertaining to the Department of Heavy Industries,  Ministry of  Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises.
2.         The Committee heard the oral evidence of the CMDs of four PSEs under the  Department of Heavy Industry, representatives of Auto Association and the Secretary and other representatives of Department
of Heavy Industry,  Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, on  the 12
th April, 2006.  This report of the Committee is based on the material supplied to it by the Ministry and other organizations and the
oral evidence tendered before it.
3.         The Committee in its meeting held on  22nd  May, 2006 considered and adopted the Report.
New Delhi:
22nd May, 2006;

Standing Committee on Industry
 
 
REPORT
 
Mandate of the Department of Heavy Industries
 
1.      Department of Heavy Industry is concerned with the development of Heavy Engineering/Electrical Industry, Auto Industry and administers 34 operating public sector enterprises.
 
2.      Department also administers two national level Institutes namely Fluid Control Research Institute at Palakkad and Automotive Research Association of India, Pune which cater to the needs of flow and
automotive Industry. This Department is also implementing a project on ‘National Automotive Testing and R&D infrastructure Project (NATRIP) through the NATIS, a society set up for this purpose.
 
3.
      Department of Heavy Industry has total 48 PSEs out of which 14 PSEs have either been closed or operations discontinued. Thus leaving the Department with 34 operating PSEs. Out of 34 operating PSEs,
13 PSEs made profit and remaining 21 made losses during the year 2005-06. The profit making PSEs made a profit of Rs.1578.55 crores and loss making PSEs made a loss of Rs. 1952 crores in 2005-06. The
anticipated overall loss for the year 2005-06 would be Rs. 373.45 crores.
 
4.
      However the Committee observes that of the aggregate profit of Rs. 1578.55 crores, the flagship BHEL alone earned a profit of Rs. 1472 crores. The Committee also recognizes that as per the target set by
DHI for year 2006-07, 9 more PSEs should start earning profit. And that the PSEs under DHI shall earn an overall profit of Rs. 497.86 crores as against the anticipated overall loss of Rs. 373.45 crores  in 2005-
06.
 
5.
      The Committee was informed that theRevival packages in respect of 9 PSEs as approved by the Government  till April 2006 on the basis of recommendations of BRPSE are as under:-

8.      The Committee was informed that the revival plans were being prepared in consultation with the PSEs as well as on recommendations of consultants appointed for this purpose. These revival plans are
further scrutinized by the Department and placed before BRPSE. BRPSE also makes a detailed appraisal and gives its recommendations after examining various projections made in the revival plan. Once the
revival plan is approved by the Government, an MOU is  signed with the management of the company based on the targets and expected revival in a specified time-frame. These MOU targets would be
reviewed regularly for monitoring and mid-course corrections which may be considered necessary.
 
9.
      The Committee observes that greater part of BRPSE approved Revival Plans includes waiver or conversion of previous loans and interest liabilities into equity and Government’s Guarantee for raising fresh
loan. However such Revival Plans do not elaborate other components that would be critical for sustainable revival like technology upgradation and absorption, enhancing marketing network, manpower training
etc. It may be recalled that previous revival efforts too pertained to similar cosmetic restructuring of financial liabilities and fresh assistance without realigning the PSEs to new market realities. As such previous
revival plans could not ensure the sustainability of revival. The Committee doubts whether these packages would be sustainable. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry of HI & PE to examine the
inclusion of these vital components in the revival packages  so that the Companies come out of protected regime and operate in the new market realities.
 
10.
  It however is  the considered view of the Committee that the revival plans pertained largely to financial reconstruction, and technology and marketing aspects are not contained in the revival plan approved
by the Government. As the nodal Department the DHI must monitor with the management of PSEs on these aspects of revival. The Committee would like to be informed of the steps taken by the DHI in this
regard.
 
11.
  The Committee cautions that DHI should bear the previous experiences in mind while assessing and ensuring the sustainability of revival. DHI  should  address the comprehensive restructuring of other
critical factors that have bearing over performance of a PSE. The Committee also suggests that the respective PSEs should be given financial targets to be achieved within a time frame.  
12.
  Moreover, in view of the details furnished by the DHI of the Planned capital expenditure,  the Committee wonders that such meager  infusion as the part of revival plan, would at all be sufficient to carry out
technological  upgradations and to realign  market network. The DHI may offer its comments on the issue.
 
13.
  As regards the cases of revival of such PSEs where Government approval was still pending, the Committee is informed thatlump sum provisions have been made in BE 2006-07 both on Plan as well as on
Non-plan side. The capital expenditure portion is likely to be met from the Plan allocations and other requirements  like loans for VRS, working capital etc. is to be met from the Non-plan side.
 
14.
  Regarding the Committee’s query whether PSEs were encouraged to raise resources by unlocking surplus assets and if Government had formulated any policy in this regard, the Committee was informed
that Government generally encourages PSEs to fund their revival plan from their own resources by either unlocking surplus assets or borrowings from banks/financial institutions. Government is providing
financial support only in those cases that neither have internal resources nor have the capacity to seek funds from external sources. However the Committee was not informed of any policy by the Government to
unlock the surplus assets of the PSEs. Though BRPSE had recommended 11 cases for the unlocking of surplus assets. 
 
15.
  The Committee strongly feels that the Government should come out with a transparent policy for unlocking of surplus assetss by the PSEs. The Committee feels that such a policy need to be uniform in
respect of all the CPSEs which fall under various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. If necessary the concerned State Government may be consulted before the formation of the policy on this

are major constraining factors. The PSEs still do not have marketing network so vital to retain the market niche and also to harness emerging. In absence of marketing network and strategy, the PSEs continue to
rely on Government and PSEs for orders, and have not been able to exploit new business opportunities in private sector and export market. In order to face the increased competition, the PSEs have been asking
for consolidation, merger or Joint Ventures with other PSEs. However, these aspects have not been included in the revival plans, whose focus is confined to the financial restructuring of the PSEs by infusion of
fresh capital or waiving off or restructuring the previous liabilities. Except for HEC, no other PSE has been asked to garner resources from internal sources by unlocking surplus assets. As a result the
Government has to make huge investment for the revival of these PSEs, who in turn have assured to earn a rather modest profit over next five years.
 
139.           The Committee seeks the elaborate response fro DHI of its observations, queries and suggestions in its ATN.
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
The Committee observes that greater part of BRPSE approved Revival Plans includes waiver or conversion of previous loans and interest liabilities into equity and Government’s Guarantee for raising fresh
loan. However such Revival Plans do not elaborate other components that would be critical for sustainable revival like technology upgradation and absorption, enhancing marketing network, manpower training
etc. It may be recalled that previous revival efforts too pertained to similar cosmetic restructuring of financial liabilities and fresh assistance without realigning the PSEs to new market realities. As such previous
revival plans could not ensure the sustainability of revival. The Committee doubts whether these packages would be sustainable. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry of HI & PE to examine the
inclusion of these vital components in the revival packages so that the Companies come out of protected regime and operate in the new market realities.
(para : 9)
It however is the considered view of the Committee that the revival plans pertained largely to financial reconstruction, and technology and marketing aspects are not contained in the revival plan approved
by the Government. As the nodal Department the DHI must monitor with the management of PSEs on  these aspects of revival. The Committee would like to be informed of the steps taken by the DHI in this
regard.
(para : 10)
The Committee cautions that DHI should bear the previous experiences in mind while assessing and ensuring the sustainability of revival. DHI  should address the comprehensive restructuring of other
critical factors that have bearing over performance of a PSE. The Committee also suggests that the respective PSEs should be given financial targets to be achieved within a time frame.  
(para : 11)
Moreover, in view of the details furnished by the DHI of the Planned capital expenditure,  the Committee wonders that such meager  infusion as the part of revival plan, would at all be sufficient to carry out
technological  upgradations and to realign  market network. The DHI may offer its comments on the issue.
(para : 12)
The Committee strongly feels that the Government should come out with a transparent policy for unlocking of surplus assetss by the PSEs. The Committee feels that such a policy need to be uniform in
respect of all the CPSEs which fall under various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. If necessary the concerned State Government may be consulted before the formation of the policy on this
issue with a view to have broad consensus. The Committee considers that in absence of a transparent policy, it would be difficult for the PSEs to generate resources by unlocking the surplus assets as it may
involve administrative issues and avoidable litigations.
(para : 15)
The Committee observes that considering that the Planned Capital expenditure is vital for a sustainable revival, and survivability of the PSEs, of the total required outlay of Rs. 1350.22 crores, a Budgetary
support of only Rs 450 crores has been given in the BE 2006-07.  The Committee wonders whether the PSEs would be able to generate the remaining Rs. 950.22 crores from non-Budgetary sources. The
Committee also wonders if the BRPSE has identified the potential sources  to generate balance funds from extra Budgetary sources. The Committee would like to have the DHI’s comments on the possibility of
such shortfalls in budgetary allocations which may result in derailing the recommended revival of the PSEs.   
(para : 19)
The Committee observes that of the total BE ( 2006-07) of  Rs. 905 crores, Rs 455 crores are Non-Planned expenditures meant for committed expenses. Of this Rs. 400 crores are meant to settle VRS and
statutory dues, salaries and wages. Though these are loans to begin with but the Committee also notes the abysmal record of PSEs in respect of Loan Repayment. The Committee finds it alarming that this
situation has remained for years. Even during the FY 2005-06, it is evident that while the Planned expenditure was enhanced only by Rs. 94 crores, the Non-Planned expenditure was enhanced by Rs. 116
crores. The non-Planned expenditure was increased to meet the salary dues of the PSEs.
(para : 32)
The Committee only wonders if the feeding the PSEs out of Budgetary support is sustainable practice.
(para : 33)
The Committee is constrained to note that in the several revival packages offering non-planned budgetary support for wages, salaries, VRS and other statutory dues did enable the loss making PSEs to turn
around but only marginally and temporarily. This could have been due to faulty and partial implementation of lop-sided revival plans. The Committee therefore cautions the Government to ensure the viability
before approving the revival plan and also strictly monitor its implementation. The Committee should be apprised of monitoring mechanism and the additional measures for successful implementation.
(para : 34)
 
The Committee observes that the Non-Planned expenditure has been higher than Planned Expenditure for last several years. Meaning thereby that the expenditure is much higher on the committed liabilities
as compared to new developmental and capacity-building initiatives under Government sponsored schemes. Even the committed liabilities reflected under Non-Planned expenditure, the majority of expenditure
has been going to meet on year to year basis the financial obligations incurred by PSEs. In view of the definition of Capital expenditure as provided by the DHI, the Committee only wonders if the lumpsum
allocations of Rs 400 crores to support to clear VRS dues and salary dues to the workers could at all be termed as Capital expenditure. The Committee desires that DHI may clarify the position.
(para : 35)
 
The Committee has not been furnished any information regarding the criteria on which any expenditure is approved by the Planning Commission and is reflected as Planned Expenditure where as other bulk
expenditures are shown as Non-Planned expenditures. The Committee desires to know whether such a division is random or based on any objective criteria.
(para : 36)
 
To consider the Cess as private sector’s contribution would be misrepresentation of fact. The Committee would like to know the initial mandate for which Cess was levied, and if the NATRIP is covered
within that mandate? The Committee is not in agreement with the DHI’s assertion calling NATRIP a joint project by public and private partnership. As is evident from the presentation given by the DHI, out of
the total investment of Rs. 1718 crores only Rs 118 crores would be contributed by the users from industry within three years, rest of the investment is to be made in one form or the other. The Committee feels

that the participation of industry should have been substantial to justify the public private partnership.
(para : 44)
For Rs. 47.4 crores required for the two-year pilot scheme for textile and machine tools sector only Rs. 1 lakh token amount has been allocated. No information has been given as to how the remaining
finance shall be garnered. Further Committee may be apprised of the method of identifying the beneficiary Units, delivery of funds and monitoring the performance of the scheme. The Committee would like to
know if the beneficiary would also include the private sector units.(para : 47)
The Committee notes the reduction in allocation for FCRI. The Committee is of the view that this project is vital R&D project and would require long-term committed allocations. The Committee therefore
feels that budgetary constraints should not come in the way. The Committee suggests that DHI may find out the ways to associate industry to meet the funds.(para : 50)
The Committee takes note of elaborate but protracted decision making procedure. However the DPR, as submitted in January 2006, broadly indicates the extent of expenditure to be incurred in the project.
Considering the relevance of the technology demonstrator project, requisite finances should have been earmarked in the BE 2006-07. Here again the Committee finds priorities of DHI flawed. The Committee
accordingly considers that such R&D projects must be catered with long-term committed finances instead of piecemeal allocations based on expeditious requirements.
(para : 51)
The Committee expresses its concern over the delay in sanctioning the project and  would like to know the factors that caused the delay to which the allocation could not be utilized in previous financial
year. Furthermore, the Committee would like to know the basis on which the allocations have been enhanced this year despite the fact the funds remained unutilized last year.(para : 55)
The Committee wonders if the beneficiaries of the previous year would be repeated this year too. The Committee is unable to comprehend the rationale behind having twin policies on VRS dues, one
through the huge lumpsum allocation and also by subsidizing the PSEs for raising resources to settle VRS dues from market.
(para : 59)
The Committee however does not appreciate waiver of loan or interest on the loan given to a PSE. The Committee is not sure whether this aspect is taken into account while extending loans to PSEs. The
Committee desires to know the circumstances under which such loans or interests thereon are waived. The Committee directs the re-examination of the whole issue and DHI should furnish a detailed note on the
issue while submitting the ATN.
(para : 64)
The Committee finds  that in view of the past experience when the Lump Sum allocations in the BE stage have remained unutilized till the last quarter of Financial year. Even in case of lump sum provision
of Rs. 95 crore in RE 2005-06 for restructuring of PSEs, only Rs. 27 crores could be spent till March 2006. The Committee also observed that of this lumpsum amonu a sizable Rs. 44.60 crores were re-
appropriated as non-planned expediture towards CCI.  And that  Rs. 2.70 crores have been surrendered at the advice of Ministry of Finance. The Committee wonders if any worthwhile capacity building of PSEs
been done as part of intended sustainable restructuring. Also observing the smaller amount that have been allocated to individual PSEs for restructuring, the Committee only wonders if the amount could have
raised from the market with requisite subsidies from the Government. The Committee should be apprised if the amounts given out of this lumpsum provision are loans or grants to the individual PSEs.
(para : 69)
The Committee notes with surprise that Rs. 44.60 crores meant for restructuring of CCI as Planned expenditure were re-appropriated to Non-Plan expenditure. The Committee feels that such steps are ad-
hoc and lack any long term strategy for prudent financial management. The Committee asks DHI to clarify under which rule or guideline, such re-appropriation was sought.(para : 70)
Committee observes that the sheer quantum of such non-planned expenditures for revival suggests that revival packages have focused largely on clearing the financial dues which the PSEs owe. Compared
to which the Lumpsum allocations for the restructuring the PSEs under Planned Capital Expenditures has been meager Rs. 87.82 crores this year which has been reduced from Rs. 95 crores.(para : 80)
The Committee also observes that of Rs. 250 crores for VRS/VSS only Rs 201 crores could be spent till the first week of March 2006. Of Rs 150 crores allocated in BE 2005-06 for revival and further
enhanced to Rs 266 crores in Second Supplementary Grant, only Rs 142 crores were spent till the first week of March 2006 of which Rs. 124 crores were spent in the second quarter of the Financial Year 2005-
06. With such uneven appropriation throughout the year and inability to actually spent the allocated money  almost till  the end of the Financial Year, the Committee wonders if there was at all a need to seek an
enhancementof Rs.166 crores in Second Supplementary Demands. The Committee therefore desires that in the ATN, the DHI may furnish the details of the actual expenditure.(para : 81)
The Committee feels strongly of the trend of creating such trench of undefined lumpsum allocations, which are released to clear the financial dues of the PSEs as and when required. Whereas, the capacity
building for sustainable restructuring remains low in priority as is evident from the allocations. (para : 82)
The Committee observes that the Engineering Industries are likely to generate internal and extra budgetary resources (IEBR) to the tune of Rs. 562 crores as compared to Rs. 241.49 crores in RE 2005-06.
Of this Rs. 440 crores will be generated by BHEL and Rs. 97.40 crores by BEML. However in cases of TCIL, REIL and SCI the  IEBR are likely to come down this year as compared to the RE 2005-06. The
Committee however expresses its concern that with most other PSEs are not earning enough IEBR, and their reliance over Budgetray support is likely to increase in coming years.  The Committee holds the
view that PSEs should be able to run on its own with only necessary minimal Budgetary support.
(para : 84)
The Committee feels that with the approval of revival plans the need for such undefined lumpsum allocations should have reduced. Instead the allocation for AMR has been increased. However the
Committee  would like to be apprised of the details of type of expenditures that were met out of the two lumpsum allocations for crucial balancing and AMR and the explanation as to why the allocations for
AMR was increased whereas allocations for crucial balancing were reduced since the revival plans were approved. (para : 95)
The Committee is distressed to note the plight of PSEs who can not pay the regular salaries to their employees and would like to know the PSEs that were given such support. Further, Committee is
bewildered by the complex procedure of decision making, where lumpsum allocations were made in the Budget in advance under presumption and the expenditure is decided later based on expediency. In such
a scenario it is obvious that the expenditure would neither be evenly distributed nor would it cater to any long-term strategy to evolve the PSEs.
 (para : 102)
The Committee is of the view  that the Government has been actually losing money given as  loans to PSEs. In several cases, eventually these loans were either waived or converted into equity, thereby
converting secure debt liability into an insecure liability. The Committee impresses upon the DHI to check this trend and to take appropriate steps to ensure the repayment of loans and interests thereon.
(para : 108)
The Committee observes that against the aggregate Paid up Capital of Government/ holding PSE to the tune of Rs 3911.96 crores, however the PSUs have accumulated loss of Rs 8795.24 crores with an
aggregate  negative net worth of Rs 5097.17 crores. The Committee apprehended that such a financial situation may eat up the modest profit, which PSEs are likely to earn this year.
(para : 111)
The Committee however noted that the efforts in the revival plans is to gradually reduce the losses and turn these companies into viable enterprises. To improve the Net worth of the PSEs the debt/loan
liabilities are being restructured as a part of revival plan. The Committee notes if such a pattern of assistance is sustainable for longer term and if it puts huge pressure on Government’s finances. The Committee
desires the DHI to find the way out.
(para : 112)
The Committee feels that the PSEs to become financially self-relient must harness the export opportunities to earn their own finances for revival.(para : 114)
 
The Committee observes that the order book position of the PSEs under the DHI has grown steadily over past few years. However the Committee expresses its serious apprehensions on the over dependence
on Government for orders.

Usage of Information Technology

of BRPSE, MOU Task Force, etc. It is also clear that  BRPSE only considers the revival package prepared by the

impresses upon the DPE to take initiative to formulate a uniform policy on the issue a nd if required, consult the 
State Government and other stakeholders.

68.       The Committee notes that the objective of the CRR scheme is to provide training to VRS optees so as to 
align them to the job market for a  gainful employmen t. A comparison between number of VRS optees and those 
actually redeployed after the being trained under CRR, reveals that the sc heme has not been effective in meeting 
this objective with only about 10% of the VRS optees actually getting redeployed. In such a scenario, manpowe r 
rationalization can only lead to wide-spread unemployment. Despite the fact that the Government is spending huge 
amount to settle the VRS and other stat utory dues of the rationalized employ ees, the entire pr ocess of man powe r 
rationalization appears to be precipitating social insecurities and unemployment among a productive section of the 
society. 
  
69.       The Committee feels that the DPE must study the experiences of other countries those have gone through 
the similar process of reforms. The Committee also re commends that with present performance where only about 
1/3 of the CRR beneficiaries actually ge t redeployment after training, there is  a huge scope of improvement in the 
present status of CRR schemes. 
  
70.            The Committee sought to know the process of selection of the nodal agencies to train CRR  beneficiaries and if there was any 
process of rating their performance.    
  
71.            The Committee was informed that the selection of Nodal agencies was done by a Committee  headed by the Developme nt 
Commissioner, SSI and represented by Ministry of Labour, Planning Commission,  Mi nistry of Finance and  Department of Public 
Enterprises. Nodal agencies are select ed based on institutional background, prof ile and activitie s carried out under simila r 
schemes/programmes, available facilities like faculties, infrastructure etc.  
  
72.            The performance of nodal agencies is dete rmined based on progress reports, wh ich includes figures on achievement against the 
assigned physical target and   redeployment of trained VRS  optees. 
  
73.       The Committee desires to know the ratings of the nodal agencies and the parameters of  their performance.
Further Committee observes that such tr aining should be imparted in the vicini ty of the existing parent company, 
so as to save the incidental costs that might prohibit the VRS optee to jo in the training. The Committee also 
observed that in several cases the location of such nodal agencies was not in the vici nity of the PSEs. Location o f 
the nodal agency should facilitate the VRS optees to take advantage of this scheme. The Committee desires if the 
parent PSE could invite the nodal agencies to conduct courses to train their employees.  
  
74.       Furthermore, the Committee wants to know  if the core competencies, skills and expertise of the personnel 
are considered before selecting the nodal agencies. Give n the poor performance in redeploying the trainees, the 
Committee apprehends that these critical issues are pe rhaps not given due importance while selecting the nodal 
agencies. Bearing such possibilities into considerati on the Committee has been impressing upon the DPE the need 
for some policy guidelines for regular skill upgradation and mid-career training for the supervisory staff and 
below. Such training will not only bene fit the PSEs but shall also enhan ce the professional prospects of its 
employees in case of VRS. The Committee seeks DPE’s comments on these issues.  
  
75.       The Committee sought further information on it s recommendation in its 168th Report  asking the DPE to 
pursue with Planning Commission to include the family of  the VRS optee in the coverage of CRR  scheme. The 
Committee on previous occasions had also suggested if th e CRR  schemes could be aligned with the Government 
sponsored employment programmes or entrepreneur development schemes.

retraining of dependents of VRS optees. Plan ning Commission has viewed that with the proposed modification in scope, the CRR  w ould 
be losing its focus on self-employment /redeployment of VR optees  apart from associated difficulties in monitoring of the programme.

2.         The Statement of Objects and Reason, states as under:
“The Cement Corporation of India Limited (CCI), being a public sector enterprise under the administrative control of
the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises (Department of Heavy Industry,), has become a sick industrial
company as defined under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 and a reference in respect of
which has been made to the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) during 1996.  The BIFR had
circulated  a Draft Rehabilitation Scheme(DRS) for revival of the CCI.  The DRS, inter alia, provide for closure and sale
of assets of the seven non-operating plants and expansion or modernization of the remaining three plants.  The assets of

one of the seven non-operating plants proposed to be closed, namely, the Charkhi Dadri Cement Plant in Haryana, were
acquired under the provisions of the Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act,

In view of the judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, in the Centre for Public Interest Litigation vs.  Union
of India, (2003) 7 SCC 532, it has been decided to suitably amend the Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. (Acquisition and
Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1981 so as to empower the CCI to close and dispose off the assets of the Charkhi Dadri
Cement Plant.”
 
 
3.         The Committee held three meetings to examine, consider and adopt the Bill. Ministry of Heavy Industries and
public Enterprises along with Cement Corporation of India explained the background and intent of the Bill in their
written and oral presentations before the Committee.
 
While examining the Bill, the Committee availed the opportunity to assess the performance of the Cement Corporation
of India Ltd. as the Bill has a critical bearing over the overall rehabilitation of the CCI.
Cement Corporation of India
In the presentation before the Committee, the CCI informed that the Company was established in January 1965 with
Paid up Capital of Rs. 446.82 crores 100% owned by Government of India.  However, by 31
st March 2006 the Company
had accumulated losses of Rs. 1321.02 crores which reduced its net worth to negative to the tune of of Rs. 874.20
crores.    At present the Company owns ten units of which only three units at Bokajan, Rajban and Tandur are
operational remaining seven units at Mandhar, Kurkunta, Naya Gaun, Akaltara, Adilabad, Charkhi Dadri and Delhi
Grinding Units have been  rendered non-operational since long.  As such of the total install capacity of 38.48 LMT, CCI
has only 36% (13.96 LMT) capacity as operative, where as remaining 64% (24.52 LMT) capacity is lying idle.  In any
case the CCIs installed capacity is meager 2.6% of the total installed capacity in the country. 
 
 
The Committee was informed that obsolete technology rendered CCI units inefficient and un-economical in a
competitive market. Plants were some thirty years old. Of the authorized capital of Rs. 700 crores, total equity capital of
Rs. 446.82 crores has been invested in the Company over a period of some 40 years. The Committee   notes that where
as Government had been injecting Non-Planned Funds to pay salary and other dues, no concerted Planned expenditure
was made to modernize these Plants.
 
 
In its written presentation, the Committee was informed that the  CCI was referred to BIFR in  1995 after its net worth
eroded and was declared sick in August, 1996.  In June, 1998,  BIFR circulated first Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (DRS)
with a proposed cost of some Rs.41.60 crores of which Rs. 35 crores were for the planned expenditure and remaining
Rs.6.60 crores were meant to clear the VRS dues.  However, Government of India did not make commitment and the
DRS lapsed.
 
The Second DRS was formulated in 1999 which projected the rehabilitation cost at Rs. 109 crores but was allowed to
lapse due to not commitment.
 
In March 2001, the process of sale for CCI was initiated. SBI Caps was  appointed as the Merchant Banker by IFCI, the
operating agency. However in response  to the Globel Tender,   only two bids were received for the Rajban Plant.  No
bid for other plants was received.  Even the two bids for the Rajban unit were below the reserved price and therefore no
sale could take place.
 
Subsequently, M/s Holtec and M/s NCMB were appointed consultants in September, 2004 to conduct the techno-
economic studies.  The recommendations of the consultants have been assessed at various levels by BIFR, BRPSE and
Committee of Secretaries.   Based on these recommendations the revival scheme for CCI was approved by the Union
Cabinet in March, 2006 and subsequently by BIFR in May, 2006.

The Committee was informed that the BRPSE even considered feasibility of a Joint Venture as a probable method for
the rehabilitation of CCI. The proposal eventually was not found feasible.
 
The Committee noted that with such financial situation, the Board of the Company did not have much options left but to
accept the DRS as approved by the BIFR. The Board of CCI in its 273
rd and 278th meetings accepted the DRS.
 
As per the revival scheme, the seven non-operative units of the CCI are to be closed and sold as per the valuation done
by Asset Sale Committee constituted by BIFR.  The revival scheme also envisages the expansion and modernization of
remaining three operational plants at Bokanjan, Tandur and Rajban with estimated cost of Rs. 141.11 crores.  The
revival scheme includes waiver of outstanding interest dues of Rs. 886.22 crores on the Government of India loans and
conversion of GOI loan of Rs. 355.43 crores into share capital.  It further seeks to freeze the interest on outstanding GOI
loan beyond March, 2005.  In addition to restructuring the previous liabilities, the revival scheme recommends a fresh
planned assistance of Rs. 30.67 crores for the expansion and modernization of operational units and also a renewed non-
plan loan of Rs. 153.62 crores to clear the outstanding dues towards creditors and VRS dues of employees. In addition
to this revival package, the Government has already provided a budgetary support of Rs. 176.30 crores over the years
for the payment of salary and other dues in non-functional units.
 
In its written reply to the Committee, the Ministry informed that after such costly rehabilitation, the capacity of
functional units will increase from present 1.39 lakh MT/ annum to 1.64 lakh MT/annum.
 
The Committee was informed that the CCI expects Rs. 617.76 crores as sale proceeds of its seven non-functional units.
Of this only Rs 141.11 crores will be used for modernization and expansion, remaining Rs. 476.65 crores will be used to
settle the dues.
 
The Committee takes serious view of the massive cost of delay in implementing the revival scheme.   The revival which
could have cost only Rs. 41.60 crores in 1998, has now swollen to Rs. 1577.05 crores in 2006.  This cost will
rehabilitate only three of the currently operational units.  For six years the losses and liabilities have been allowed to
accumulate whereas assets have eroded during the same period. With a negative net worth of the Company, a major part
of the sale proceeds of the seven units are likely to be used in settling the old dues instead of funding upgradation and
expansion of the remaining units. This fact is corroborated by the representatives of the CCI, who confirmed that only
Rs. 141.11 crores will be used for expansion and modernization out total Rs. 617.76 crores as probable sale proceeds.
And only 0.25 lakh MT of additional capacity will be added to the three operational plants. The remaining fund that
could have been used for capital expenditure will be used in settling the dues that have mounted due to delay.   On the
other hand, as a part of rehabilitation, the Government will be required to infuse another Rs. 30.67 crores for capital
expenditure and shall have to waive its dues worth  Rs. 1250 crores.  The Committee finds it alarming waste of
resources.  It is alarming that this wastage took place despite the fact that the Government held 100% of equity stake in
the Company. In view of the Government’s ownership of the CCI, the Committee specifically asked the Ministry about
the views and opinions of the Government Directors on the Board of CCI during the loss making years. However no
specific reply was provided by the Ministry on this specific query. Neither any accountability has been fixed for such
situation.
 
The Committee expresses its  apprehension that if most of the sale proceed are to be spent on settling previous dues
instead of expanding prospective business, there was only a limited chance of long term viability of CCI even after such
rehabilitation, as there will be only a very limited addition in the capacity. The Committee observes that the
Government should take a view of the current trends in the cement sector, where private players were expanding their
capacities, acquiring new plants and even global cement giants picking up stakes in Indian cement sector. In competition
with such players the CCI, with its limited capacity will remain untenable and may eventually seek Budgetary support
from the Government.
The Committee recommends that the Government must take into account the current trends and prospects in cement
sector and also factor  above mentioned facts while disposing off the seven non-operational units of the CCI and should
try to maximize the sale proceeds of these units.

Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited
In a written reply by the Ministry the Committee was informed regarding the circumstances under which the Dalmia
Dadri Cement Ltd. was acquired by the Government of India in 1981. The Company was rendered non-functional in
March, 1980, and the case for its liquidation was pending before High Court of Punjab and Haryana. The Government
of India had however acquired it with a view of securing proper management so as to serve the interest of general public
by ensuring the continued manufacture, production and distribution of Cement. 
After acquisition in 1981 by Government of India the unit was actually commissioned in May,1982.  The Government
incurred a rehabilitation cost of Rs. 2.51 crores.  The original installed capacity of the unit was 1.74 lakh MT per
annum. The unit has 201 acres of land for its factory and township.   It also has 1232.77 acres of leased mines.
However, the objective with which the Units was acquired, was defeated   within four years of its acquisition as the unit
started incurring losses  from 1985 and was eventually rendered non-operational in 1996.  Till 31
st March, 2006 the unit
had accumulated losses of Rs. 130.93 crores.  It is paying Rs. 5.43 lakhs monthly in idle wages to 25 regular employees.
During its examination the Committee sought to know the circumstances under which the units started incurring losses
within four years off its acquisition.   The Committee was informed that the poor quality of limestone and the semi dry
process of production were the two major causes which had major bearing over the performance of the unit.   The
Committee was informed that as the conversion to dry process entailed huge investment, therefore Government did not
consider it feasible to convert the Unit to Dry process, though it should have been more efficient process.
The Committee observes that the Government had not assessed quality of the limestone prior to Unit’s acquisition, an
omission that eventually had a critical bearing over its financial viability.
The Committee however recommends Asset Sale Committee should re-assess the valuation of the plant and the land of
the Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd.  in transparent manner.   In context of prevailing price of land in that region and the
current growth in the Cement sector.
The Committee recommends that the Government should consider these observations of the Committee while disposing
of Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. under the provision of proposed Amendment Bill.

Recommendation in 178th Report
 
1.         The Committee observes that since their inception the CPSEs had initiated a wave of industrialization in their adjoining region. The CPSEs
were direct mainstay for several small  scale ancillaries and supplies and many more indirectly. These Units had thrived on the orders from CPSEs.
The Committee is of the view that if the trend could continue this would have benefited both parent company and the ancillary units.
(Para 27)
Action Taken Report
 
2.         Originally, Ancillaries were established as suppliers for components to mother factories during 1960-70’s when manufacturing was at its
infancy in the country.
 
3.         Manufacturing industry started growing from 1980 onwards, with industries being set up viz, State Government Assisted, Small Scale and
Private Enterprises as small and medium Units. The larger units (automobile or capital goods like Machine Tools etc.) in turn commenced sourcing
their requirement of components and assemblies from these units, also, in order to obtain competitive process and advanced technology.
 
4.         Today the Small Scale Units, other than Ancillary Units established in the country have taken a lead to upgrade and equip their facilities with
modern high-tech machines viz, CNC machines, adopting processes and manufacturing methods that have significantly reduced the cost of
manufacture.
 
5.         Simultaneously with   this development, the requirements of the mother Industries’ also changed and in order to compete effectively the large
industries shifted to products of higher standards and higher technologies that require higher quality parts, in low volumes with shortened  deliveries.
 
6.         While these transformations were taking place the Ancillaries failed to upgrade the manufacturing facilities and with their existing old units
and machinery are able to take up only primary machining operations on the raw material supplied by the mother factories and are not in a position to
supply the high quality components required by the manufacturing industries.
 
7.         Today outsourcing has permeated to such an extent that finished components ready for assembly, are available. This has been the primary
reason for the shift that has taken place in out-sourcing by mother industries from Ancillary to other small scale and medium industries.
 
8.         However, the Ancillaries are still being supported by mother industries to the extent they are able to supply high quality parts. In addition to
the above mother factories have been providing technology support by way of engineering, inspection etc. despite the limitation for utilizing the
services of ancillaries as on date.
 
Further Recommendation of the Committee
 
9.         The Committee acknowledges the efforts made by the mother CPSEs to enable the ancillaries to meet their requirements. The Committee also
impresses upon the ancillaries to upgrade technologically and diversify their products and market profile so that the CPSE does not suffer due to the
drawbacks of ancillaries. The Committee is of the view that   in a competitive and open market, the CPSE is entitled to minimize its cost to remain
competitive, yet efforts should be made to utilize these  existing facilities by upgrading them.

1.         Considering the resource requirement of the HMT for its revival and the Committee’s consistent   emphasis on need to encourage the CPSE to
generate their own resources to assume full autonomy, also appreciating the long association of ancillaries with their present HMT Company and
taking a view of their offer to purchase the sheds at the price ascertained by State Government agency TECSOK as against the market prices which is
demanded by the HMT,  the Committee recommends that the CMD of the HMT, in exercise of the powers vested  in him, on taking a lenient and
favourable view  on demand of the ancillary owners, constitute a sub-committee in the Board of Directors to review the issue in consultation with
stakeholders within the parameters  of the Company’s financial requirements, such sub- committee should furnish its report to the Board of Directors
of the Company with in a time frame who may then take a final view on the issue in its earliest meeting.

Director, HMT Machine Tools, Company Secretary and the Chief of Asset Management to examine all the relevant issues concerning the demands of
the HMT Ancillary Units Entrepreneur’s Association including the transfer of the industrial sheds. The Committee has submitted its report which was
