              The P.E.S.B was set up with the objective of evolving a sound managerial policy for the Central Public Sector Enterprises and, in particular, to
advise Government on appointments to their top management posts.  While taking cognizance of the current composition of the PESB, the Committee
observes PESB too has been reduced to a parking bay for retired bureaucrats.
 
64.
              The Committee feels that the objective is not likely to be achieved as is evident from the current composition of PESB which is not at all in tune
with the spirit of the objective.  The Committee desires the Government to ensure that Board is constituted accordingly. 
 
65.              The Committee finds the nuanced interpretation of rules and provisions to accommodate certain groups of people as downright subversion of the
policy intent and in contradiction with its mandated autonomy. Behind the window-dressing of autonomy, the Government servants try to retain their
pre-eminence at every stage of selection in PSEs.
Government Directors
 
66.
              While the Guidelines propose that maximum two Government Directors could join the Board of Directors of a PSE, only in such cases where
the stakes of more than one Government agencies were involved, the Committee observes that the presence of Government Directors in maximum
permissible strength of two or often more than two is in gross violation of the guidelines. In almost all the cases, the Committee observes that both the
Government Directors belonged to same Ministry/ Department and in several cases the representatives of other Government agencies too were included
as Government Directors over and above this limit in gross violation of policy provision.  The Committee dismisses the argument that the Financial
Advisor of the Ministry being representative of the Ministry of Finance and as such can not be considered as representing the Ministry. The Committee
finds such argument too nuanced to be of any merit. The Committee recommends that this practice must be dispensed with urgently.
 
67.
              The Committee also finds the presence of Government Directors without any expertise relevant for the Sector. The Government Directors do not
have the academic or professional expertise required to independently discharge the onerous responsibilities required by the assignment. The Committee
finds such practice patently contradictory to the objective of Professionalisation  of Boards. The Committee recommends that notwithstanding their
assignments in the Administrative Ministry or Department, relevant expertise should be made mandatory for the Government Directors.  Government
Directors, in view of the Committee do not passively represent the Ministry or Department but should also actively espouse the interest of their
respective PSEs.  Government Directors should act independently as the Directors of the PSEs and should have the knowledge of its business scenario in
domestic and international markets and align the Company’s business with the Government’s policies, RBI’s regulations and the statutory requirements.
 
68.
              Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the Government must take actionable measures on the recommendations and observations of the
Ad Hoc Group of Experts on the Empowerment of CPSEs. The Committee is in agreement with recommendations of the Ad Hoc Group of Experts that
the Ministries should not communicate directly or indirectly with the managements of the CPSEs instead they should communicate through the Boards
of Directors.  Subject to Government policy, RBI guidelines and the statutory requirements, the Board of Directors should have powers to pursue
independent business line.  
 
69.
              The Committee is of the view that as Government is entitled to safeguard its investments in the CPSEs and the returns thereon, the Ministry or
Department should be represented with Financial Advisor on the Boards of the PSE. Presence of another representative concerned with the PSE in the
Ministry, is not required as the obligations of the PSE and the Administrative Ministry are clearly defined in the MoU.  Any interference in the routine
commercial, corporate or HR policy by the Ministry through its representative Director on the Board of Directors should amount to undermining of such
MoU.
Independent Directors
 
70.
              The Committee was informed by the Secretary, DPE that till October 2006 there were 200 posts of CMDs, 469 post of Functional Directors and
700 positions of Independent Directors of which only 240 were in position. Of the remaining 460 vacancies recommendations for about 250 positions
have been made and were at various stages of approval. Still action to fill up remaining 210 vacancies needs to be initiated expediently.  The Committee
impresses upon the DPE that it should actively pursue with the concerned Ministries and ensure that remaining vacancies are filled up expeditiously. 
The Committee directs the DPE to apprise the progress made in this regard. 
 
71.
              The Committee is particularly concerned about the Ministries’ reluctance in filling up the requisite vacancies of the Independent Directors in the
Boards of Directors of the CPSEs. The Committee during its interactions with the Ministries repeatedly encountered lame alibis for delays in
appointment of such Directors. It was observed by the Committee that the Ministries or Departments have not appointed Independent Directors for years
together.
 
72.
              Even in such cases where the selection process was underway, the procedural complexities and layers of approvals have led to delays. The
Committee was informed in response to its recommendations in 168 th Report that necessary directions had been duly reiterated by the Department of
Public Enterprises to the Administrative Ministries/Departments.  However the Committee was constrained to note during its interactions the abysmal
performance of the Administrative Ministries and Departments in following up with the repeated exhortations by the Department of Public Enterprises
and this Committee, to initiate the process of selection for the forthcoming vacancies in time.  The Committee strongly feels that there is a need to
streamline the procedure.  DPE must assess which are the stages of approval that are most time consuming and if layer of approvals could be reduced.
The DPE may also consider framing sector-wise panels or database of such professionals who could join the Boards as Independent Directors.
 
73.
              The Committee feels there is an obvious reluctance on the part of the administrative Ministries or Departments to dilute their control over the
PSEs. In view of the reluctance on the part of the Administrative Ministries or Departments in implementing the guidelines in respect of appointments of
independent directors, the Committee recommends that the DPE must assume a more pro-active role in ensuring the timely appointment of appropriate
Independent Directors, instead of remaining a hapless mute spectator. The Committee recommends that the Government should come out with the

198th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/198th%20Report%20of%20Committee%20on%20Industry.htm[04-07-2016 13:08:09]
guidelines empowering the DPE not merely to take proactive role in the earnest implementation of this Policy but also monitor religiously.  The
Committee directs the DPE to furnish the report to the Committee where delay takes place in appointment alongwith reasons therefore. 
 
74.              The Committee’s view is further strengthened by the fact that as against the professed objective to professionalise the Boards to make them
independent of the respective Ministries or Departments, in most of the cases the Independent Directors were retired bureaucrats, Government servants
or former Executives. In most of the cases, the retired Government servants had no proven expertise relevant for the Company. The Committee finds
that such state patently contradicts the very objective of this policy.
 
75.
              A perusal of the Database of Independent Directors compiled by the Department of Public Enterprises shows conspicuous predominance of
former bureaucrats and retired CPSE Executives in this   database. The Database is a sure evidence of Department’s reluctance in reaching out to a
wider spectrum of talented professionals and attracts them to join CPSEs as its Independent Directors, the Committee observes.  The Committee directs
the DPE to be more proactive in reaching out to a wider spectrum of talented professionals. 
 
76.
              The Committee had observed in its 168 th Report that the minimum educational criterion for the Independent Directors has been very basic to
render any professional expertise.  The Committee had therefore recommended to raise the minimum educational qualification to the Post Graduate
Degree/Diploma from a premier institution in a professional course. Regarding the CMDs and MDs joining the Boards of PSEs, the Committee had
recommended that the size of the corporate body should be specified. The Committee further recommends that the CMDs/MDs of only listed corporate
entities should be considered as Independent Directors.  Further, former bureaucrats with ten year of more experience as Joint Secretary and above are
eligible to become the Independent Director. The Committee reiterates its view that a Joint Secretary belongs to a generalized service and may not have
expertise required of an Independent Director of a PSE unless he has experience in the field relevant to the PSE. The Committee therefore asks DPE to
modify the eligibility criteria.
 
77.
              Further, the Committee finds it  remarkable that majority of Independent Directors were towards the higher limit of the permissible age-band of
45-65 years, indicating that they were appointed Independent Directors only upon attaining the superannuation in their respective careers.  Even a survey
of the Database for Independent Directors compiled by the DPE, indicates predominance of only such candidates. The Committee wonders if this was
the objective of the Policy of Professionalisation  to make the Boards of Directors the parking lot for retired government servants.  The Committee
recommends that the Ministries/Departments should appoint younger professionals from non-Governmental agencies as Independent Directors.
 
78.
              The Committee considers it to be yet another evidence of Government’s preference for Government Servants. It was with this objective that the
Committee in its 168th Report had suggested to reduce the maximum age limit to 60 years, which is also the age of superannuation in Government.  The
Committee reiterates its recommendation. 
 
79.
              The Committee also observes that in several cases the term of Independent Directors was renewed.  The Department of Public Enterprises has
chosen not to act upon the Committee’s previous recommendations para 21.5 of 168 th Report.  The DPE has neither informed the Committee of the
sound logic behind not accepting its recommendations in this regard.  The Committee impresses upon the Government to review the guidelines and
inform the Committee of the decisions along with the reasons.  The Committee views such renewal as another manifestation of reluctance on the part of
Ministries or Departments to allow a broader and wider talent to join CPSEs Boards as Independent Directors.
 
80.
              In its 168th Report (para 21.5) Committee, while commenting upon the appointment of former bureaucrats in the boards of PSU as independent
director also their re-appointment, observed that such arrangement falls short of spirit of objective of the policy.  The Committee urged the DPE to
ascertain the implementation of the policy in consonance with its true objectives. Having considered the reply of DPE to this recommendation, the
Committee in its 179th Report observed that the reply lacked earnestness in implementing the spirit. 
 
81.              In their further reply to the Committee’s observation, the DPE informed the Committee that of 145 recommendations made by the Search
Committee during last two years, 100 were academicians/technocrats/professionals/former PSE executives/ CAs or Private Sector experts, Similarly, of
the 105 names recommended by the PSEB, 65 persons belonged to these categories.  The existing Independent Directors can be re-appointed for another
term depending on specific need of the CPSE, provided they continue to fulfil the laid down eligibility conditions and their name is proposed again by
the concerned Administrative Ministry/Department is recommended by the Search Committee/PESB and is approved by the competent authority. 
However, the Committee is not convinced with the reply by the Department regarding the renewal of term of the independent Directors. The Committee
reiterates its recommendation in its 168th Report that the term of independent Directors should not be renewed and fresh professional expertise should be
given chance as independent Directors. 
 
82.
              The Committee while acknowledges some representations of the academicians and management professionals on the Boards, yet there was
virtually negligible representation of the corporate sector.
 
83.
              In an era of close cooperation between private and public sectors, and considering the recent global acquisitions by the Indian companies, the
Committee finds it an imperative that the Directors of the Companies should have much broader vision of the global trade. The repeated exhortation of
public-private partnership should actually be reflected in the structure and functioning of the Boards of  CPSEs.
 
84.
              While the Committee does not wish to preclude any group from becoming the Independent Director, it certainly expresses its serious reservation
over predominance of former bureaucrats and the executives of the PSEs, at the cost of a larger spectrum of professionals. The committee, therefore,
desires the Government to explore availability of talent from a wider spectrum of larger society. In respect of selection of the Independent Directors the
Government should not confine its choice largely to a select group of retired persons but include young entrepreneurs and professionals and if required,
revise the guidelines.
 
85.
              Delay in appointment or not filling up the posts of Independent Director for considerable period of time has been the concern of Committee

constantly.  The Committee noted that the Administrative Ministries and Departments are actually responsible for it.  The Committee accordingly
recommends that they must assume a more pro-active role in ensuring the timely appointment of appropriate Independent Directors. The Committee
strongly feels that in the case of non-compliance of guidelines, DPE should take appropriate action.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should come out with the guidelines empowering the DPE to take even punitive measures against the respective PSUs for the earnest
implementation of this Policy.
 
86.
              The Committee acknowledges the initiative taken by the Ministry of Company Affairs in setting up the National Foundation for Corporate
Governance, which should organize intensive training programmes for the Independent Directors. In this respect the Directors Certification Programmes
organized by the SCOPE, Academy of Corporate Governance and the DPE, could be useful. The Committee recommends that such Certification should
be also made mandatory for the Government Directors.
 
87.
              The Committee is in agreement with the recommendation of the Ad-hoc group of Experts for Empowerment of CPSEs that some mechanism
must be created to monitor and assess the performance and contribution made by the Independent Directors.
 
88.
              The Committee takes note of the broader dynamics in Indian corporate sector with which the PSEs have to compete to survive even in the
domestic market. The Committee also acknowledges the buoyancy in the PSEs in those sectors that have been opened up for private sector and where
the PSEs have been granted greater autonomy. In an era when Indian industries are charting out larger Joint ventures, mergers and acquisitions in global
market, the PSEs must not be allowed to remain stymied by a limited choice of personnel in their Boards of Directors to give the enterprise a strategic
direction in this era.
 
89.
              The Committee recommends that the DPE must revise its Guidelines accordingly to attract such talent with global vision of the business.
 
90.
              In this respect the Committee takes an affirmative view of the recent statement of the Prime Minister at the Conference of Chief Executives of
the Public Enterprises on 8 th March 2007- “ Induction of Independent Directors on the Boards of PSEs would,…., ensure greater efficiency and
effectiveness in the decision making processes as well. We must, therefore, pay greater attention to how we identify “independent” Directors and ensure
that they are truly independent “professionals”.
 
91.
              Prime Minister further, underlined the nature of impending competition in market “ public enterprises also need a new strategic vision. In the
increasingly globalised world that they operate in now, they must learn from private sector and seize opportunities for mergers, acquisitions,
amalgamations, takeovers and creating new joint ventures”   
 
92.
              The Committee expects that the remaining vacancies of Independent Directors in all the PSEs shall be filled up expeditiously with appropriate
persons give due cognizance to the recommendations of this Committee.
 
93.
              The Committee notes a remarkable under representation of women as independent Directors on the Boards of the CPSEs.  The Committee
recommends that the priority should be accorded to include at least one such women professional having the expertise relevant to the CPSEs, as the
independent Director on the Boards of CPSEs. 
 
94.
              The Committee reiterates its recommendations in 168 th Report and commends the Government to take cognizance of the observations and
concerns expressed by the Committee in lackadaisical implementation of the Policy of Professionalisation of Boards of the CPSEs. The
 
95.              Government and administrative Ministries should be more forthcoming in involving new sets of experts from outside the government agencies.
The vision set by the Prime Minister in his address to the Conference of Chief Executives must be followed up earnestly with actionable measures. The
Committee also seeks a detailed explanation from the Government on the status of implementation of the recommendations of the Ad hoc expert Group.
 
            The Committee directs the Ministry to furnish the detailed action taken and if recommendation is not acceptable, the reasons therefore.

REPORT
 
                  1.0 AN    OVERVIEW
1.1    The Agro and Rural Industries Sector has been envisaged as an important avenue for creation of employment opportunities   in the rural non-farm sector
for the balanced economic growth of the country.  The importance of this sector lies in the fact that it seeks to establish village industries at low cost  based on
the local raw materials, skills and technology for providing employment opportunities to the local population and artisans who have been traditionally engaged
in village level economic activities.

1.3       The main contribution of ARI sector to the national economy has been in terms of production and employment generation
through setting up of village industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. Over the past five decades, there has been a big growth in
Village Industries (VI) Sector in terms of production and employment. The Committee was informed by the Ministry of ARI that
while in the year 1955-56, the production in terms of value under village industries was at the level of Rs.10.93 crore, the same had
gone up to Rs.11915.54 crore in 2005-06 and Rs. 12773 crore in 2006-07 (up to February 2007). Similarly, employment level in VI
sector has also increased from 3.07 lakh persons in 1955-56 to 77.65 lakh persons up to February 2007.
 
 
1.4       The Committee notes the performance of VIs but feels still much remains to be achieved keeping in view of size of  population
that lies in rural India and also the scope of   VI, have to grow.  The Committee,   therefore,   feels that the  contribution  of VI can be 
further strengthened and  streamlined by  ensuring timely and adequate delivery of credit by the banks, technology upgradation and 
marketing support in the    form  of  financial support  for exhibitions, product design intervention and packaging etc.
 
       
        The Ministry guides and coordinates with the implementing agencies to ensure development and achievement as per the set mandate.
 
1.5            To generate additional employment opportunities in rural areas, the Government launched the “Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP)”
throughout the country on 01.04.1995. In the 10th plan, a target of 2 million jobs under REGP was fixed.  This target was enhanced to 2.5 million jobs in 2003-04.
Accordingly, the employment targets were revised and fixed for 2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-07 as 5 lakh, 5.25 lakh, 5.50 lakh and 5.90 lakh respectively.
During 10th Plan period (upto February 2007), 22.87 lakh job opportunities have already been generated under this programme. The Ministry informed that 3.56 lakh
additional employment opportunities (60 per cent of the target) have been generated as against the target of creation of 5.90 lakh job opportunities.  It has been
reported that a number of projects are at sanction stage and it is expected that the target set under the programme  would be achieved. During 2005-06, an
achievement of 5.68 lakh number of additional employment opportunities was made against the target of 5.50 lakh. In order to meet the enhanced employment target,
the budgetary allocation for REGP was also enhanced from Rs. 366.60 crore in 2005-06 to Rs. 372.63 crore in 2006-07 which has been further enhanced to Rs. 445
crore in BE 2007-08.  Based  on the expected performance in  2006-07, the outlay  to the extent of Rs.445 crore for 2007-08 under REGP is expected to generate
additional employment opportunities for 7.04 lakh persons as against 5.90 lakh  opportunities targeted for 2006-07.

7.2            The Khadi and Village Industries Commission functions in the rural and
 towns to provide employment opportunities at low cost to local artisans by utilizing the local raw materials. To support such traditional industries, Government
had been giving loans for Khadi and Village Industries to be set up in rural areas through the KVIC. The KVIC in turn was lending this money to Khadi and VI
institutions for meeting their working capital fund requirements.  As the Khadi institutions were to pay zero per cent interest on this loan till 2003 and 4 per cent
thereafter, KVIC have hardly been able to pay any interest or return the loan advanced by Government to KVIC. The amount of interest accrued to KVIC on loan has
been subsidized by the Government through payment of subsidy in lieu of interest over the years.  Thus, this subsidy in lieu of interest is not actually released to the
KVIC but is provided for in the budgetary provision both Plan and Non-Plan for book adjustments, against the interest payable by KVIC to Government. . The
subsidy is therefore towards this difference in the rate at which KVIC borrows from the Government and the rate at which it lends to beneficiaries. Since the amount
of interest subsidy has been accumulating every year, the budgetary provision for interest subsidy has been kept at the level of Rs. 39.10 crore to meet the
requirements of annual book adjustment. The budgetary provision for interest subsidy is only the book adjustment of interest on past loans.

1.0       INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The small scale industries (SSI) sector constitute one of the vibrant sectors of the Indian economy in terms of
employment generation; the strong entrepreneurial base it helps to create and; its share in industrial production and
exports.  The Ministry of SSI designs policies, programmes , projects and schemes in consultation with its organizations
and various stakeholders and monitors their implementation with a view to assisting   the promotion and growth of small
scale industries. The Ministry also performs the function of policy advocacy on behalf of the SSI sector with other
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government and the State and Union Territories.  Taking into account the high
potential for growth in the SSI sector in terms of output, employment and exports, the role of the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries is to strengthen the SSI sector, to enable it to remain competitive in market-led economy and generate
additional employment opportunities. For achieving these objectives, the endeavor of the Ministry is to provide the SSI
sector proper and timely inputs like:
 
(i)
               adequate credit from financial institutions/banks;
(ii)             funds for technology upgradation and modernization;
(iii)            adequate infrastructural facilities;
(iv)           modern testing facilities and quality certification laboratories;
(v)             modern management practices and skill upgradation through advanced training    facilities;
(vi)           marketing assistance; and
(vii)          level playing field at par with the large industries sector.
 
1.2       Worldwide, the Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are recognized as an “engine of growth”. In our country
however, it is necessary to refer to the “Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises” (MSMEs) on account of the significance
of the micro enterprises, both in the total population of MSME and in the economy as a whole. The process of
globalisation has, on the one hand, opened the gateways of opportunities to the MSME: of closer interactions and access
to much larger markets, to name only a few. It has, on the other hand, exposed the segment, particularly the micro and
small enterprises (MSEs) in the country, to the challenges of intense competition, both domestic and global.
 
1.3       The contribution of this segment to the economic sinews of the country is no less significant. Nearly 39 per cent
of the gross manufacturing output and 34 per cent of the exports of the nation arise from these enterprises.  The
estimated number of MSE units in the country is 123.42 lakh of which 18.71 lakh are registered and 104.71 lakh
unregistered. At the end of 2005-06, total production of the MSEs was estimated at Rs. 4, 76,201 crore at current prices
and Rs. 2, 77,668 crore at constant (1993-94) prices.  During the first four years of the Tenth Plan, the output of the
segment has recorded a real growth rate of 8.87 per cent annually. Over six thousand products are manufactured by the
MSEs, they include several sophisticated items used in high technology areas like nuclear power, missile and space
programmes, information technology, biotechnology, etc. The level of exports by this segment also testifies to its overall
competitiveness in the global markets.
 
 1.4      In the present context the Government in its National Common Minimum Programme  (NCMP) declares that the

200th Report of Committee on Industry

most employment-intensive segment of small-scale industries would be freed from the “Inspector Raj” and given full
credit, technological and marketing support. The NCMP also states that a major promotional package for the sector
would be announced and infrastructure upgradation in major industrial clusters will receive urgent attention.
 
1.5       By enacting the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, one of the needs felt and
articulated by this segment for long has been met. This Act seeks to facilitate promotion and development and
enhancing competitiveness of these enterprises. It provides the first-ever legal framework for recognition of the concept
of “enterprise” (comprising both manufacturing and service entities), definition of medium enterprises and integrating
the three tiers of these enterprises, namely, micro, small and medium.
 
1.6       The Government has announced a Policy Package for stepping up Credit to Small and Medium Enterprises
assuring, inter alia, a 20 per cent year-on-year growth in credit flow. The flow of net bank credit has, as a result,
increased considerably during the first year of implementation of the Package.
 
1.7       The Package for Promotion of Micro and Small Enterprises has also been approved. This Package, in turn,
covers further legislative measures (viz., a law on limited liability partnerships, the bill for which has been introduced in
Parliament), credit support, fiscal support, support for cluster based development, technology and quality upgradation
support, support for entrepreneurial and managerial development, empowerment of women owned enterprises,
strengthening of Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) and strengthening of data base for MSME Sector. The
measures in the Package would run concurrently with the Eleventh Plan.
           
1.8       In the National Manufacturing Strategy adopted by the National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council
(NMCC), it has been concluded that to increase the share of manufacturing in the gross domestic product and to
accordingly enhance competitiveness of the Indian manufacturing sector, particular attention needs to be paid to the
small and medium (manufacturing) enterprises. 
 
1.9       The Tenth Plan recognized the vital role of the SSI segment in the process of industrialization, regional spread of
industry and employment generation. Ministry of SSI informed that  there was no major policy shift for the year 2007-
08 as compared to 2006-   -07.
 
1.10     This trend is expected to continue during the current year (2007-08). In consonance with the past trend, for the
Eleventh Five Year Plan also, a higher growth rate for the SME sector has been projected as compared with both the
industrial sector as a whole and the manufacturing sector.
 
1.11     With the aim of improving manufacturing competitiveness of the segment, the launching of a National
Manufacturing Competitiveness Programme (NMCP) has been announced. The Planning Commission has given in-
principle approval for implementation of the NMCP during the 11
th Five Year Plan. The schemes under this Programme
will be implemented mainly in the Public-Private Partnership mode.
 
1.12     An Empowered Group of Ministers (EGoM) under the chairmanship of the External Affairs Minister has
recently been constituted to lay down the comprehensive policy for cluster development and oversee its implementation.
The Ministry of Small Scale Industries will service the EGoM.
 
1.13     Under the Credit Guarantee Scheme, life insurance cover for Chief Promoters of units provided guarantee cover
by the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries (CGTSI) has been introduced.  Further, the one-time guarantee
fee under the scheme has been reduced from 2.5 per cent to 1.5 per cent w.e.f.1
stApril, 2006
 
1.14     After due consultation with the stakeholders, 180 items reserved for exclusive manufacture in small scale sector
have been dereserved in 2006-07.

1.16     The Committee notes the trend of growth of SSI sector vis-a-vis Industrial sector.  During 2005-06 the Micro
and Small enterprises sector registered a growth rate of 12.3 per cent as against a growth rate of 8.1 per cent for the
overall industrial sector, showing better performance of SSI sector.  The Committee impresses upon the Government to
realize the importance of SSI sector which still has large potential to grow. The Committee solicits all out support, from
all the concerned agencies specially the financial institutions to come forward and provide their best services to this
sector for its overall growth and recommends the Ministry to continue its endeavor to bring together all the agencies so
as to ensure tapping the growth potential of the SSI sector in the country.
 
1.17     Considering that the policy package announced for stepping up of credit to SME sector by providing 20% year
on year growth in credit flow is a positive step, still much remains to be done.  The Committee is constrained to observe
that number of SSI accounts, have drastically gone down from 29.64 lakh in 1998 to 16.33 lakh in 2003.  However, a
slight rise to 18.85 lakh in 2006 is no solace.  Similarly the credit in terms of percentage of Net Bank Credit (NBC) to
SSI has also witnessed the same fate.  It went down from 17.5 % of NBC to 8.1% in 2006.   The Committee is of the
considered opinion that the credit to SSI in terms of percentage of NBC should also not be less than 20% and therefore
calls upon the Ministry of SSI and Ministry of Finance, RBI and the Banks to be more considerate   to SSIs for their
growth and prosperity in the national interest.
 
 
1.18     The Committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should undertake requisite steps  to enable the Micro, Small and
Medium Enterprises  to imbibe the potential to drive  the bases of growth rate, large number of employment-generation
and enhancing to national exchequer, combating the problem of poverty and improving the standard of living hence
contributing to the National Economy.
 
1.19.    The Committee however, endorses the following initiatives of Ministry of SSI :-
 
(i)
                  Providing requisite credit, technology upgradation, modernization and marketing support to the SSI sector;
(ii)                Infrastructure upgradation in general and particularly in the major small enterprises clusters; these would
include road connectivity, regular supply of power, common effluent treatment facility and water supply, etc.
(iii)               Reduction in the plethora of rules and regulations presently applicable to the micro and small enterprises
sector;
(iv)              Providing necessary support to the service industry to fulfill its growth and employment generation potential;
and
(v)                Providing training to existing and potential entrepreneurs and workers on an extensive scale and facilitating
modern management practices and skill upgradation through advanced training facilities for capacity building in
the small enterprises sector.
 
1.20     Ministry of SSI informed the Committee that the Action Plan for the Ministry for the year 2007-08 provides for
implementation of the Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises Development (SMED) Act, 2006 to promote the growth of
the sector; implementation of Promotional Package announced for the SSI sector; examination of problems facing
Enterprises in the Unorganized / Informal Sector through the National Commission set up for this purpose; facilitate
credit flow to the SSI Sector – by implementing the Performance and credit Rating Scheme for Small Enterprises,
through NSIC; and; infrastructure up gradation in major industrial clusters.  As a precautionary measure to achieve the
Action Plan constant review and monitoring of the Action Plan is being done.
 
1.21     The Committee feels these initiatives need to be translated in to result oriented actions.  The Committee hopes

3.0       DEVELOPMENT COMMISSIONER FOR SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
 
3.1       The Office of the Development Commissioner, Small Scale Industries, DC(SSI)  is an attached office of the
Ministry of Small Scale Industries and performs a dual role with regard to the promotion and development of small
enterprises. On the one hand, it advised the Government on formulation of appropriate policies, schemes, projects and
programmes and on the other, implements these policies, schemes, etc. for the overall development of the small
enterprises.
 
3.2       The Ministry informed that in the changing scenario of liberalization and globalization, the role of the Office of
DC (SSI) is in the process of being reoriented, broadly on the following lines:
 
(i)         The Office of the DC (SSI) would need to be equipped and strengthened to view the sector as a
composite whole, without losing the focus on the need for generation of employment as well as the
specific developmental/promotional requirements and inter-linkages of each distinct component of the
composite sector and the products and services produced by them.
(ii)        To address the issues of liberalization and globalization, the Ofiice of DC (SSI) need to widen and
continuously update its knowledge base regarding global trends in policies and Government interventions
as well as ascertain ‘best practices’ in this field, within the country and abroad, and appropriately adopt
them.
(iii)       It would need to strengthen its linkages with the State Governments, other Central
Ministries/Departments and associations of SMEs to achieve the objectives more effectively.
(iv)       Finally , it would need to forge stronger links with the relevant international institutions and bilateral
organizations for more effective cooperation so as to derive full advantage of the comparative strengths
of the Indian SME sector.
 
3.3       The Committee also feels that DC’s office needs to  be reoriented in view of changing scenario of the day.  The
Committee desires that a time frame be set up for doing so and ensure that DC’s office successfully implements the
policies and programmes for promotion and development of SSIs.  It’s role remains incomplete if it does not provide

effective monitoring mechanism.  The Committee accordingly solicits progress report on the functioning of National
Board of MSME constituted under the MSMED Act. 2006.
           
3.4       Further the Committee considers the role of DC(SSI) very critical in execution of cluster development
programme.  The Committee desires that DC’s office actively involve the beneficiary units through their associations. 
The Committee hopes CDPs would certainly result in technology and skill upgradations, increased production and
exports and overall increase in competitiveness of the clusters.    Since the scheme is demand based DC’s office has also
to play proactive role in persuading the States where response is not forthcoming.

that year.   This year i.e. 2007-08 an outlay (non-plan) of Rs. 9.89 has been proposed it includes   advertising  &

Headquarter office (Rs.0.26 crore). The Ministry has informed that allocation is sufficient to meet the requirement.

7.0       CENTRAL INSTITUTE OF TOOLS DESIGN
 
7.1       The Central Institute of Tool Design was established at Hyderabad in 1968 by the Government of India with the
assistance of UNDP & ILO. It was the first of its kind in the country established by Government of India. The aim was
to fulfil the tooling needs of the small scale Industries in the field of Tool Design & Manufacture   and training of
technical personnel in these fields.
 
7.2       The Institute promotes growth of SMEs by facilitating development and production of tools, moulds, dies etc.
and making available trained manpower and technical consultancy services to SMEs etc.  The Institute also assists
industry in upgrading their technology and developing the skill of their employees, through various vocational training
programmes.
 
7.3       CITD has trained around 10000 persons in various skill upgradation  courses like CAD/CAM, CNC Technology
etc. during the last five years (2001-06). The number of candidates trained during 2006-07 is likely to be around 3000.
In addition, more than 500 units are being provided tooling services both production and design every year.
 
7.4       The support to SMEs is being further enhanced by regularly upgrading the facilities and services of the Institute,
by way of introducing state-of-the-art machinery & training facilities etc.
 
8.0       THE NATIONAL MANUFACTURING COMPETITIVENESS PROGRAMME (NMCP)
 
8.1       The 10 point initiative under NMCP aims to provide SMEs, micro and small enterprises in particular, to enable
them to adjust to the competitive pressure caused by liberalization and moderation of tariff rates by way of providing
supportive measures to facilitate technological upgradation, assistance to improve their manufacturing systems and
competitiveness, helping in developing the alternative design strategy and design interventions, promote ICT, awareness
about Intellectual Property Rights (IPR), awareness of latest manufacturing techniques and manufacturing tools, support
for entrepreneurial and management development, marketing assistance, etc. The supportive measures provided under
the NMCP would enable the Small Scale Industries to have sensitization about the existing global scenario and adopt to
the international global manufacturing processes and practices so as to enable them to become competitive both at
domestic and international level.
 
8.2       The Planning Commission has granted in-principle clearance to implement  10 point initiative under the National
Manufacturing Competitiveness Programme (NMCP), only during Eleventh Plan.  The initial proposed total financial
outlay of Rs.956 crore was revised to Rs.852.90 crore and public private partnership (PPP) mode tried out where
enterprises level assistance comes forward.  Currently, the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) Memos for these
stand alone schemes are under the consideration of the Integrated Finance Wing (IFW) of the Ministry of SSI, before
they are circulated to the Ministries concerned for seeking their comments, which is a pre-requisite step before their
consideration by the Expenditure Finance Committee.
 
8.3       Budget Estimate for 2007-08 provide token provision for NMCP of Rs.15 crore (including NE region) with a
view to increase competitiveness in the manufacturing sector of SMEs on application of lean manufacturing; promotion
of ICT in Indian manufacturing sector; mini tool rooms to be set up by Ministry SSI; technology and quality upgradation
support for SMEs; support for entrepreneurial and managerial development of SMEs; set up design clinic to bring
design expertise to manufacturing sector; enable manufacturing sector to be competitive through quality management
standard and quality technology tools and; market assistance and technical upgradation activities of Ministry of SSI in
co-operation with TIFAC/CSIR.
 
8.4       The Committee welcomes the initiatives undertaken by Ministry under NMCP proposing an outlay of Rs. 852.90
crore for 11
th five year plan.  The Committee however notes with concern that only a token provision has been made in
BE 2007-08 without setting the targets to be achieved during the year nor does it explains the reasons for delay in doing

9.0       CREDIT LINKED CAPITAL SUBSIDY SCHEME

9.1       The Ministry of Small Scale Industries (SSI) is operating a scheme for technology upgradation of micro, tiny and
small enterprises called the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS). The Scheme aims at facilitating
technology upgradation by providing   upfront capital subsidy to  small scale units, including tiny, khadi, village and
coir industrial units, on institutional finance (credit) availed of by them for modernisation  of their production equipment
(plant and machinery) and techniques.  The Scheme (pre-revised) provided for 12 percent capital subsidy to SSI units,
including tiny units, on institutional finance availed of by them for induction of well established and improved
technology in selected sub-sectors/products approved under the Scheme. The eligible amount of subsidy calculated
under the pre-revised scheme was based on the actual loan amount not exceeding Rs.40 lakh.  The CLCSS has been
revised with effect from September 29, 2005.  The revised scheme, inter-alia, include raising of ceiling on loans from 
Rs. 40 lakh to Rs. 1 crore and the  rate of subsidy from 12 per cent to 15 per cent.  Presently, the scheme is in operation
upto March 31, 2007 or till the time sanction of aggregate capital subsidy disbursed by the Nodal Agencies/Banks
reaches to Rs. 600 crore, whichever is earlier.  The amount of subsidy disbursed between 2001-02 to 2005-06 is
approximately Rs.36 crore. However, most of it has been disbursed after the revision of the scheme. During the year
2006-07, approximately Rs. 60.0 crore has already been disbursed till end February 2007.  Thus, the scheme has gained
momentum after the revision of the scheme, i.e., from 29.09.2005
           
9.2       The target groups for the scheme are SSI units, including tiny and micro units.  The scope of the scheme has
been widened to include khadi, village and coir industrial products (falling under the purview of the Ministry of ARI).
 
9.3       The basis for the selection of the target group is that the scheme has primarily been conceived for providing
subsidy to the small and micro enterprises in the country.  However, industry  graduating from small scale to medium
scale on account of sanction of additional loan under CLCSS are also eligible for assistance under the scheme. Thus the
scheme will help SMEs in upgrading their technology and remaining competitive in the global market.  
           
9.4       The scheme is implemented through eligible Primary Lending Institutions (PLIs) which include Scheduled  
Commercial  Banks , Scheduled Cooperative Banks [including urban cooperative banks co-opted by the SIDBI under
the TUFS of the Ministry of Textiles], Regional Rural Banks (RRBs),  State Financial Corporations (SFCs) and North
Eastern Development Financial Institution (NEDFI).  The capital subsidy is released to Nodal Banks/Agencies for on-
ward disbursements to the beneficiary units through eligible PLIs.  An advance of Rs. 5 crore and Rs. 3 crore has been
placed with SIDBI and NABARD respectively for operationalising the scheme. Besides, an advance of Rs. 1 crore each
has also been placed with the Public Sector Banks/Government Agencies, which have been inducted as additional nodal
banks/agencies for disbursement of subsidy by them.   The funds utilized by these Agencies towards disbursement of
subsidy under the CLCSS is replenished by the Office of the DC(SSI) from the budgetary  provisions made for the
CLCSS.
 
 
10.0     The monitoring mechanism governing the scheme
 
10.1     The Governing and Technology Approval Board (GTAB) of the CLCSS monitor the scheme. The Secretary (SSI
& ARI) is the Chairperson of the Board and the Additional Secretary & Development Commissioner (SSI) is its
Member-Secretary. The GTAB periodically reviews the functioning of the scheme. There is a Technical Sub-Committee
(TSC) under the GTAB to consider inclusion of new sub-sectors/products and Well Established and Improved
Technologies under the Scheme. With the help of the existing monitoring mechanism, the scheme is implemented
effectively and its progress monitored regularly.  The progress of the implementation of the scheme has been boost up
with the effective working of the GTAB.  The GTAB, in its last meeting, decided to include 9 more Nodal
Banks/Agencies for implementation and release of subsidy directly   through them. The products/sub
sectors/technologies eligible for subsidy under this scheme is demand driven. Initially, the scheme was launched with
only 13 products/sub-sectors. However, over a period of time, 35 new products/sub-sectors have been included, making
it more broad-based for micro and small enterprises.  
                       
10.2     During the year 2006-07, upto end of February 2007, 1702 units have already benefited by disbursing subsidy of
approximately Rs. 60.0 crore to them as against Rs. 18 crore (approx.) to 699 units during the year 2005-06.  In the year
2005-06 itself, only 200 units were covered before raising the subsidy from 12 per cent to 15 per cent, while in the post

15.0     CREDIT SUPPORT PROGRAMME
 
15.1     The Credit Guarantee Scheme was launched with a view to alleviate the problems of collateral security faced by
the small enterprises, particularly first generation entrepreneurs, and to remove the impediments in flow of credit to
small enterprises sector.  It provides contribution to the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises
(CGTMSE) for providing Guarantee Cover to Commercial Banks for extending loans to small/tiny Units without any
collateral. Under this head Government will provide assistance to SIDBI to create Portfolio Risk Fund for credit
operations for micro enterprises under this scheme, assistance will be given for empowerment of Women Owned
Enterprises and Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes and Minorities.  This year the Government provides Rs.190 crores
(including NE region) to provide guarantee cover for 30000 micro and small enterprises with a view to generate higher
confidence level of Banks for lending better credit flow to Small and Micro sector.
 
15.2     The main problem in the implementation of the scheme pertains to low level of awareness about the scheme
amongst the field level officers of MLIs, negative mindset of the MLIs due to greater volume of administrative work in
the small enterprises lending, bankers’ traditional/usual comfort with collateral security and perceived high risk for
providing loans to the small enterprises sector. These problems need to be seriously addressed by the management of the
banks,  by enhancing awareness about the scheme among the field level officers of MLIs through seminars/training,
progress under the scheme could be enhanced. Furthermore, raising of the Corpus Fund up to Rs.2500 crore would
increase the comfort level of participating MLIs and encourage them to avail the scheme on a much wider scale.
 
15.3     The Credit Guarantee Scheme aims to alleviate the problem of collateral security among the small enterprises,
particularly to tiny enterprises.  To cover the entire micro sector, which is defined as units having investment in plant
and machinery upto Rs.25 lakh, the loan limit under the scheme was set at Rs.25 lakh.  As announced in the ‘Package
for Promotion of Micro and Small Enterprises’, appropriate steps are being taken by the CGTSI for enhancing the loan
limit from Rs.25 lakh to Rs.50 lakh.

15.6     The monitoring mechanism
 
15.7     The performance of the Credit Guarantee Scheme, being operated by CGTSI, is regularly monitored by the
Board of Trustees of CGTSI, which comprises the CMD, SIDBI, AS & DC (SSI), Ministry of SSI, GoI, Chairman, IBA,
and CEO, CGTSI.  The performance under the scheme is also reported to Ministry of SSI, GoI, on monthly and
quarterly basis.  The performance has also been reviewed in the past by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry.  CGTSI also has interface with the banking industry through IBA Review Forum, which helps in streamlining
the policy level impediments, if any.  DC (SSI) reviews the performance of banks under the scheme. Further, the
progress under the scheme by the banks are reviewed periodically in seminars and conferences organised by industry
associations, etc., which is attended by senior officers of the Ministry of SSI. The performance of MLIs participating in
the Credit Guarantee Scheme also comes up for review by the SLBCs, which are held on regular basis in various States
across the country. 
           
15.8     One of the main objectives of the Scheme is to generate more employment opportunities spreading across length
and breadth of the country. It is estimated that the loans guaranteed by the Trust were instrumental in creating around
3.41 lakh new job opportunities as on December 31, 2006. It may also be mentioned that the major beneficiaries under
the Scheme are in the tiny sector comprising of rural artisans, self-employed entrepreneurs, etc.  In fact, number-wise,
loans below Rs.2 lakh comprise 76% of the cases covered.
 
15.9     The Committee welcomes the scheme as it has come as a relief  to credit  starved  micro and small industries
who were denied lending for not furnishing the collateral security to the Banks.  No, doubt it is a good begining , the
Committee feels there is still a long way to go.
 
15.10   The Committee is constrained to note that credit to micro and small enterprises is still not smooth and adequate. 
The Banks still demand collateral security despite the RBI guidelines.  The Committee feels that the mindset at the

200th Report of Committee on Industry

branch level of Banks needs to be changed.  In this scenario this scheme covers loans upto Rs. 25 lakh only  going by
the current business trend this needs to be enhanced as many entrepreneurs in this sector would like to go for higher
loans and in that case they have to furnish collateral or third party guarantee. 
 
15.11   The Committee,  therefore, recommends for the following modifications in the Scheme  for strengthening of the
scheme:
 
            (i)         Raising the loan limit from Rs.25 lakh to Rs.50 lakh;
(ii)        Raising the guarantee cover from 75% to 80% for micro enterprises for loans upto Rs.5 lakh; and
(iii)   Raising the guarantee cover from 75% to 80% for micro and small        enterprises   owned and/or operated
by women.
 
15.12   The Committee observes that there is a need for strengthening monitoring mechanism of the scheme.  The
Committee therefore suggests that :-
 
(i)         RBI may include “review of Credit Guarantee Scheme” as one of the items in its agenda for regular
meetings held with commercial banks.
 
(ii)        Ministry of Finance may create  a monitoring mechanism for reviewing the progress made under Credit
Guarantee Scheme by Banks.
(iii)       Directorate  of Industries in various States may be requested to carry out review of coverage of credit
under Credit Guarantee Scheme by banks in their respective States.
iv)        Commercial banks may be requested to apprise the Ministry of SSI, regularly, on the progress made by
their respective banks under the Credit Guarantee Scheme.
 
15.13   The Committee notes that the The Plan Outlay under the Scheme during 2006-07 was Rs.118.10 crore and has
helped in enhancing the size of the corpus fund from Rs.1188.93 crore to Rs.1336.55 crore. The outlay provided during
2006-07 was, however, lower than the projected demand of Rs.206 crore. This year also  the requirement under the
scheme was projected at Rs. 232 crore for 2007-08.  Thus the allocation of Rs. 190 crore made for 2007-08 is lower than
the projected requirement. The Committee strongly feels that cut in projected requirements adversely affects the
progress particularly when the package for promotion of micro and small enterprises aims for raising the corpus fund to
Rs. 2500 crore by the end of 2010-11.  The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Ministry SSI to take up the issue
with Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission at the  RE stage for enhancement of allocation under the Scheme
and inform the Committee of the outcome thereof.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS  OF THE COMMITTEE-AT A GLANCE
 
 
1.0       INTRODUCTION
 
The Committee notes the trend of growth of SSI sector vis-a-vis Industrial sector.  During 2005-06 the Micro
and Small enterprises sector registered a growth rate of 12.3 per cent as against a growth rate of 8.1 per cent for the
overall industrial sector, showing better performance of SSI sector.  The Committee impresses upon the Government to
realize the importance of SSI sector which still has large potential to grow. The Committee solicits all out support, from
all the concerned agencies specially the financial institutions to come forward and provide their best services to this
sector for its overall growth and recommends the Ministry to continue its endeavor to bring together all the agencies so
as to ensure tapping the growth potential of the SSI sector in the country.
 
                                                                                                                        (Para 1.16)
 
Considering that the policy package announced for stepping up of credit to SME sector by providing 20% year
on year growth in credit flow is a positive step, still much remains to be done.  The Committee is constrained to observe
that number of SSI accounts, have drastically gone down from 29.64 lakh in 1998 to 16.33 lakh in 2003.  However, a
slight rise to 18.85 lakh in 2006 is no solace.  Similarly the credit in terms of percentage of Net Banking Credit (NBC)
to SSI has also witnessed the same fate.  It went down from 17.5 % of NBC to 8.1% in 2006.   The Committee is of the
considered opinion that the credit to SSI in terms of percentage of NBC should also not be less than 20% and therefore
calls upon the Ministry of SSI and Ministry of Finance, RBI and the Banks to be more considerate   to SSIs for their
growth and prosperity in the national interest.
           
(Para 1.17)
 
            The Committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should undertake requisite steps  to enable the Micro, Small and
Medium Enterprises  to imbibe the potential to drive  the bases of growth rate, large number of employment-generation
and enhancing to national exchequer, combating the problem of poverty and improving the standard of living hence
contributing to the National Economy.
    (Para 1.18)
 
            The Committee feels these initiatives need to be translated in to result oriented actions.  The Committee hopes
that action plan prepared by the Ministry of SSI will certainly take care of the fact.  The Committee would however, like
to see the progress in the ATR to be submitted by the Ministry of SSI.
 
 (Para 1.21)
 
2.0
              DEMAND NO. 86
 
            The Committee considers these two schemes i.e. Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme and MSME cluster
development scheme as instrumental in promotion and development of MSMEs.  The Committee does not want these
schemes to suffer from budgetary constraints and accordingly impresses upon the Ministry to aggressively pursue with
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for adequate funds at RE stage and inform the Committee of the outcome
thereof.
 
(Para 2.2)

small enterprises.  It is proposed that the NSIC will organize 5 exhibitions, participate in 45 exhibitions, organize 15

1.14     The Committee takes note of the cost of  revival of the PSEs. The Committee was also informed that if needed
the PSEs will raise the resources for revival from either internal or extra budgetary sources against the guarantees
provided by the Government.
 
1.15   The Committee notes with concern that more than half of budget support of Rs 4733 crores to the revival will go
into waivers and conversions of outstanding dues. Fresh infusions of about Rs. 1100 crores will be required. Only less
than 10% of the total cost, about Rs 400 crores will go into capital investments. ##
 
1.16     The Committee finds that revival package is largely about restructuring the manpower, waiving or converting
the financial liabilities over the PSEs. It is apparent that not much of the Budgetary support is available to the more
critical issues of technology upgradation and strengthening the marketing of PSEs. PSE are left to generate IEBRs for
capital investments. This is despite the fact that DHI has recognized technological obsolescence as one of the factors of
PSEs’ losing competitive edge.   The Committee therefore observes that the Government should consider this aspect
while preparing  revival  packages for the sick PSEs.
 
1.17     In this regard, the Committee also assessed the previous revival efforts for the same PSEs that have again been
referred to BRPSE. During the period of 1995-2004, an effort to revive these very PSEs was made with an aggregate
cost of some Rs. 6400 crores. Even at that time these PSEs faced similar constraints from global/domestic competition,
technological obsolescence, old machines and over-dependence on Government for marketing and within couple of
years of approval of such costly revival plans, these PSEs relapsed into losses.
 
1.18     From the Demands for Grants of last few years, it appears that no lessons have been learnt from the failures of
the previous revival attempts. The Committee considers that even the current efforts of revival may remain only a costly
window dressing unless the more critical issues of marketing and technological alliances are not effectively addressed.
The Committee however is constrained to note that in successive Budgets this aspect of rehabilitating the PSEs, has
been ignored. It appears from the Demands for Grants that while liabilities are being liquidated with the budgetary
support, for the capital investment the PSEs are being asked to generate IEBRs. The Committee wonders if such an
arrangement could make the revival of PSEs sustainable.  The Committee therefore recommends that Government
should review and re-assess the revival plans of the PSEs.
 
2.0       Impact of Budget proposals on Heavy Industries and Auto Sector
 

201st report of Industry

2.1       The Committee enquired about the overall impact of Budget proposals on the Sectors under the purview of DHI. 
The Committee was informed that:
 
1.      Custom duty has been reduced across the board from a peak level of 12.5% to 10%.  This would benefit
PSEs having high level of import content.
 
2.      Increase in the dividend tax (from 12.5% to 15%) and education cess (from 2% to 3%) would erode the
profitability of profit making companies like BHEL, HPC etc.
 
3.      Reduction in custom duty on Dials and movements of Watches from 12.5% to 5% would adversely
affect HMT (Watches).
 
2.2       The Committee was further informed that the positive features of the budget in respect of the auto sector were
the reduction of CST from 4% to 3%, the continuation of the weighted deduction of R&D expenditure under Income
Tax Act for the automobile sector for the next 5 years, and the retention of current customs duty structure on cars and
two wheelers which are likely to encourage local value addition in the domestic economy and generate employment.
 2.3      The Committee observes the divergence in the opinion of DHI and SIAM in respect of reduction of customs
duty on commercial vehicles and auto components from 12.5% to 10%. In the view of DHI, the step is likely to benefit
the PSEs with high import content, however in the view of SIAM   such reduction in duty is likely to affect the industry
adversely, as this would open up imports from low cost economies and deflect investment in the sector.   The
Committee therefore desires the Department of Heavy Industries to take up the issue with Ministry of Finance and
ensure that the interests of Auto sector too are protected.
 
2.4       The Committee was also informed thatincrease in spending on roads both national highways and rural roads will
have some positive impact on the sector. The increase in outlay for the Urban Renewal Mission and its focus on
transport will help increase public transportation in the country.
 
3.0       Plan Outlay for 2007-08
 
3.1       The Committee noted that total Plan Outlay for 2007-08, is estimated at Rs. 2485.22 crores of which Rs. 450
crores will be provided as budgetary support, and remaining Rs. 2035.22 crores are to be generated through internal and
extra budgetary resources. Given the negative growth in engineering and machine tool sector, largest chunk of
Budgetary support has been allocated to this sector.  Only the 14 PSEs are expected to generate IEBR.  
 
3.2            However, the Committee noted that last year in BE 2006-07 too, Rs 1360.22 were allocated for the Plan
outlay, however the estimates were reduced to Rs. 1127.82 crores in RE 2006-07, with both Budgetary support and
IEBR being lowered. Last year too, the larger part of the Plan outlay was allocated to engineering and machine tools
sector that could not utilize the allocations.
 
3.3       The Committee desires DHI to explain the reduction in budgetary support and IEBR and the steps taken to help
PSEs to generate IEBRs in order to reduce their continuous dependence on budgetary support. The Committee observes
that despite Government’s guarantees the PSEs have not been able to meet IEBR  targets which needs to be reviewed
seriously.  
 
3.4       The Committee expresses its serious concern over the constraints faced by the engineering and machine tools
sector in generating the IEBR and even utilizing the allocations, despite the healthy growth of more than 15 % in
successive years 2005-06 and 2006-07. 
 
3.5       The Committee observes with concern that as per the Outcome Budget 2007-08, a substantial part of Rs 1807.84
crores of IEBRs are committed for settling the VRS/statutory dues and salaries, in addition to Rs 150 crores of
Budgetary support. Only Rs. 227.88 crores of IEBR in addition to Rs 5 crores of Budgetary support will be used for
capital investments in PSEs. The Committee considers it as an evidence of a lopsided revival and restructuring of PSEs
where greater stress is being laid on restructuring the manpower instead of capital investments in the PSEs.  ##

4.4       In this context the Committee finds it rather intriguing that the lumpsum allocations of Rs. 400 crores meant for
the loans to the PSEs to settle the VRS and other statutory dues and to pay the salaries to the employees are categorized
as Non-Planned Capital expenditure, whereas  the Salary under the Major Head of Secretariat is placed as a Revenue
expenditure.   The Committee finds the explanation of the Department untenable  that allocations for ‘Loans’ per se are
Capital expenditure even if it is meant for payment of Salaries or VRS dues to the staff. Similarly Rs 25 crores meant
for R&D in Auto Sector, other than NATRIP,, is classified as a Non-Planned Revenue expenditure.  The Committee
directs the Department to take note of the Government Accounting Rules 1990, which states “ the classification of the
transactions in Government Accounts, shall have closer reference to the function, programme and activity of the
Government and the object of revenue or expenditure …”   If that  be the case how can  allocation  meant  for salary  be
classified differently in the  same  Demand.   In this context the Committee also finds it relevant to  mention the recent
pattern  of loans eventually being waived or converted into unsecured equity.    The Committee observes that the 
definition of  capital expenditure  has been contrived and directs the Government to take appropriate  measures to avoid
such inconsistencies.
 
4.5       The Committee notes the definition of Planned and Non-Planned expenditure, as given in GFR 78, which states
“Plan expenditure represents expenditure on Plan outlays approved for each scheme by the Planning Commission and
indicates the extent to which such outlays are met out of budgetary provisions.  Expenditure other than these are
categorised as Non-Plan expenditure.” The obvious corollary to this definition is that the allocations to the tune of Rs
456.30 crores have not been approved by the Planning Commission. However no clarification  has been  offered about
the criteria on which any scheme is approved by the Planning Commission.
 
 4.6      The Committee noted that RE-2006-07 indicated reduced planned revenue and capital expenditure whereas the
non-planned capital and revenue expenditure have exceeded the BE -2006-07.   The Committee was informed that the
Plan expenditure in 2006-07 was reduced due to transfer of one scheme relating to Bharat Earth Movers Ltd.,  having an
allocation of Rs.64 cr. in BE 2006-07  to M/o Defence. Increase in Non-plan allocation has been mainly for revival of
PSEs and VRS/statutory dues etc. Many of the PSEs have been defaulting on payment of wages/salary and statutory
dues. Govt. has provided budgetary support to tide over this situation. An amount of Rs.250 cr. has been sanctioned in
two tranches  of Rs.125 cr. each for payment of wages/salaries upto Dec. 2006 in defaulting PSEs.

7.0  Modernisation of Capital Goods Sector
 
7.1       The Committee wanted to know  if any purpose was served for the Modernization of Capital Goods Sector with
only Rs.1.00 lakh allocated in BE-2006-07, considering no additional resources had been sought  in supplementary
demands during 2006-07, yet the allocation has been enhanced to Rs.20.00 crores in BE-2007-08.
 
7.2       In the written reply Department of Heavy Industries informed that it proposed to launch a Pilot Scheme for
Competitive Enhancement and Modernization of Machine Tools and Textile Machinery Industry.  To start with, the
scheme was to address three core areas of constraints identified in the industry, namely (i) modernization and
technology upgradation (ii) R&D facilities and (iii) Business Development Services to ensure capacity increase and to
enhance competitiveness of the industry in the context of  ongoing globalization. However, as 2006-07 was the last year
of the 10
th five year plan , it was decided to have a pilot scheme for two years covering the sub sectors of machine tools
and textile machinery  at a total cost of Rs. 47.40 crore.  The scheme was under scrutiny of Planning Commission.  In
order to make the scheme operational in the current financial year, a token amount of Rs. 1.00 lakh  was allocated in the
Demand for Grants of Department of Heavy Industries  for the year 2006-07. The Pilot Scheme could not be approved
by the Planning Commission.  However, it was decided that a comprehensive proposal for capital goods sector should
be worked out and presented for the 11
th Plan period.  Accordingly, a presentation has been made to the Planning
Commission and in-principle approval is awaited before finalizing the details and obtaining final approval for the
scheme. The allocation of Rs. 20.00 crore for the financial year 2007-08 is based on the tentative outlay indicated at the
level of Advisor, Planning Commission during plan discussions for DHI.  Activities taken up under the scheme during
2007-08 would either be completed during the same year or may receive additional support during subsequent years
depending upon the gestation period involved.
           
7.3       The Committee was further informed that the proposed scheme was meant to support all capital goods
manufacturers to modernize their technology and to promote setting up of common facilities, R&D centres and business
development services.
 
7.4       The four strands of the scheme include Technology upgradation, Common facility centers, R&D Centers and
Sector specific parks. The Committee was also informed that the project will require Rs. 1328 crore. While the DHI had
sought a Budgetary support of Rs. 150 crores for 2007-08, however Planning Commission recommended  Rs 20 crores
for this year. 
 
7.5       The Committee finds it to be a  typical example of misplaced priorities where a critical project for the revival of
capital goods sector has been delayed due to extraneous considerations,  administrative complexities and layers of
approval. A project that was allocated funds by the Government in the Budget has been over-ridden by the Planning
Commission. The Committee feels that the administrative constraints of the last year of the  Five Year Plan can not be
an alibi for delaying a project for modernizing the capital goods sector. The Committee desires the DHI to inform the
Committee  of the business model, backward and forward linkages and commercial viability of the project. And if DHI
has done a survey of the stakeholders and their stakes in the project. DHI needs to ascertain about the management
structure of the scheme.

21.0  Auto Sector
21.1     The Committee noted that there has been a gradual decline in the growth of Auto Sector from 18.13% in 2002-
03 to estimated 13.5% in 2006-07, though the share of exports to the turn over has grown from 5.05% to 8.36% in the
corresponding period.  However, given the slow down in overall growth of the auto sector, an increase of export share
indicates export orientation of this sector. The Sector expected the reduction of excise duty from 24% to 16% that was
limited to small vehicle segment in 2006-07 should be expanded to other segments of MUV and passenger vehicles. The
Sector also expected fiscal and tax incentives for in House R&D in the auto sector.
 
21.2     The Committee also noted that the Government has provided necessary policy environment to this sector. Auto
Policy was launched in 2002 and 100% FDI without cap on investment has been allowed. In 2005 the Government
launched the major R&D project NATRIP. The Government has also launched the Automotive Mission 2006-16  that
sets to double the contribution of Auto Sector to the GDP, and ten-fold increase in its export earnings by 2016.
 
21.3     The Auto Sector  is technology intensive sector which has massive scope of investments in R&D.
 
21.4     The Committee observed that planned expenditure in respect of R&D for auto sector was reduced from Rs. 200
crores to Rs.130 crores in RE 2006-07. The Committee also noted that in previous years the planned allocation for
NATRIP was part of   overall allocation for R&D for the Auto Sector, however the two have been bifurcated this year.
The Committee sought to know about the time frame that Government has decided for the NATRIP and as to how long
the Government proposes to provide the Planned Budgetary support. The Committee wondered that the Government has
been providing for the annual budgetary support for the Non-Planned expenditure of Rs 25 crores, given the fact that
this project is being run by a Society which is free to generate its own resources.
 
21.5     Given the fact that Indian auto industry has a sizable presence of private players, who would be benefiting from
the NATRIP, the Committee has been espousing the case that the NATRIP  should be modeled as public –private
partnership. The Committee therefore sought to know the contribution of the Auto industry into the NATIS.

six    years from September, 2005 to August, 2011.  The Government will provide budgetary support of Rs. 1600 crores
for setting up the project            
and the remaining Rs. 118 crores will be the internal generation for  the project on account of users charges.
