COMMITTEE’S OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
            Summary of  Committee’s observation
 
            In view of the reply of the DHI regarding the classification of allocations into four categories, there is a fair
scope of arbitrariness in such classification in absence of specific criterion. The Committee also observed that the
practice of allocating lumpsum had been continuing for last several year since 1998-1999 despite failure of previous
failed revival efforts. No lessons have been learnt to protect Government’s new investments for the revival of PSEs.
 
            The revival and restructuring have remained unspecified in DHI’s response. The two terms have been used as
inter-changeably and to avoid specific details e.g. the ‘lumpsum for revival scheme of PSEs’ is actually meant to pay
salaries to the employees. Similarly in its responses to Committee’s specific queries, the DHI has tried to shift the
responsibility to the BRPSE which in fact considers only the draft revival plan prepared by the concerned PSE. The DHI
appears to have reduced to mere fund raising agency for BRPSE. Considering that the BRPSE’s recommendations are
eventually approved by the Government, the Committee wonders if BRPSE’s recommendations pertain only to the
limited issue of waivers and liquidation of liabilities, or wider problems pertaining more basic issues like marketing,
technological profile of products, consolidation through possible acquisition and merger etc. too have been considered
by the BRPSE and if the Government has accepted the BRPSE’s recommendation in totality. And if such issues require
any Budgetary support?  DHI’s replies lack specific information on these issues.   The Committee recommends that DHI
must apprise it of the broad framework of the strategy for revival of the PSEs. 
 
            In this regard the Committee observed that while Non-Planned allocations have been higher than Planned
expenditure in BE, the mid year Supplementary demands often seek costly waivers that add to the Non-Planned
expenditures. As per the definition provided in GFR it is clear that budgetary resources are being used only to clear the
commitments and liabilities. Such investments by the Government may have added the notional value to the Company

201st report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/201streport.htm[04-07-2016 13:12:15]
instead of adding to it worth.  
 
            As the PSEs are required to generate IEBRs to meet their capital expenditures, the Committee observed that
except for a few PSEs, most of the PSEs are not in a position to generate IEBR as indicated from the RE 2006-07, yet
the annual target for IEBR has been raised without explaining the reasons for such optimism. As for the meeting the
requirements of capital expenditure, minimal budgetary support is available by the way of multiple schemes like AMR
or Crucial balancing meant largely for same purpose. The meager money was supposed to be used for minor expenses
towards addition or replacement or modification, however remained largely unutilized. The promise of providing
budgetary support to the capital investments remained only a promise as the token allocations were never enhanced. 
 
            The Committee also noted that capital investments are being generated from the IEBRs whereas the revenue
expenditures like salary and retirement dues are being financed through budget support. Budgetary allocations are being
made to provide loans to liquidate the liabilities however, going by the current practice, the Committee apprehended that
these loans might be waived or converted into unsecured equity in future. Despite Committee’s repeated queries
regarding the steps taken by the DHI to secure these loans as per the OM of Ministry of Finance, the replies were non-
committal. The Committee believed that the amount of such lumpsum allocations should have come down over
successive year with the revival of PSEs and after clearing the VRS and statutory dues of rationalized employees.
However, the lumpsum allocations have remained the same every year.    The Committee would like to know if the
beneficiary PSEs have begun to repay the loans and interest there on or they have been granted moratorium. The DHI
must apprise.
 
            In addition to waivers and conversions, the Government is also loosing money by providing Interest subsidies to
the PSEs. Guarantee fee of which should have accrued to the Government is too has to be waived. And yet the PSEs
have to seek loans from the Government out of budgetary allocations. The Committee considers it to be a clear
indication of credit worthiness of the PSEs.
 
            The Committee also observed the practice that despite retaining the allocations in RE, a significant part of the
allocations are committed only towards last quarter of the FY without actually meeting the proposed outcome. The
Committee takes serious view of this FY-end rush in expenditures. It is for this reason that the Committee has been
asking the DHI to seek Supplementary Demands as and when the BRPSE recommendations are approved by the
competent authority. The Committee found DHI’s reply not convincing particularly in the view of practice where DHI
have been seeking token amounts for certain capital expenditures with an understanding to enhance them through
Supplementary Demands as per the requirement. The Committee found the DHI’s response inconsistent.
 
            On the critical R&D projects like Coal Gassification, the Committee considers  that the avoidable delay in
commissioning the project due to  lack of coordination between the managements of BHEL and NTPC  is patently
unacceptable and  holds the management of the two PSEs accountable for any possible escalation of cost. Given the fact
that power sector in the country is opening up to newer technologies, a delay may affect the commercial prospects of
this project. The Committee feels that the managements of the two Navratna PSEs need to be more alive to the urgent
technology requirements of the country in power sector. The Committee asks the DHI to ensure that the issues between
the two PSEs are resolved and provide the status report to the Committee.
 
            Regarding the NATRIP, it has been Committee’s view that since the Auto Sector in the country has sizable
presence of private players, the project should be modeled as a public-private partnership with an enhanced contribution
from automobile companies and lesser dependence on budgetary support. Considering that the lands for the NATRIP
are being provided by the State Governments at much cheaper rates and the Budgetary support of Rs 1090 crores being
provided as Planned resources, a meager Rs 118 crores  as annual user charges hardly qualifies NATRIP as an ideal
Public –Private partnership. The Committee reiterates that there is still a scope for private contribution in the project.
 
            Furthermore, the Committee takes a very serious view of the diverting funds collected from Road Cess to Auto
research. Road cess was meant for the maintenance of national highways and rural roads, to divert fund from this pool
for auto research is a violation of its mandate. The Committee asks the DHI to explain the circumstances causing such
diversion of fund meant for public interest to a patently commercial use.

COMMITTEE’S OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
            In view of the sectoral growth rates, the Committee observes that with 29 of the 48 PSEs of DHI belonging to
Engineering and machine tools sector, it is obvious that negative growth in this sector is reflected in the performance of
the PSEs. It is a matter of concern for Department of Heavy Industries and corrective measures need to be taken in this
regard.                                                                                                            ( Para 1.3 )
                 
            The Committee observes steep decline in profits of HMT ( Holdg.). REIL, HNL, Hoogly Printing and  PTL and
desires that the Committee may be apprised of the reasons therefor. The Committee may also be  apprised  whether the 
current loss making Companies which are likely  to make profit in 2007-08 would be making notional or actual profit,
break  up  of each such Company may be provided.                      ( Para 1.9 )
 
            The Committee notes with concern that more than  half of budget support of Rs 4733 crores to the revival will
go into waivers and conversions of outstanding dues. Fresh infusions of about Rs. 1100 crores will be required. Only
less than 10% of the total cost, about Rs 400 crores will go into capital investments.                              ( Para 1.15)
 
            The Committee finds that revival package is largely about restructuring the manpower, waiving or converting
the financial liabilities over the PSEs. It is apparent that not much of the Budgetary support is available to the more
critical issues of technology upgradation and strengthening the marketing of PSEs. PSE are left to generate IEBRs for
capital investments. This is despite the fact that DHI has recognized technological obsolescence as one of the factors of
PSEs’ losing competitive edge.   The Committee therefore observes that the Government should  consider this aspect
while preparing   revival  packages for the sick PSEs..                                            ( Para 1.16 )
 
            From the Demands for Grants of last few years, it appears that no lessons have been learnt from the failures of
the previous revival attempts. The Committee considers that even the current efforts of revival may remain only a costly
window dressing unless the more critical issues of marketing and technological alliances are not effectively addressed.
The Committee however is constrained to note that in successive Budgets this aspect of rehabilitating the PSEs, has
been ignored. It appears from the Demands for Grants that while liabilities are being liquidated with the budgetary
support, for the capital investment the PSEs are being asked to generate IEBRs. The Committee wonders if such an
arrangement could make the revival of PSEs sustainable.  The Committee therefore recommends that Government
should review and re-assess the revival plans of the PSEs.                                                                                                    
( Para 1.18 )
 
            The Committee observes the divergence in the opinion of DHI and SIAM in respect of reduction of customs
duty on commercial vehicles and auto components from 12.5% to 10%. In the view of DHI, the step is likely to benefit
the PSEs with high import content, however in the view of SIAM   such reduction in duty is likely to affect the industry
adversely, as this would open up imports from low cost economies and deflect investment in the sector.   The
Committee therefore desires the Department of Heavy Industries to take up the issue with Ministry of Finance and
ensure that the interests of Auto sector too are protected.                                                                           ( Para 2.3 )      
 
            The Committee desires DHI to explain the reduction in budgetary support and IEBR and the steps taken to help
PSEs to generate IEBRs in order to reduce their continuous dependence on budgetary support. The Committee observes
that despite Government’s guarantees the PSEs have not been able to meet IEBR  targets which needs to be reviewed

4.4       In this context the Committee finds it rather intriguing that the lumpsum allocations of Rs. 400 crores meant for
the loans to the PSEs to settle the VRS and other statutory dues and to pay the salaries to the employees are categorized
as Non-Planned Capital expenditure, whereas  the Salary under the Major Head of Secretariat is placed as a Revenue

direct the Department to  take note of the Government Accounting Rules 1990, which states “ the classification of the
transactions in Government Accounts, shall have closer reference to the function, programme and activity of the

definition of  capital expenditure  has been contrived and directs the Government to take appropriate  measures to avoid
such inconsistencies.                                                             ( Para  4.4 )
 
            The Committee notes the definition of Planned and Non-Planned expenditure, as given in GFR 78, which states
“Plan expenditure represents expenditure on Plan outlays approved for each scheme by the Planning Commission and
indicates the extent to which such outlays are met out of budgetary provisions.  Expenditure other than these are
categorised as Non-Plan expenditure.” The obvious corollary to this definition is that the allocations to the tune of Rs

the criteria on which any scheme is approved by the Planning Commission.                                            ( Para 4.5 )

Report
1.0            Introduction
 
1.1       The Department of Public Enterprises of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and public Enterprises plays the nodal role in coordinating the matters of general policy of non-financial nature affecting all the public sector industrial and commercial undertakings. Its functions include formation of policy guidelines for PSEs in areas like performance improvement and evaluation, personnel management, Board
structures, pay structures, wage settlement, training, vigilance, performance appraisal   etc. The mandate also includes the matters relating to MoU mechanism to improve the performance of PSUs . The Department is also the mandated with the issues pertaining to the Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment of the rationalized employees of the CPSEs. The DPE is also the administrative Department   for the
Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises and the Bureau of Public Enterprises and looks after the issues relating to Permanent Machinery of Arbitration for PSUs..
 
1.2       The Committee sought the views of the Department about the measures to strengthen its role in view of mandate to formulate the non-financial policies for all the PSEs.
1.3       The Committee was informed that Department of Public Enterprises collected, evaluated and maintained information on several areas in respect of CPSEs. The Committee agrees that DPE is the vital interface between the administrative Ministries/Departments and the CPSEs. It appreciated that the DPE has ample scope and potential to encompass in the following areas:
 
                  (i)      Support to training institutes;
                (ii)      Improving  corporate governance
               (iii)      Survey of State Level Public Enterprises
              (iv)      Thematic consultancies and studies
                (v)       Seminars and workshops on generic issues of CPSEs.
 
1.4       In its interaction with the respective Ministries over the compliance of certain guidelines issued by the DPE, the Committee is constrained to observe recurrent violations. The Committee therefore reiterates its recommendation that the DPE must also be proactive and persuasive in collecting, collating and monitoring the performance and progress of the guidelines for PSE. In this regard the Committee
further recommends that the DPE must undertake thematic consultancies and studies, seminars and workshop on the issues concerning PSEs more regularly. And that the Planning Commission should be approached to allocate more funds for this purpose. The DPE must also conduct annual survey of the State PSEs with the help of Institute of Public Enterprises, Hyderabad.  The Committee also recommends
that Institute of Public Enterprises, Central Manufacturing Technology Institute, Bangalore should be brought under the administrative control of Ministry of HI & PE. The Department must also contribute funds to the National Foundation for Corporate Governance. The Committee also recommends that DPE must be represented on the Boards of Governors of the premier management institutes in consonance
with the autonomy of these institutes. The Committee believes that greater interaction with the professional academia will help the DPE to evolve modern management practices for the PSEs. The Committee suggests that DPE should contact these institutions to conduct periodic surveys on the constraints faced by the PSEs and bring out recommendations that could become a useful input for the BRPSE.
 
2.0            Demands for Grants
 
2.1       The Committee was informed that the DPE had demanded a grant of Rs 45.31 crores  of which Rs 40.30 crores were asked for the Planned expenditure and Rs 5.01 crores for Non-Planned expenditure. However actual allocation was reduced to only Rs 14.43 crores, with sizable reduction in planned allocations at Rs. 10 crores. The Non-Planned allocation has been Rs 4.43 crores.

4.6       The Committee observes that maximum PSEs for which revival has been recommended by the BRPSE belonged to the capital goods sector under Department of Heavy Industries followed by the chemicals  and fertilizer sector. The Committee expresses serious concern over the costly revivals that largely entail waivers and conversions of the secured loans and interest dues towards Government of India.
The Committee notes that as per the revival plan, the revived units are likely to earn meager profits by the 2009-10. The Committee seeks information from the DPE that of the fresh cash infusions how much would be inform of secured loans, unsecured equity and grants respectively. The Committee also seeks information  regarding the steps taken to secure the government loans and interest there on.
 
4.7       The Committee   also observes among the administrative Ministries, the practice of using the recommendations of the BRPSE as the alibi without actually justifying the revival package. The Committee recommends that once a revival package is approved by the competent authority, the onus of justifying the revival package must be one the administrative Ministries. The NCMP states “While every
effort will be made to modernize and restructure sick public sector companies and  revive sick industry, chronically loss-making companies will either be sold-off, or closed, after all workers have got their legitimate dues and compensation”. However the Committee observes that the revival plans have been largely confined to the manpower rationalization, cutting the wage cost and liquidating the liabilities for
the accounting adjustments. The Committee wonders that after such accounting adjustments the PSEs will be earning only the notional profits or the actual profit. Taking lesson from the earlier failed attempts of reviva  such as HMT etc, it is evident that such window dressing of accounts will result only in notional revival that may not be sustainable in longer run. The Committee wonders if measures to secure
Government investments are built in the revival package. The BRPSE must suggest measures to secure Government’s investments as a substantial part of Government’s investments are in form of unsecured equity. The Committee suggests that instead of waiving the loans and interests dues towards Government, they can be deferred till a prescribed period till such time PSE should attain profitability.
 
5.0       ICPE
 
5.1       The Committee sought to know the reason for increase in the contribution to ICPE from Rs.0.37 crores in BE 2006-07 to Rs.0.73 crore in RE 2006-07 and same amount has been retained this year too. The Committee also required the information regarding the impact of such costly courses.
 
5.2       The Committee was informed that the ICPE was set up at the initiative of United Nations for promoting public enterprises in developing countries. It is an inter-Governmental organization of developing countries for improving the performances of their public enterprise, a strategic instrument of economic and social development. With the passage of time financial position of ICPE has been adversely
affected due to non-payment of membership contributions and inadequate generation of internal resources from programmes  and activities undertaken at the center. After the erstwhile State of Yugoslavia disintegration and winds of economic liberalization swept throughout world, too much emphasis on public sector became somewhat of an anachronism in the changing world scenario. As a result many
member countries have withdrawn there membership and only 19 countries now remain members of ICPE out of 42. Out of these only India and Slovenia  are paying regular membership contributions. The survival of ICPE now critically dependents on India and Slovenia . The hope of survival of ICPE gathered momentum when Slovenia became member of EU and is assuming  presidency of EU by 2008.
Government of India’s contribution to ICPE is paid in advance. During the financial year 2005-06, the membership contribution for the year 2006 could not be paid in advance due to late receipt of demand letter from ICPE.   Therefore, in BE 2006-07, the membership contribution could be paid for the year 2006 only. Thus, contribution for the year 2007 yet remained un-paid, which has been taken care of in
RE 2006-07. And as such in RE 2006-07 an amount of Rs. 72 lakh has been provided. Taking into account these factors and for the revival and revitalization of  ICPE, the annual contribution of Government of India has been enhanced from Rs.36 lakh to Rs.72 lakh per annum from the year 2007-08 on wards. The Ambassador of India, Budapest who was accredited to Slovenia also supported the enhancement
of India’s contribution, as ICPE can provide an intellectual platform for India to project its image in Europe.
 
5.3       In view of absence of Department’s specific reply on the query regarding the impact of costly courses of ICPE and also considering the depleting membership of the ICPE, the Committee feels if the erstwhile members of ICPE did not consider the organization as worthwhile, the rationale for continuing with the costly contribution should be more robust than mere survival  of a moribund  organization.
The Committee, therefore desires DPE to review its stand on ICPE and inform the Committee the outcome thereof.
  
5.4       The Committee was informed that ICPE conducts one year MBA programme  and short duration courses for the Government employees as well as CPSE executives. During 2006-07 ICPE conducted one year MBA programme  in which 4 Executives one each from Hindustan Paper Corporation Ltd., Hindustan Machine Tools and two from Bharat  Heavy Electricals Ltd were nominated. Candidates are
sponsored by the concerned CPSEs and nominated by DPE. Entire expenditure is met by the concerned CPSE. For the one year MBA programme the expenditure per candidate is as under:

5.5       The Committee observes that over and above annual contribution an amount of Euros 15450 (about Rs 8 lakhs per candidate) is spent on every candidate. The Committee feels that performance of the Company must justify this expenditure.  However no assessment based on tangible benchmarks regarding the impact of such courses was given to the Committee. The Committee considers such cost-
benefit assessment is essential given the financial stakes involved in such training. The DPE may inform the Committee if such an assessment has at all been formulated. The DPE must initiate a survey of the efficacy of ICPE training.
 
5.6       The Committee in its 168
th Report (2005) underlined the need for organizing similar ED programmes  with Indian Institutions for other member countries of ICPE, so as to enhance and project the academic profile of premier academic and research institutions of the country. In this regard the Committee sought to know that beyond the initial communication of DPE with the relevant institutions, if any
such course for ICPE-member countries has actually been organized by Indian Institutions.
 
5.7       The Committee was informed that in pursuance to its recommendation the matter was taken up with Secretary, Deptt. of Scientific and Industrial Research, Secretary, Secondary and Higher Education and DG, ICPE followed by reminders. DPE received response from DG, CSIR agreeing for imparting training to the participant member countries of ICPE in consultation with ICPE. DG, ICPE has already
been advised in this regard. The response from Secretary, Higher Education was still awaited.
 
5.8       The Committee is constrained to note the tardy progress made after passage of two years. The Secretary, M/O HRD has not even responded to the DPE’s reminder, whereas the DG, ICPE has not followed up on the advise to contact the CSIR. The Committee recommends that India as the prominent contributor and founder member of the ICPE, must persuade the ICPE for such academic cooperation
between  CSIR and ICPE. The Committee strongly disapproves the lackadaisical approach of the M/O HRD. DPE must secure an early and elaborate response from the M/O HRD in this respect.
 
6.0            Training for skill upgradation  
 
6.1       The Committee in its 168
th report had recommended that DPE organize orientation and skill development programmes for shop-floor level technical functionaries, as they are the end users of new material management and production techniques.
 
6.2       In its response the DPE informed that it supplemented the efforts of the public sector enterprises in regard to training and skill development in respect of middle and senior level executives through EDPs in collaboration with premier management and training institutes in the country. The recommendations of the Committee have also been conveyed to all the administrative Ministries/Departments and
Chief Executives of all CPSEs. DPE has since received feedback from a number of CPSEs stating that they have been giving due weightage to skill development of shop-floor technical functionaries by conducting internal programmes as and when required. Training programmes are also being organized by the respective CPSEs for shop-floor employees to enhance their skills.
 
6.3   The Committee finds the reply too general without any specific information. Given the upgradation of tools and machines and increasing computer-based automation it is necessary that the supervisory and lower levels of workers must be trained to align their skill sets with new modifications on floorshops and in production processes. Absence of such skill upgradation will seriously jeopardize the
redeployability of the workers and may cause redundancies leading to possible protest against modernisation , which in itself is essential for retaining competitive edge in the open market. The Committee is constrainted  to note that while DPE and concerned PSEs facilitate expensive trainings  for Middle and Higher management levels, the lower cadre remains vulnerable to changes in company structures and
modernization in technology due to lack of regular training. A fact glaringly borne out by the number of rationalized employees in these cadres and low redeployment rate of employees even after CRR scheme. The Committee finds such large redundancies a telling   example of poor HR management practices and lack of sufficient emphasis on training/skill upgradation and therefore recommends a more
structured approach to this issue. The DPE should  formulate  comprehensive guidelines  in this respect in consultation with the stakeholders and independent resource agencies. The Committee feels that HR management should be held accountable for large redundancies in the PSEs  resulting in large liability towards VRS/VSS cases.

The Committee also reiterates its recommendation that the CRR should be aligned with the existing employment schemes of the Central Government. The benefits of these schemes should also be available to CRR trainees.

of four nodal agencies namely CDAC, Mohali; CIPET, Guwahati; SISI, Chennai and SISI, Indore could be redeployed. The performance of most of the nodal agencies has remained indifferent despite significant allocations by DPE under the CRR scheme. DPE to extend the coverage and scope of   the scheme to include one of the dependent   of the VRS optee. 7.20     The Committee is of view that the Planning Commission should have given adequate reasons for reducing the funds  from this scheme which is important to fulfill the Government’s commitment with the VRS optees. In its previous reports the Committee has been recommending to expand the scope of the CRR scheme to cover the families of the VRS optees to raise the family income, instead the
Planning Commission has even reduced the allocation. The Committee finds the reduction unacceptable. Instead the Committee recommends that the Scheme should be accordingly redesigned to increase its coverage and scope.
 
7.21     The Committee further recommends that the PSEs should impart on-job or in-campus training for skill upgradation or vocational training to its employees to facilitate a smoother transition to new vocation. The Committee recommends that the HR Department of the concerned PSE should be made accountable and responsible for the VRS optees not availing the CRR scheme. The gap between VRS
optees and CRR trainees and their redeployment suggest that the PSEs are seriously lacking in their efforts. The Committee recommends that beyond customary communication with the PSEs and the Ministries, the DPE must make pro-active efforts to persuade the PSEs about CRR scheme.
 
8.0       North Eastern Region
 
8.1       The Committee sought the reasons for reducing the allocations for NE region from Rs.3.15 crores in RE 2006-07 to Rs. 1 crore this year and also about the usage of the money in 2006-07.
 
8.2       The DPE informed the Committee that during 2007-08, Planning commission has reduced the overall budget allocation under CRR Scheme. As per instant norm, 10% of the total allocation is earmarked for NE Region. For the year 2007-08 total allocation is Rs. 10.00 crore. Therefore, allocation for NE region has also been reduced to Rs. 1.00 crore. During 2006-07, Rs. 3.15 crore was earmarked for
NE region under CRR Scheme against which a sum of Rs. 3.95 lakhs  has been released to Indian Council of Small Industry to cover a physical target of 50 VRS optees. Central Institute of Plastics Engineering & Technology, Guwahati has also been assigned a physical target of 50 to be covered against balance fund available with them pertaining to 2005-06. The balance fund of Rs. 3.11 crore pertaining to NE
Region for 2006-07 would be transferred to ‘non-lapsable central resources pool’. The coverage under CRR Scheme in NE Region is lower mainly because of non-availability of sufficient VRS optees in the region. VRS is not very sizeable in the units located in NE Region. Also, a number of VRS optees, immediately after separation, leave NE region to settle in their native place.
 
8.3       The Committee observes that the money is not given as per the requirement of the region but for the sake of a norm that stipulates 10% of funds  be earmarked for North East. A larger part of the funds remain unutilized and transferred to a non lapsable central resource pool. The Committee expresses its reservation over such under utilization of scarce resources and recommends that allocation of funds
should be a function of need and not an administrative fiat.

that Institute of Public Enterprises, Central Manufacturing Technology Institute, Bangalore should be brought under the administrative control of Ministry of HI & PE. The Department must also contribute funds to the National Foundation for Corporate Governance. The Committee also recommends that DPE must be represented on the Boards of Governors of the premier management institutes in consonance
with the autonomy of these institutes. The Committee believes that greater interaction with the professional academia will help the DPE to evolve modern management practices for the PSEs. The Committee suggests that DPE should contact these institutions to conduct periodic surveys on the constraints faced by the PSEs and bring out recommendations that could become a useful input for the BRPSE.
 ( Para 1.4 )

The Committee expresses serious concern over the costly revivals that largely entail waivers and conversions of the secured loans and interest dues towards Government of India.
The Committee notes that as per the revival plan, the revived units are likely to earn meager profits by the 2009-10. The Committee seeks information from the DPE that of the fresh cash infusions how much would be inform of secured loans, unsecured equity and grants respectively. ( Para 4.6)

The NCMP states “While every
effort will be made to modernize and restructure sick public sector companies and  revive sick industry, chronically loss-making companies will either be sold-off, or closed, after all workers have got their legitimate dues and compensation”. However the Committee observes that the revival plans have been largely confined to the manpower rationalization, cutting the wage cost and liquidating the liabilities for
the accounting adjustments. The Committee wonders that after such accounting adjustments the PSEs will be earning only the notional profits or the actual profit. Taking lesson from the earlier failed attempts of revival such as HMT etc, it is evident that such window dressing of accounts will result only in notional revival that may not be sustainable in longer run. The Committee wonders if measures to secure
Government investments are built in the revival package. The BRPSE must suggest measures to secure Government’s investments as a substantial part of Government’s investments are in form of unsecured equity. Overview of the Tyre Industry in the country
1.         Tyre Industry was delicensed  in the year 1989.  There are 43 tyre companies in India.  MRF, Apollo, JK and Ceat  account for
88% of sales.  Bus and Truck tyres account for 65% of production.  The tyre industry has been growing at the rate of 11% per annum. 
The total export of tyres during 2006-07 was 54.49 lakh  an increase by 1.15% over previous year.
 
2.         The Committee was informed about the SWOT analysis of the domestic tyre industry as under:-
 
Strength:
 
1. Availability of qualified manpower and technical professionals
2. Domestic demand can be fully met from the domestic supplies
3. Export of tyres from India has increased acceptance in the world market
4. Competitive domestic market with multiple brands
5. Indian tyres conform to product and safety standards
 
Weaknesses
 
6. Lower spending on basic R&D in comparison to global tyre majors
7. Lower productivity of labour in comparison to world standards.
8. Infrastructural and related bottlenecks.
9. Higher cost of raw-materials.
 
Opportunities
 
10. Robust growth in economy and automobile industry.
11. More export opportunities.
12. Increased investment on highway projects and other roadways.
 
Threats

Background of Acquisition
 
18.       The Committee sought to know the objective and the rationale of the nationalization as the Company could never become

19.       The Committee was informed of the background of the acquisition by the DHI. Prior to acquisition by the Government of
India, M/s. National Rubber Manufacturer Limited (NRM) at Tangra was engaged in the field of industrial product like Conveyer
Belt, Transmission Belt, Hoses, V-Belts etc. and M/s. Inchek Tyre Limited (ITL) at Kankinara was engaged in the field of
manufacturing automotive tyres and tubes. These two private sector companies were chronically sick and their management was taken
over under Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 in the years 1977 and 1978 respectively. The total number of
employees was 4400 and they were not getting their salaries regularly. 
 
20.       At the time of nationalization, the two units were in poor financial condition.   The poor condition of machinery, non-
availability of drawings and molds, uneconomic production, labour problems and constraints in the availability of working capital
were main causes for the sickness of these units. 
 
21.       The Committee was further informed that the purpose of the nationalization was to secure proper management of the two
undertakings and to sub-serve the interest of the general public by ensuring continued manufacture, production and distribution of
tyres, tubes and other rubbers goods which are essential to the needs of the economy of the country. 
 
22.       An amount of Rs.4.91 Crore was paid by Government of India to the Commissioner of Payment (COP) as compensation to
settle the liabilities of the two companies at the time of nationalization in 1984.

General Observation and Recommendation of the Committee
 
1.   The Committee has taken a serious view of the chronology of revival efforts and found that right from the beginning the
Company had suffered due to crippling delays at the crucial stages.  After the nationalization in 1984, it took three years till 1987
to recommend modernization plan which lacked long term perspective in respect of technology and market requirements.
Considering that the Company was already suffering from sickness as it was taken over and subsequent foreign exchange crisis in
early 90’s had sever impact over the sustainability of the Company.   The Committee feels that the cost of delay was never taken
into account while deciding upon its revival. The long gaps in above chronology indicate the lack of sensitivity on the part of
Government and management towards ever escalating price of revival and accumulating losses and liabilities that eventually
sealed the fate of the Company.
 
2.   The Committee feels that as envisaged the TCIL was never in a position to breach the oligopoly in tyre industry, which was
one of the stated objectives of Public Sector. The Company lacked resources and technology to harness the growth in the auto
sector domestically and internationally. Despite repeated though  delayed revival no serious effort was made by the Government to
make the Company viable with a long term strategy for technology upgradation or reviving the marketing network. Instead the
Government had initiated process of locating JV partner in 1997. A process that is likely to fructify now after a decade long delay
with the passage of this Bill. In the meantime the Company has accumulated huge liabilities in its balance sheets which need to be
cleared at a huge cost on the Government and creditor Banks. The Committee feels that the Bill as introduced in the Parliament
does not elaborate the obligations for the prospective JV partner. The Committee is of the view that while the conditions on which
the JV proposals were rejected in 1997, have been substantially relaxed in the current Bill, the cost of delay by a decade has only
mounted for the Government and creditors. The Committee takes a serious view of the delay in decision making in the
Government.  
 
3.   The Committee also takes a serious view of the practice of seeking Parliamentary approval as suggested by Committee of
Secretaries, without providing requisite   information regarding valuation of the Company, terms of proposed JV and the prospects
of the Company. Such information is essential for a considered parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation. The Committee therefore
recommends that such information should be furnished by the Government to the Parliament as and when it takes up the Bill for
its consideration and passage. The Committee sought the rationale of bringing the Bill without providing any substantive
information. It questioned if the objectives of the Bill could have been better served with an Amendment to the existing Inchek
Tyres Ltd and National Rubber Manufacturers Limited (Nationalisation ) Act, 1984. The Committee also wondered if the Bill
could coexist without making such amendments to the existing Act.  The Committee accordingly recommends that necessary
Clauses should be incorporated in the Bill to avoid any conflict with existing Bill/Ordinance/Act.
 
4.   The Committee also recommends that the Bill should incorporate broader provisions regarding the valuation of lands, assets
and liabilities that are aligned with the valuation methodology prescribed by Department of Disinvestment instead of confining the
valuation on the basis of book value.
 
5.   The Committee further recommends that the relevant provisions must be incorporated in the Bill to prevent diversion of usage
of land as per the norms of valuation prescribed by the Department of Disinvestment.
 
6.   The Committee is in consonance with the recommendation of the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Finance which had found the asset valuation guidelines inadequate and vague on the issue of valuation of land and had
accordingly recommended “the land should be valued separately.”

Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
1.            The Committee observes with concern that as per the Outcome Budget 2007-08, a substantial part of Rs 1807.84 crores of IEBRs are committed for settling
the VRS/statutory dues and salaries, in addition to Rs 150 crores of Budgetary support. Only Rs. 227.88 crores of IEBR in addition to Rs 5 crores  of Budgetary
support will be used for capital investments in PSEs. The Committee considers it as an evidence of a lopsided revival and restructuring of PSEs where greater stress
is being laid on restructuring the manpower instead of capital investments in the PSEs.                                    
 (Para 3.5)

purpose of payment of VRS/statutory dues.
 
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
4.         The Committee expresses its reservations over the DHI’s inability to spend allocated funds for NE region. Yet the planned allocation has been hiked to Rs.
100 crores in the year 2007-08 for the very same projects as in 2006-07. The Committee wants the DHI to explain the causes of such lackluster performance  in NE
and steps taken to improve the situation.
(Para 14.3)
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
5.         In the previous years, capital expenditure in North East was envisaged for AYCL and CCI. Budget was being kept at least at 10% of the total plan budgetary support.
However, enough schemes were not available for fully utilizing the funds of NE region.  However, now a decision has been taken by Government to revive NPPC with an
estimated cost of over Rs. 500 crore.  Therefore, allocated funds for the current financial   year (2007-08) are likely to be utilized fully.
 
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
6.       The Committee would  like to have the DHI’s comments on certain discrepancies in the figures furnished by the Department at different places in its replies. 
The Committee noted one such discrepancy in case of Rs. 150 crore  allocation as loans for the revival to settle salary dues of the PSE employees. As per the
information furnished Rs 257 crores had already been spent and another Rs 50 crores were likely to be spent by the end of march 2007. Whereas only Rs 120 crores
out of the allocation of  Rs 250 crores  meant for loans to settle VRS dues, have been spent. The reply of the DHI does not match with the written replies to the
subsequent questions.
(Para 16.7)
 
ACTION TAKEN
           
7.         In order to mitigate the hardship of the employees of the sick and loss making PSEs whose revival schemes are under consideration of BRPSE or the Govt. and the
PSEs are not able to meet the expenditure on account of salary and wages of their employees, non-plan budgetary support is provided to PSEs.  During the last financial year
the funds fell short in the lump sum provision of Rs.150 crore for revival schemes and hence the funds were re-appropriated from the other lump sum provision of Rs.250
crore for VRS and other statutory dues with the approval of Ministry of Finance to meet the requirement of funds for salary and wages of the employees of the PSEs.  With

these re-appropriations and further supplementary grants, the Department of Heavy Industry could be able to release the non-plan loans to the sick and loss making PSEs to
pay the salary and wages of their employees till December, 2006.
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
 8.           The Committee is concerned that same PSEs may be repeated over the successive years.  It presumes that these PSEs can not even raise funds from the
market against VRS Bonds and seeks that DHI must inform it of the road map as to how long such allocations are likely to continue and from when the PSEs shall
start paying back the loans.  The Committee  apprehends that the DHI as the Government department has been reduced to fund raising agency for the PSEs. The
Committee finds such situation unacceptable.
 (Para 16.10)
 
9.            In reply to a query the Committee was informed that these non-planned loans ostensibly meant for the revival of PSEs, are in fact utilized in paying the
salary dues to the employees. The Committee accordingly, recommends that the DHI should change the nomenclature from a generic heading “Lumpsum  Loans for
the Revival Schemes of PSEs” to a more specific “Lumpsum  for salaries”.  Such a change in heading will give greater clarity about the specific objective of
allocation.
(Para 16.19)
ACTION TAKEN      
 
10.       Government is only releasing funds as non-plan loans only to sick and loss making PSEs whose revival is under consideration of BRPSE and to mitigate the  hardship
of the employees of the PSEs who are not able to generate sufficient funds to meet their requirements of funds for payment of salary and wages to their employees. This
Department is not releasing funds directly for salaries, hence, the nomenclature of the head of account “Lumpsum provision for implementation of revival schemes of PSEs-
Loans and Advances” appears to be the right nomenclature instead of lumpsum for salaries.
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
11.          In response to Committee’s view on modeling the NATRIP on the lines of Public -Private Partnership, the DHI informed that of the Rs. 1728 crore  project
Rs 1090 crores will come from planned resources, Rs. 519 crores from non-planned cess funds and only Rs 118 crores as user charges.  The Committee is of the view
that the private component in this project is very less and should be increased substantially.
(Para 21.13)
 
 
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
12.       Out of the investment of Rs. 1718 crore, Rs. 1090 crore is from the Plan support by the Government and Rs. 273 crore of this Plan support is in the form of loan which
has to be re-paid back by the industry, Rs. 510 crore is being contributed through automotive cess and Rs. 118 crore will be collected through user charges.  DHI agrees with
the view of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee that Cess cannot be taken as a contribution of the Automotive Industry.  NATRIP is largely a public
project of development nature being financed by the Govt. funds for establishment of facilities.    The Project has been conceived, designed and being implemented in total
tandem with the automotive industry and its running is also proposed to be looked after by the autonomous bodies having complete involvement of the industry.
 
13.       Automotive Industry is also contributing to NATRIP in the following way:
 
Automotive Industry is providing their experience, expertise assistance and support by way of formation and interaction with Technical Advisory Team (TAT)
which comprises of the technical experts of the automotive industry.  The TAT consisting of R&D heads of various OEM and Manufacturers is meeting
regularly with NATRIP and guiding the technical architecture of the project.
 
Automotive industry is providing specific advisory service on a regular basis as and when required by NATRIP.

Comments of Committee
14.       While Committee welcomes close interaction with industry, greater financial stakes from the industry will not only reduce the burden on budget but will also
give the project financial autonomy.
15.       NATRIP is in the process of selecting a HR consultant firm to device the overall HR Policy, manpower requirement and recruitment strategy for NATRIP
and its centres.  HR consultant shall be interacting with the Automotive Industry in developing the overall HR architecture for the project, as and when the
consultants start their work.
16.       Facilities being developed under NATRIP are being publicized through brochure, newsletters, video presentations, seminars, conclaves etc. being organized
from time to time.  The Automotive Industry has already envisaged great interest in using NATRIP facilities once these have been commissioned.
17.       Automotive Industry will facilitate and assist in the process of accreditation of the test and the R&D facility of NATRIP overseas and collaborate in their
upgradation such Indian facilities to world standards.
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
 
18.       The Committee also takes an exception of using non-planned Road Cess funds for the Auto sector. The Road Cess was meant for maintenance of national
highways and rural roads and certainly not for the auto sector, where going by current growth, the private players have sufficient resources to contribute into such
world class R&D facility. The Committee notes that the DHI is funding some 124 R&D projects out of the cess fund.  The Committee seeks information from the
DHI about the basis of such diversion of cess funds from their stated objective of maintenance of   national highways and rural roads and if these stated objectives
have been fully met.  
(Para 21.14)
ACTION TAKEN
19.         Road Cess fund is not being used by the Automotive Sector for undertaking R&D in Automotive Sector.  For undertaking R&D in Automotive Sector, Cess @ 1/8%
is levied on the sale of vehicle which is collected by Ministry of Finance and deposited in the Consolidated Fund of India.  A part of it is allocated by Ministry of Finance
through the Budget of Department of Heavy Industry for undertaking R&D projects in the automotive sector.  Therefore, automobile Cell and not Road Cess is used for R&D
in Automotive Sector.
 
       
 
 
 
CHAPTER – III
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS EITHER NOT ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY OR
HAS ASKED THE MINISTRY TO REVIEW ITS REPLY
 
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
 
1.         The Committee notes with concern that more than  half of budget support of Rs 4733 crores to the revival will go into waivers and conversions of outstanding
dues. Fresh infusions of about Rs. 1100 crores will be required. Only less than 10% of the total cost, about Rs 400 crores will go into capital investments.                 
           
(Para 1.15)
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/204threport.htm[04-07-2016 13:15:19]
2.            The Committee finds that revival package is largely about restructuring the manpower, waiving or converting the financial liabilities over the PSEs. It is
apparent that not much of the Budgetary support is available to the more critical issues of technology upgradation and strengthening the marketing of PSEs. PSE
are left to generate Internal and External Budgetary Resources for capital investments. This is despite the fact that DHI has recognized technological obsolescence
as one of the factors of PSEs’ losing competitive edge.   The Committee therefore observes that the Government should  consider this aspect while preparing 
 revival  packages for the sick PSEs.
(Para 1.16)
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.         Some of the PSEs had gone into losses due to problems specific to each PSE.  There are PSEs where major element of input is financial restructuring for cleaning their
balance sheet.  Capital investment is kept at a level where the Company can be turned viable.   All these aspects are kept in view/considered by the Consultants, BRPSE and
the Govt. before a comprehensive revival package is approved.  However, as suggested by the Hon’ble Committee, greater emphasis shall be laid on technological
upgradation in future revival plans.
(Para 1.15 & 1.16)
Committee’s Further Recommendations
4.         Taking in view the reply of the  Department justifying  the meager allocations for capital expenditure, it appears that PSEs mostly suffered due to financial
mismanagement requiring clearing their balance sheet.  Same pattern was reflected in the previous revival attempts.  However even the new  revival  plans are
limited to clearing the balance sheet and manpower rationalization.   The Committee feels that if the fundamental of the Companies are so   firm    and do not
require capital investment and that financial problems  were only transient,  the Company should have been able to generate funds from  market even against
Government’s guarantees instead of relying on the  outright Budgetary support.
           
5.         In view of meager capital allocations, the Committee is apprehensive of the Ministry’s assurance  regarding greater emphasis and technological upgradation,
this needs to be looked into seriously.
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
6.         The Committee in its 169th Report had raised question regarding the criterion for dividing the allocations under  four categories of Plan, Non-Plan, Revenue
and Capital Expenditure. This year too, the Committee had sought clarification on such division. Though the GFR 78 and 79 define the Planned and Non-Planned
expenditures and Revenue and Capital expenditures respectively.  No clarification has been furnished by the Ministry on the hybridized four categories. In absence
of such clarification, the Committee apprehends a fair scope of arbitrariness in the classification of allocations,   which  must be avoided.                                 
(Para 4.3)
ACTION TAKEN
 
7.         Allocations are divided in the four categories as per the definition given in the GFR, which are as follow :-
 
7.1       Plan Expenditure
 : Plan expenditure represents expenditure on Plan outlays approved for each scheme or Organization by the Planning Commission and indicating
the extent to which such outlays are met out of budgetary provisions an is shown distinctly from the other Non-Plan expenditure.
 
7.2       Non-Plan 
Expenditure : Non-plan expenditure is used to cover all expenditure of Government not included in the Plan expenditure.
 
7.3       Revenue 
Expenditure : Subsequent charges on maintenance, repair, upkeep and working expenses which are required to maintain the assets in a running order as also
all other expenses incurred for the day to day running of the organisation, including establishment and administrative expenses are classified as Revenue expenditure..
 
7.4       Capital 
Expenditure : Expenditure incurred with the object of acquiring tangible assets of a permanent nature (for use in the Organization and not for sale in the
ordinary course of business) or enhancing the utility of existing assets.

Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
63.    The figures provided by the DHI substantiate the apprehensions of the Committee.
After 2004-05, the Department of Heavy Industries could never exhaust Rs.250 crore  meant to disburse loans to settle VRS dues, rather only small fraction was
released for the purpose. Further the  number of VRS optees has been coming down since 2003-04. Yet Department of Heavy Industries demands have remained
stagnant at Rs.250 crores. Further it has not been informed if the same PSEs were extended loans to settle VRS dues in successive years. The Committee also noted
that after the completion of second quarter only Rs 34 crores  out of Rs 250 crores  could be spent on some 11 CPSEs. These are the same PSEs that have been
receiving such loans for years in succession.
 
64.       Similarly the Government has provided budgetary support in seven trenches since October 2004 to liquidate salary and statutory dues. The total sum has
been coming down significantly in each successive trench. Yet the annual lumpsum allocations to liquidate such liabilities have remained the same for years.  The
Committee noted that even this year, against an allocation of Rs 150 crores, only Rs 53 crores have been spent till the completion of second quarter. The beneficiary
PSEs are the same as those that availed loans to clear VRS dues. Such PSEs have been thriving on such Government loans for successive years. 
 
65.      The Committee takes a strong view of this continuing trend in DHI to keep the resources unutilized and yet seek huge lumpsum allocations annually to
provide loans to  clear  the liabilities of PSEs. While taking such view the Committee also bears in consideration the trend of converting the loans/interests into
equity or waiving them altogether.
 
66.       The Committee may also be informed about the terms of repayment of these loans for VRS dues/salaries. Has the Department of Heavy Industries
formulated any model terms of such loans for PSEs to avail these loans?
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
67.     The Committee observes inconsistency in seeking lumpsum. For certain prospective planned capital investments only token sum of Rupees one lakh was
allocated in BE 2006-07 with an understanding to enlarge the allocation through Supplementary Demands as and when required. However same criterion is not
applied for the massive lumpsum allocations made for the prospective non-planned  expenditures. The Committee is of the view that instead of providing large
lumpsum allocations, it is more appropriate that PSE-wise specific grants are sought in the Supplementary Demands.
(Para 16.6)
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
68.       The two non-plan lump sum provisions are made for providing budgetary support to sick units for fresh fund infusion under the approved restructuring schemes; for
meeting the short-fall in expenditure on salary & wages and for meeting the expenditure on VRS etc. as approved under the revival schemes of sick PSEs.  Until a revival
scheme of each sick PSE  is approved, the requirement of funds cannot be explained PSE wise in details.   Keeping in view the number of restructuring schemes likely to be
cleared during the year,  the  lumpsum provisions have been made.

security of such loans. The Committee apprehends that going by the current practice, such loans may either be waived off or converted into unsecured- equity some
time in future.

ACTION TAKEN
 
89.       Current policy of the Govt. as per NCMP is to revive sick PSEs which can be made viable. Accordingly revival plans are being attempted. Such revival plans
invariably have provisions for treatment of past loans/interest so that the Company can start with a clean slate.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
90.       The Committee should be informed if there is any objective criteria to determine the revivability  and sustainability of a PSE.  It has often been observed that
while the revival is limited to clearing the liabilities without making any effort towards ensuring the sustainability for which technical modernization,  marketing
etc., are critical for these facts, the Government looks for strategic partners to bring in technology and capital investment
91.       It is also observed that the Government looks for JV partners to bring capital investments only after clearing the books of PSEs at a huge cost. The
Committee should be informed of the rationale of clearing the books of a PSE whose management is eventually to be transferred to a JV partner.
 
 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
 
92.       The Committee observes that only a few select PSEs are able to generate IEBRs. In view of under performance in generating the IEBRs by the PSEs, the
Committee apprehends that majority of PSEs have to be funded through the budgetary resources to liquidate their outstanding liabilities or to meet their working
capital requirements. The fact that the PSEs are not able to generate IEBRs is indicative of the long term credit worthiness of the PSEs, this is despite the fact that
the Government has been providing the guarantees and interest subsidies.
(Para 19.4)

93.       With the revival of some PSEs, the Companies in the coming years are expected to generate higher IEBR.  During 2007-08, IEBR expected to be generated is Rs.
2368.52 crore against an actual IEBR of Rs. 401.28 crore in 2006-07.
 
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
94.       The Department of Heavy Industry’s response does not address the Committee’s observation regarding under achievement in generating IEBR as against
the annual target.  Also, the reply does not deal with Committee’s  impression regarding low credit worthiness as indicated by PSEs inability to generate IEBRs
despite Government’s guarantees  and subsidies towards guarantee fees and interest liabilities, Committee should be informed about the steps taken by Department

Report
 
 
1.         This Two Hundred Fifth Report  deals with action taken by the Government on the Two Hundred Second  Report of the Committee.
 
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Department of Public Enterprises in respect of the recommendations contained in that Report. These have been
categorized as follows:-
Chapter -I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Department.
Chapter -II- The recommendation/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies.
Chapter -III- The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has either not accepted replies of the Department or has asked the Department to review
its reply.
Chapter -IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Department have not been received. In respect of recommendations placed in
Chapter-IV. The Department has either furnished the interim replies or mater has been forwarded to other agency/Department whose reply is awaited or couched its language
in vague terms like noted for compliance/guidance.
